playbooks.name: Create a marketing kit
playbooks.description: Turn a product brief into a launch kit. Get positioning angles, landing copy, 5 social posts, and a 1-page PDF leave-behind.
steps: Draft 3 positioning angles and recommend one
Produce 5 social posts (LinkedIn, X, Threads, Instagram)
playbooks.prompt:
I want to create a launch marketing kit for my product.

Product brief:
- Name: [product name]
- One-liner: [10-15 word summary]
- Target customer: [role + company shape]
- Top 3 problems it solves: [problems]
- Primary value props: [3-5 props]
- Pricing model: [model + price points]
- Competitors I differentiate against: [names]
- Launch date: [date]
- Tone / brand voice notes: [punchy / authoritative / playful / etc.]

Deliverables, in this order:

1) Positioning angles (3 options). For each: angle name, headline (<=12 words), the audience segment it lands hardest with, why it works, and the biggest risk. End with your pick and one paragraph of reasoning. Wait for my approval before moving on.

2) Landing page copy, based on the picked angle:
   - Hero: headline (<=10 words), subhead (<=25 words), primary CTA copy
   - "What it is" section (~80 words, no jargon)
   - 3 feature/benefit blocks (label + 1-sentence benefit + concrete proof point each)
   - Social proof / objection-handling section
   - Final CTA section
   Keep total copy under 600 words. Ban: "revolutionary", "seamless", "unlock", "leverage", "in today's landscape".

3) 5 social posts, tailored per platform — not the same copy reflowed:
   - 1x LinkedIn (150-250 words, narrative or contrarian hook, 3 niche hashtags at the end only)
   - 2x X / Twitter (one <=280 char standalone, one 4-tweet thread with a hook tweet)
   - 1x Threads (conversational, <=500 chars, 1-2 emoji max)
   - 1x Instagram caption (hook line + body + soft CTA + 5 niche hashtags)

4) 1-page PDF leave-behind, written to my workspace as an actual .pdf file. Include: product one-liner, the 3 problems mapped to the 3 solutions, a screenshot placeholder block, 2 testimonial placeholders, pricing summary, and a contact line. Clean, high-contrast layout — no stock-photo clichés.

Quality bar:
- Cross-check the entire kit against the brand voice notes before handing it back
- Every claim that names a number or fact must be either from my brief or flagged as "placeholder — verify"
- At the bottom, list anything you had to invent so I can replace it

playbooks.name: Plan a weekly content calendar
playbooks.description: Plan 7 days of social content. Get a hook, post copy, CTA, and visual idea for every day.
steps: Confirm brand voice, audience, and active campaigns
Draft each day's hook, body, and CTA
Suggest a concrete visual per post
Output the week as one shareable plan
playbooks.prompt:
Plan a 7-day social content calendar.

Inputs:
- Brand: [name + 1-line description]
- Audience: [who, in 1-2 sentences, including their job and pain]
- Platforms (rank by priority): [LinkedIn / X / Instagram / Threads / TikTok / ...]
- This week's theme or active campaign (optional): [theme]
- 2-3 recent posts that worked well (for voice reference): [paste or links]
- Tone: [e.g. dry-witty, authoritative-but-warm, founder-voice]

For each of the 7 days (Mon -> Sun), produce:
1. Date label and primary platform for the day (vary platforms across the week so the mix matches my priority list)
2. Theme / angle for the day
3. Hook (one line — the scroll-stopper)
4. Full post copy, formatted for that platform's norms (LinkedIn long-form, X tight, IG caption with line breaks, etc.)
5. CTA (specific — not "let me know what you think")
6. Visual concept (1-2 sentences describing what's actually in the image/video — not a stock-photo brief)
7. 3-5 hashtags, niche over broad

Constraints:
- No two days share the same hook structure (don't open every day with a stat or a question)
- At least 2 posts must be narrative or personal-story shaped
- At least 1 post must be a contrarian or pattern-break take
- Voice must be consistent across the week — every post should sound like the same author

Output as a single shareable plan I can paste into a doc. Flag any day where you couldn't fill a field without inventing facts.

playbooks.name: Run competitive research
playbooks.description: Profile 3-5 competitors. Get a positioning map and concrete differentiation angles to act on.
steps: Profile each (positioning, pricing, strengths, gaps, recent moves)
Build a positioning map with justified axes
playbooks.prompt:
Run a competitive research pass for my product.

My product:
- Name + 1-liner: [paste]
- Segment / category: [segment]
- Primary buyer + their job-to-be-done: [who buys this and what outcome they want]
- Pricing model: [model]
- What I think my edge is (so you can pressure-test it): [edge]

Process:

1) Identify competitors. Find the 3-5 most relevant for this segment. Give me your shortlist with one sentence per name on why it's in (and which obvious-but-wrong picks you ruled out and why). Wait for my approval before profiling.

2) For each competitor, produce a profile with:
   - Name + 1-line positioning in their own words (quote their homepage)
   - Target customer: be specific — company size, role, industry
   - Core product description: what it actually does, not what they claim
   - Pricing: every plan and price; note enterprise tier if hidden
   - Distribution: how they acquire customers (SEO, paid, partnerships, PLG, sales-led) — with evidence
   - Top 3 strengths, each with a piece of evidence (URL, review quote, public metric)
   - Top 3 weaknesses, each with evidence (negative reviews, missing features, public complaints, slow updates)
   - Recent moves in the last 6 months (funding, launches, hires, pricing changes, GTM shifts)

3) Positioning map. Pick two meaningful axes — NOT "price vs features". Pick axes that actually segment this market (depth-vs-breadth, self-serve-vs-sales-led, technical-vs-business-user, vertical-vs-horizontal, etc.). Plot every competitor and me. Justify the axis choice in 2-3 sentences.

4) Differentiation recommendations. Give me 3 concrete angles I should consider. For each:
   - The angle (one sentence)
   - The segment it lands hardest with
   - The proof points I'd need to credibly own it
   - The biggest risk if I commit to it
   - Which competitor it most directly threatens

Quality bar:
- Cite a real URL for every non-obvious claim
- Pull from at least 3 source types per competitor (homepage, review site like G2/Capterra, recent news or blog)
- If you can't verify something, say "unverified" — never invent ARR, customer counts, funding amounts, or headcount
- If a competitor's docs/site are paywalled or behind login, say so and work from what's public

playbooks.name: Write a deep research report
playbooks.description: Research a topic end-to-end. Get a long-form report with inline citations as Word and PDF.
steps: Clarify topic, audience, depth, and constraints
Propose outline + source plan; wait for approval
Draft every section with inline citations
playbooks.prompt:
I want a deep research report.

Brief:
- Topic: [topic]
- Audience: [who reads this — their seniority, role, existing knowledge level]
- Why they care: [the decision or question this informs]
- Desired depth: [e.g. ~3000 words, 8-10 sections, exec-readable]
- Hard constraints: [paywalled sources OK? recency requirement (e.g. nothing older than 2 years)? specific perspectives to cover or avoid?]
- Style references (optional): [links or names of reports whose tone I like]

Phase 1 — Outline. Wait for my approval before drafting prose.
Propose:
1. Working title + a 2-sentence framing of the report's argument or central finding
2. Section list. For each section: title, 1-sentence purpose, the 3-5 sub-points it will cover, and an estimated word count
3. The 2-3 questions the report MUST answer for the reader (this is the success bar)
4. A source plan: 8-15 sources you intend to use, grouped by category (primary research, peer-reviewed, industry analyst, journalism, expert blog/practitioner), with a 1-line note on why each one is in the list and what perspective it brings
5. What you're choosing NOT to cover, and why

I'll reply with edits or "approved". Do not draft prose until I approve.

Phase 2 — Draft.
- Write every section in full to the estimated word count (±15%)
- Inline-cite using [Author, Year] or [Source name] — every non-obvious claim needs a citation
- Lead each section with the conclusion / takeaway, then support it (BLUF, not buildup)
- Where sources disagree, surface both sides in 2-3 sentences and tell me which is better-supported and why
- If a section's evidence is thin, say so plainly — don't pad with adjacent material
- Include at least one concrete example, case, or data point per section

Phase 3 — References + deliverables.
- Build a numbered references list at the end with full URLs, author, publication, date
- Produce two output files in my workspace:
  1. Word document (.docx) with consistent heading styles
  2. PDF version of the same content

Quality bar:
- Zero invented statistics, dates, quotes, or studies. If a claim has no source, drop it.
- No filler intros ("In today's fast-paced world...", "It is widely known that...")
- No AI-slop tells: ban "delve", "tapestry", "leverage", "in the realm of", "navigate the complexities", "unlock the potential"
- A reader skimming only the section openers should still get the report's argument
- At the very end, list any open questions or weak spots in the evidence so I know where to push back

playbooks.name: Generate a weekly finance report
playbooks.description: Summarize the week's revenue, spend, and runway. Get a one-page digest with WoW deltas and decisions needed.
steps: Flag movers (>10% WoW or >5% of total spend)
playbooks.prompt:
Generate this week's finance report.

Inputs:
- Data sources to read: [list dashboards, sheets, warehouse tables, accounting export — with paths or URLs]
- Last week's report (for delta comparison): [link / paste]
- Period: this week = [start date] -> [end date]
- Currency: [USD / EUR / etc.]

Produce a one-page report with these sections, in this order:

1) Headline (2 lines max). The single most important takeaway about the week's financials.

2) Numbers table:
   | Metric | This week | Last week | Delta | % change |
   At minimum include: gross revenue, net revenue, total spend (broken into COGS, payroll, marketing, infra, other), gross margin %, cash balance, runway (months).

3) Movers. Every line item that moved >10% week-over-week OR >5% of total spend. For each: what moved, by how much, and the most likely cause based on the data (cite the source).

4) Trends (3 sentences max). What the 4-week direction looks like for revenue, spend, and runway.

5) Needs your decision. Numbered list of items requiring my call this week. Each: the item, the deadline, the dollar amount at stake, and your recommendation in one line.

Constraints:
- Round to thousands (or appropriate magnitude); no false precision
- If a number is unavailable, write "n/a" — never guess or silently extrapolate
- Don't editorialize beyond the data — if you say "likely caused by X", point at the row/dashboard that backs it
- Output as a single one-pager PDF in my workspace, suitable to forward to investors or co-founders without further editing

playbooks.name: Plan my day
playbooks.description: Build a focused day plan from your calendar and todos. Get a time-blocked schedule and the single top priority.
steps: Pick the single most important outcome
Batch shallow work into one block
playbooks.prompt:
Plan my day.

Inputs:
- Today's calendar: [paste or link]
- Open todos / priorities: [paste or link]
- Energy notes (optional): [e.g. focus best in the morning, fade after 3pm]

Give me, in this exact order:
1. One sentence — the single most important outcome for today.
2. A time-blocked schedule. Keep my fixed meetings in place, then fill gaps with: at least one deep-work block (>=90 min, protected, named with the task) for the top priority, and one batched block for shallow work (email, replies, admin).
3. End-of-day checkpoint — what I should review at 5pm to call today a win.

Keep the whole plan under 200 words. Skip motivational language.

playbooks.name: Draft a blog post
playbooks.description: Outline and draft a blog post. Get a publish-ready post with a strong hook and SEO basics covered.
steps: Clarify topic, audience, angle, target length
Propose outline + opening hook; wait for approval
Polish: AI-slop strip, fact-check, SEO meta
playbooks.prompt:
Draft a blog post.

Brief:
- Topic: [topic]
- Audience: [who reads this + what they already know]
- Angle / POV: [the take, the contrarian framing, or the specific lens — be sharp]
- Target length: [e.g. 1200 words]
- Primary keyword (optional, for SEO): [keyword]
- 2-3 posts whose voice I like (for reference): [links]

Phase 1 — Outline. Wait for my approval before drafting.
Give me:
- 2 working title options
- A one-sentence thesis (the single claim the post makes)
- Section list (H2/H3 structure) with a 1-line purpose per section
- The opening hook, written out in full — this is what'll make me say yes or no

Phase 2 — Full draft, once I approve.
- Hit the target length within ±10%
- Use the H2/H3 structure from the outline; keep paragraphs <=4 sentences
- End every section with a one-line takeaway
- Include a concrete example, anecdote, or data point in at least 3 sections
- Close with a sharp final line — not a generic CTA, not a summary

Phase 3 — Polish pass.
- Strip AI-slop phrasing: "delve", "in today's landscape", "navigate the complexities", "unlock", "leverage", "tapestry", "in the realm of"
- Verify every fact, stat, or quote you used; cite or remove
- Produce: title tag (<=60 chars), meta description (<=155 chars), suggested slug, and 2 alt-text strings for hero image options

Output the final post as a single markdown block I can paste into my CMS, with the SEO meta in a small block at the top.

playbooks.name: Triage customer support inbox
playbooks.description: Triage your support inbox. Get a table with urgency, theme, draft replies, and human-needed flags.
steps: Draft a first-pass reply per ticket
Flag tickets needing a human or product call
playbooks.prompt:
Triage my customer support inbox.

Inputs:
- Source to read: [Gmail label / Zendesk view / Front / Intercom — be specific]
- Time window: [e.g. last 48 hours, unresolved only]
- Tone guide / brand voice notes (optional): [paste or link]
- Common-issue runbook (optional, so you reuse approved answers): [paste or link]

For every ticket, produce a row:
| Customer | Subject | Urgency (P0-P3) | Theme | Sentiment | First-pass reply | Needs human? | Why |

Urgency rubric:
- P0: production-down, data loss, security incident, churn-risk customer threatening to leave, billing failure on enterprise account
- P1: blocked workflow, billing errors on paid tier, paid-tier customer waiting >24h, broken integration
- P2: feature request from active user, small UX bugs, free-tier issues, how-to questions
- P3: vague feedback, spam, marketing-list reply-alls, opt-outs

First-pass reply rules:
- Open by restating the customer's specific issue in one sentence — NOT "Thanks for reaching out!"
- Either resolve the issue or explain the next step with a concrete timeline
- One action per reply — don't bundle
- Sign-off matching the tone guide (if no guide, default to warm + direct)
- Keep replies under 120 words

At the end of the table, add two sections:
- Patterns: any theme that appeared in 3+ tickets — flag as a possible product or doc issue, with the affected ticket count and a 1-line hypothesis
- Needs your call: tickets where Needs human = yes, listed with one-line context each, ranked by urgency

Don't send anything. Drafts only, for me to review.

playbooks.name: Repurpose a video into a content pack
playbooks.description: Turn a long video into multi-platform content. Get a thread, LinkedIn post, 3 shorts scripts, a newsletter draft, and a blog post.
steps: Draft thread, LinkedIn post, and 3 shorts scripts
Write a newsletter draft and an SEO blog post
Compile as a single shareable doc
playbooks.prompt:
Turn this video into a multi-platform content pack.

Inputs:
- Video URL (YouTube / Vimeo / Loom): [paste URL]
- Creator / brand voice: [1-2 sentence description; link a recent post if I have one]
- Target audience: [who this content is for]
- Primary CTA across platforms (optional): [e.g. subscribe to newsletter, book a call]

Step 1 — Source the material.
Pull the transcript and chapter markers. Read end-to-end — don't skim. Then identify the 5-8 highest-engagement moments: places where the speaker says something quotable, contrarian, or unexpectedly concrete. List them with timestamps before drafting anything.

Step 2 — Produce these deliverables, in this order:

1) Twitter / X thread (5-9 tweets, <=280 chars each)
   - Hook tweet must work as a standalone — no "thread below" filler
   - One concrete claim per tweet, no rhetorical questions
   - Final tweet: a sharp summary or soft CTA, NOT "follow me for more"

2) LinkedIn post (200-350 words)
   - Narrative or contrarian hook — no "here are 5 things I learned" listicles
   - One personal angle, one concrete payoff
   - Optional 3 niche hashtags at the very bottom only

3) Three short-form video scripts (1x 30s, 1x 60s, 1x 90s)
   - Each: a 3-second hook, the payoff, one CTA line
   - Tag scripts as TikTok / Reels / Shorts friendly — vertical, fast pace, no slow burns

4) Newsletter draft (400-600 words)
   - Standalone — must make sense to a reader who never saw the video
   - Structure: opening anecdote -> the insight -> why it matters -> one takeaway
   - End with a link back to the original video

5) SEO blog post (1000-1400 words)
   - H2/H3 structure derived from the chapters
   - Embed the most quotable moments as pull-quotes with timestamps
   - Title tag (<=60 chars), meta description (<=155 chars), suggested slug

Quality bar:
- Every deliverable must sound like the same author — no register drift across formats
- Strip AI-slop: "delve", "unlock", "navigate the complexities", "in today's landscape"
- At the bottom, mark which lines are verbatim quotes vs paraphrased so I can fact-check
- Flag any claim where you extrapolated beyond what was said in the video

playbooks.name: Personalize cold outreach to a lead list
playbooks.description: Research a lead list and write 3-touch sequences. Get a per-lead hook, intro email, follow-up, and breakup email.
steps: Research each lead for a specific hook
playbooks.prompt:
Personalize cold outreach for my lead list.

Inputs:
- Lead list (CSV with at least name, company, role, email; LinkedIn URL is a big plus): [paste or path]
- My company + 1-liner: [name + what we do]
- Who we serve and the outcome we deliver: [ICP + outcome]
- The single most-credible proof point I have (case study, logo, metric, certification): [paste]
- Tone: [warm + direct / playful / technical-peer]
- Sending account + signature block: [paste]

Step 1 — Clean the list.
Read every row. Drop generic mailboxes (info@, contact@, support@). Drop rows missing role or company. Tell me how many leads you started with and how many remain.

Step 2 — Research per lead.
For each remaining lead, find ONE specific recent hook. In order of preference:
1. A recent post they wrote (LinkedIn, blog, podcast)
2. A recent move at their company (funding, launch, hiring spike, layoff, acquisition)
3. A concrete job-to-be-done for their role at their company size
Never use lazy "I saw you work at [company]" personalization. If you cannot find a real hook, mark the lead "skip" — don't fake it.

Step 3 — Write a 3-touch sequence per lead.

Email 1 (initial, <=80 words):
- Open with the specific hook in one sentence — NOT "I hope this finds you well"
- One credible proof point that maps to the hook
- One low-friction CTA (15-min call OR a single-question reply)

Email 2 (follow-up, +3 days, <=60 words):
- A different angle or proof point — never "just bumping this up"

Email 3 (breakup, +7 days, <=40 words):
- Honest, slightly self-deprecating, leaves the door open
- No guilt trips, no "this is my last email" pressure

Output format:
- One markdown table: Name | Company | Hook | Subject Line | Email 1 | Email 2 | Email 3 | Notes
- Subject lines: <=6 words, lowercase, no salesy words ("opportunity", "connect", "quick question")
- Plain text only — no HTML, no images, no tracking pixels
- At the end, list any leads marked "skip" with a 1-line reason

Quality bar:
- Every email passes the "would a busy person bother replying?" test
- No template scent — each sequence must read like a 1:1 message
- Banned: "I hope this email finds you well", "just wanted to reach out", "synergy", "thought leader"

playbooks.name: Audit my codebase for tech debt
playbooks.description: Walk a codebase and write a refactor report. Get a file-cited list of dead code, hot-spot files, and ranked refactor opportunities.
steps: Map the repo structure and tech stack
Identify dead code, hot files, dependency issues
Detect duplication, coupling, and test gaps
Rank findings by effort and risk
Output a markdown report with file:line citations
playbooks.prompt:
Audit this codebase for technical debt and produce a written report.

Scope:
- Repo root: [path or URL]
- Focus areas (defaults to whole repo): [paths or modules]
- What I'm optimizing for: [readability / perf / shipping speed / onboarding / safety]
- Leave alone: [generated code, vendored deps, soon-to-be-deleted modules]

Phase 1 — Map the territory.
Walk the repo and identify:
- Tech stack (language, framework, build, test runner)
- Top-level architecture (modules + responsibilities)
- Where complexity concentrates (file LOC, cyclomatic complexity, churn from git log)
- Test coverage shape (which dirs are tested, which aren't)

Output this map FIRST, before any recommendations. I'll sanity-check it before you continue.

Phase 2 — Find the debt.
Categorize findings into these buckets. Every finding MUST cite file:line.

1. Dead code — unused exports, unreachable branches, orphaned files. Verify with grep before claiming.
2. Hot-spot files — high churn + high complexity + low test coverage. These are the riskiest to change today.
3. Duplication — copy-pasted logic that should be extracted. Show the 2-3 most painful examples with file:line for each copy.
4. Dependency issues — outdated, unused, duplicate, deprecated, or improperly pinned.
5. Coupling problems — circular imports, layers reaching across boundaries, leaky abstractions.
6. Test gaps — modules where critical paths have no tests, flaky tests, tests that don't actually assert behavior.

Phase 3 — Rank by ROI.
Score each finding on:
- Effort (S / M / L / XL)
- Risk if untouched (Low / Med / High)
- Confidence we can fix it safely (Low / Med / High)

Then recommend a top-10 list to action this quarter. For each: what to do, what to leave alone, the smallest possible PR shape, and what could break.

Quality bar:
- Every claim cites file:line — "this file is messy" without evidence is not allowed
- No suggestions that would require rewriting the whole repo
- If you can't be sure (e.g. you can't run the tests), say so — never assume green is green
- Don't propose adopting a trendy framework or rewriting in a new language unless I asked
- Output the final report as REFACTOR_AUDIT.md in the repo root

playbooks.name: Tailor my resume to a job posting
playbooks.description: Tailor a resume to a specific job. Get an ATS-friendly resume, a custom cover letter, and a follow-up email.
steps: Read the JD and extract keywords
playbooks.prompt:
Tailor my resume and cover letter for a specific job posting.

Inputs:
- Job posting URL or pasted text: [paste]
- My master resume: [paste or path]
- 2-3 achievements I'm proud of that aren't on the resume yet (optional): [paste]
- Constraints: [visa status, remote-only, target compensation if I want it referenced]

Phase 1 — Read the JD.
Extract:
- The 5-8 must-have skills / keywords (rank by how often they appear)
- 2-3 nice-to-haves
- The signal that says what the team actually cares about (e.g. "reduce on-call load", "ship to enterprise customers", "work cross-functionally with PM")
- Likely ATS / keyword-filter style based on the company (big-tech / startup / agency)

Show me this analysis before rewriting anything. I'll confirm or correct.

Phase 2 — Rewrite the resume.
- Keep my real experience — never invent roles, titles, dates, or metrics
- Reorder bullets so the most relevant ones for THIS job rise to the top of each role
- Rewrite each bullet as: action verb -> what I did -> measurable result. If I don't have a real metric, ASK me before inventing — placeholder "X%" is OK if marked TODO
- Match resume wording to the JD's vocabulary (e.g. if they say "observability", don't write "monitoring")
- Keep it to 1 page unless I'm senior (15+ years)
- Output as .docx — clean, ATS-friendly, no tables, no columns, no images

Phase 3 — Cover letter (250-350 words).
- Open with a specific reason I want THIS role — not "I'm excited to apply"
- One concrete story that proves I can do the job
- One paragraph on why I'm a fit for THEIR signal (from Phase 1)
- Close with a clear ask (a conversation) — no "thank you for your consideration" filler
- Output as .docx and as plain text I can paste

Phase 4 — Follow-up email (for +7 days if no response).
- <=80 words
- Add a new piece of value: link to a project, a thought on the role, a relevant data point
- Never "just bumping this up"

Quality bar:
- Strip AI-slop: "passionate", "results-driven", "team player", "hit the ground running"
- Never invent a metric, employer, or skill I don't have
- Flag every TODO at the bottom so I know what to fill in

playbooks.name: Write a Xiaohongshu (小红书) viral note
playbooks.description: Write a 小红书 note in viral platform style. Get a clickable title, cover concept, body in 姐妹们 voice, and a hashtag stack.
steps: Confirm 痛点 / 产品 / 目标人群
Generate 5 title options in 小红书 标题党 style
Draft 封面 concept + body in 小红书 voice
Run a 平台合规 review pass
playbooks.prompt:
Write a Xiaohongshu (小红书) note that has a real shot at going viral.

Inputs:
- Product / topic / experience I'm posting about: [paste]
- Target reader (be specific — 大学生 / 宝妈 / 职场女性 / 健身党 / etc.): [audience]
- My voice / 人设: [e.g. 都市白领分享好物 / 大学生省钱党 / 健身教练]
- The single transformation I want the reader to feel: [涨知识 / 长草 / 治愈 / 解决一个具体痛点]
- Goal: [纯种草 / 引流私域 / 涨粉 / 推广自家产品]
- Past high-performing note from this account (optional): [link]

Step 1 — Title options (5).
Draft 5 titles in 小红书 爆款 style. Each must:
- Be <=20 Chinese characters
- Use 1-3 fitting emoji (NOT generic ✨🌟)
- Use at least one 标题党 pattern: 数字 ("3款..." / "99%人不知道..."), 反差/感叹 ("姐妹们冲！" / "我宣布"), 痛点提问 ("为什么我..."), 经验沉淀 ("30天我..."), or 干货承诺 ("一篇讲清...")
- Pick one as your recommendation and explain in one sentence why it lands hardest with this reader.

Wait for me to pick before drafting the body.

Step 2 — Cover page (封面).
Suggest a 封面 design with:
- 大字报 title text (a 5-8 character punchline — usually a sharper version of the title)
- 1-line supporting subtitle
- Concrete background description (real-life shot / 桌面平铺 / 对比图 / 步骤拼图 — NOT "a beautiful image")

Step 3 — Body copy.
- First-person voice
- Reader address: 姐妹们 / 宝子们 / 大家 (pick what fits the 人设)
- Hard structure: 痛点钩子 (2-3 lines) -> 解决方案 / 产品 / 方法 -> 真实使用感 OR 对比 -> 总结 + 软性 CTA
- Line breaks every 1-2 sentences — never long paragraphs
- 1-2 emoji per section to break the wall of text — don't over-emoji
- 200-400 字 total, depending on the topic
- Mark 2-3 places where I should insert an image (e.g. "📸 这里放对比图")

Step 4 — Hashtag stack.
5-10 hashtags at the end, mixed:
- 2-3 broad volume tags (#好物分享 #生活记录)
- 3-5 niche tags specific to the topic (#xx 测评 #平价 xx)
- 1-2 community tags if relevant (#姐妹们种草 #打工人日常)

Step 5 — Compliance check.
Flag anything that risks 限流: 极限词 ("最" / "第一" / "100%"), unverified medical or efficacy claims, brand-name comparison with negatives, hard sells. Rewrite the flagged lines.

Quality bar:
- Must NOT read like translated Instagram copy
- Must NOT use 朋友们 (it reads 抖音, not 小红书)
- If the goal is 引流, the CTA stays soft — never "私信我加微信"

playbooks.name: Triage and reply to my inbox
playbooks.description: Triage unread email into Reply / Review / Noise. Get drafted replies in your voice, summaries, and a decisions list.
steps: Pull unread email in the window
Classify each as Reply / Review / Noise
Draft replies for the Reply bucket
Summarize the Review bucket in one line each
playbooks.prompt:
Triage my inbox and draft replies for everything I should touch today.

Inputs:
- Source: [Gmail label / Outlook folder / etc.]
- Time window: [e.g. last 24 hours, unread only]
- My top 1-2 priorities this week (so you can judge what's urgent for ME): [paste]
- Voice samples — 2-3 emails I sent recently that sound like me: [paste]
- Out-of-scope senders to never touch (boss / spouse / a specific client): [list]

Step 1 — Classify every email into one bucket:
- REPLY — needs an actual response from me
- REVIEW — I should see it but no reply needed (FYI, status update, calendar invite to accept/decline)
- NOISE — newsletters, automated alerts, marketing

For each email, output: Sender | Subject | Bucket | One-line reason.

Step 2 — For every REPLY email, draft a response.
Rules:
- Match my voice samples — same register, same opener style, same sign-off
- Address the actual question / ask in the first sentence
- One concrete action or timeline per reply
- <=120 words unless the email genuinely needs more
- If I'd need to make a decision before replying, write "NEEDS YOUR CALL: [the decision]" at the top of the draft and leave a stub

Step 3 — For REVIEW emails:
- Summarize each in one line ("FYI: Q3 board meeting moved to Thursday")
- If there's a calendar invite I should accept/decline, suggest which
- Don't draft replies for these

Step 4 — For NOISE:
- Suggest a filter / label rule for repeat senders so I don't see them again
- Do NOT auto-archive without my approval the first time

Step 5 — Output a single triage report:
1. Counts: how many REPLY / REVIEW / NOISE
2. REPLY section with drafts ready to send
3. REVIEW section with 1-line summaries
4. NEEDS YOUR CALL section bubbling up anything that requires a decision
5. Suggested filter rules at the bottom

Quality bar:
- Never send anything — drafts only, saved to my Drafts folder
- Never fabricate context (e.g. "As I mentioned in our last meeting...") unless it's true
- If the voice sample doesn't include enough signal, ask before guessing

playbooks.name: Build an investment thesis on a stock
playbooks.description: Research a ticker and write a 1-page thesis. Get a bull case, bear case, valuation, catalysts, and a recommended action.
steps: Read the latest filings and recent news
Read 2-4 earnings call transcripts for tone shifts
Build the bull and bear cases with cited evidence
Sketch valuation vs history and peers
playbooks.prompt:
Build a 1-page investment thesis on this stock.

Inputs:
- Ticker + company: [e.g. NVDA / Nvidia]
- My time horizon: [3-6mo / 1-3yr / 5yr+]
- My current view going in: [bull / bear / curious / no view]
- Position context (optional): [thinking of opening / sizing up / averaging down / trimming]
- Sources to prioritize: [10-K, last 4 earnings call transcripts, recent analyst notes, my past notes — paste or link]

Step 1 — Read primary sources.
In this order:
1. Latest 10-K / 10-Q
2. Last 2-4 earnings call transcripts (management tone shifts ARE signal)
3. Recent (last 90 days) news and analyst notes
4. The 2-3 closest competitor 10-Ks for context

Tell me what's MISSING before drafting (e.g. "next earnings call isn't out yet", "private competitor X has no public filings"). Don't fabricate around gaps.

Step 2 — Build the thesis.

A. The business in 2 sentences. What it does, how it makes money. No jargon.

B. Bull case (3-5 numbered points). Each point: the claim, the supporting evidence (cite filing / transcript / report with page or timestamp), the implied upside.

C. Bear case (3-5 numbered points). Same structure. Steelman it — don't soft-pedal the risks.

D. Valuation sketch. Current P/E, EV/EBITDA, P/S where relevant. Compare to: (a) the company's own 5-year average, (b) 2-3 closest peers. State whether it screens cheap, fair, or expensive AT TODAY'S PRICE.

E. Catalysts to watch. 3-5 dated events in the next 6-12 months (earnings, product launches, regulatory rulings, debt rolls) and what each would prove or disprove.

F. What would make me change my mind? 2-3 specific signals that would flip the thesis.

G. Recommended next action. Open / size up / hold / trim / pass, with one sentence on why. ALWAYS express position size as % of portfolio, never $.

Step 3 — Output.
- 1-page memo as .pdf to my workspace
- References list at the end with every citation (URL, page or timestamp)
- A "questions I couldn't answer" section flagging what I should check before acting

Quality bar:
- Zero invented numbers. If you can't find revenue/margin/guidance, say so — don't estimate silently.
- This is analysis, not financial advice — frame it as such
- No "to the moon", no "clear winner", no "trust me"

playbooks.name: Launch a digital product on Etsy / Gumroad
playbooks.description: Pick a niche and launch a digital product. Get a niche brief, SEO listing, cover-image briefs, and storefront copy.
steps: Scope a viable niche from my interests + skills
Write the SEO listing (title, tags, description)
Brief cover images + draft storefront copy
playbooks.prompt:
Help me launch a digital product on Etsy / Gumroad / Payhip.

Inputs:
- My interests + skills + spare time per week (be honest): [paste]
- Target platform: [Etsy / Gumroad / Payhip / Shopify]
- Product type I'm leaning toward (optional): [printables / planners / Notion templates / wedding suite / etc.]
- Brand voice + visual style: [e.g. minimal beige / playful kid-friendly / spicy spreadsheet-bro]
- Budget for design tools / ads ($0 is fine): [budget]

Phase 1 — Niche brief. Wait for my approval before writing the listing.

Propose 3 niche options. For each:
- The niche in one specific sentence ("perpetual budget tracker for couples splitting bills proportionally" — NOT "budget tracker")
- Why it has demand: cite 3-5 real Etsy/Gumroad listings already selling something nearby, with seller name, price, and estimated monthly sales (or "established shop, can't tell volume")
- Why I can credibly own it given my skills + voice
- The smallest possible v1 product (1 file, deliverable in a weekend)
- A realistic price (don't underprice)

Recommend one and explain why. Wait for me to confirm.

Phase 2 — Listing.

Once I confirm the niche:

1. Title (140 chars max for Etsy). Front-load with the highest-intent keyword. Pattern: [Product type] + [Specific use case] + [Variant], e.g. "Wedding Budget Spreadsheet | Excel + Google Sheets | Couples Cost Split + Vendor Tracker".

2. Tags (13 for Etsy, all <=20 chars, lowercase). Mix: 3 broad volume, 7 mid-volume long-tail, 3 hyper-niche. Note search volume tier where you can estimate.

3. Description (400-600 words, scannable):
   - Hook line (one sentence — the transformation)
   - What's included (bulleted, exact file names + formats)
   - How it works (3-5 steps)
   - Who it's for / not for (sets expectations, reduces refund rate)
   - FAQ (4-6 real questions buyers ask)
   - Delivery note (instant download, file types, license terms)

4. Cover image briefs (5 images for the carousel). For each: composition, text overlay, color palette suggestion.
   - Image 1: hero mockup with the value-prop overlay text
   - Image 2: feature breakdown
   - Image 3: in-use / lifestyle shot
   - Image 4: "what you get" file manifest
   - Image 5: social proof or testimonial placeholder

5. Storefront copy:
   - Shop announcement banner (<=140 chars)
   - About section (200-300 words in my voice)
   - Welcome message + post-purchase email

Quality bar:
- Don't fake "100+ sold" social proof — leave placeholders for real numbers
- No "limited time offer" pressure tactics
- Banned: "high-quality", "perfect for", "must-have" — say something specific instead
- At the bottom, list every assumption you made about my niche, voice, or buyers so I can correct them

playbooks.name: Write a real estate listing
playbooks.description: Turn property details into a polished listing. Get an MLS-ready description plus social variants for IG, TikTok, and email.
steps: Spin into IG, TikTok, and email variants
playbooks.prompt:
Write a complete listing pack for this property.

Inputs:
- Property data (address, beds, baths, sqft, lot, year, key features): [paste]
- 5-15 photos with brief captions of what each shows: [paste or path]
- Asking price + days-on-market context: [paste]
- Neighborhood notes (school district, walkability, recent comps, vibe): [paste]
- Target buyer (be specific — first-timers / families / downsizers / investors): [audience]
- Agent voice / brokerage style: [warm-and-personal / luxury-minimalist / data-driven / etc.]

Step 1 — Identify the 3 strongest selling points.
Don't list everything good about the house. Pick the 3 things that make THIS property different from the comps. Each: the feature, why it matters to the target buyer, the evidence (which photo or data point backs it).

Tell me your three before drafting. I'll confirm or swap.

Step 2 — MLS description (150-220 words).
- Open with a specific hook tied to selling point #1 — NOT "Welcome home" or "Step into"
- Walk the buyer through the property in a logical order (front -> public spaces -> private spaces -> outdoor)
- Mention all three selling points, with the strongest as the anchor
- End with a single concrete CTA tied to the brokerage style (book a tour / open house date / agent direct line)

Step 3 — Social variants.
1. Instagram caption (120-180 words): one strong hook, the story of the home, 5-8 niche hashtags
2. TikTok hook (script for a 30-45s walk-through, 3-second hook + 3 highlight beats + close)
3. Email blast subject + body (subject <=7 words, body <=200 words, one image suggestion per section)

Step 4 — Compliance scan.
Flag anything that touches fair-housing risk language:
- Descriptors about who the home is "for" (kids, families, professionals — risky)
- Neighborhood characterizations that signal race, religion, national origin
- Steering language
Rewrite the flagged lines with safer alternatives.

Quality bar:
- Never invent a feature ("newly renovated" if the data doesn't say so)
- Never reference schools by name unless I confirm zoning
- Banned: "must see", "hidden gem", "won't last long", "motivated seller"
- If a selling point would require an inspection / appraisal claim, mark it "verify"

playbooks.name: Reproduce a bug and ship the fix
playbooks.description: Take a stack trace and ship a real fix. Get a failing test, a patch, and a PR that goes red-to-green with a postmortem stub.
steps: Locate the failing code from the trace
Run the broader suite for regressions
Open a PR with a postmortem stub
playbooks.prompt:
Reproduce this bug and ship the fix.

Inputs:
- Stack trace or production log line (paste the whole thing): [paste]
- Failing test command (optional): [e.g. pytest tests/foo_test.py::test_x]
- Recent suspect commit(s) (optional): [shas or PR links]
- Branch to work on: [branch name — create new from main if blank]
- Test scope: [whole suite / affected module only]

Phase 1 — Locate.
- Walk the stack trace from outermost frame to innermost. For each frame, open the file and read the function.
- State your current understanding: which file, which function, what the trace is telling us.
- Do NOT patch anything yet. If you can't pinpoint the failing line, say so and ask for more context (env, inputs, version).

Phase 2 — Write a failing test (RED).
- Write the smallest possible test that reproduces this bug. Place it in the matching test file (or create one).
- Run the test. It must fail with an error that maps cleanly to the original stack trace.
- If your test passes on the first run, the repro is wrong — iterate until it fails for the right reason.
- Commit the failing test on its own commit: `test: reproduce <bug-id>`. Do NOT amend later — keep red-then-green visible in git history.

Phase 3 — Patch (GREEN).
- Write the minimum patch that makes the failing test pass.
- Re-run the new test — it must go green.
- Re-run the broader test suite for the affected module (and integration tests if the bug touches I/O).
- If anything else breaks, surface the regression and ask before pressing on.
- Commit the fix on its own commit with a Conventional Commit message: `fix(<area>): <one-line summary>`.

Phase 4 — Open the PR.
Title: `fix(<area>): <summary>`
Body sections:
- What broke
- Why it broke
- The fix
- How I tested it (mention the new test by name)
Keep the repro-test commit and the fix commit visible separately — don't squash before review. Link the issue / incident if I gave you one.

Phase 5 — Postmortem stub (at the bottom of the PR body).
- Was this caught by tests before prod? Why not?
- What test or guardrail would catch a CLASS of bugs like this one?
- One-sentence recommendation (a new test, a type, a lint rule, a runbook entry).

Quality bar:
- Never "fix" by changing the test to match the bug — the test encodes correct behavior, the fix changes the code
- Never silently catch the exception to make things green
- If the root cause is in a dependency or env config, say so plainly — don't patch around it

playbooks.name: Ship a GitHub issue end-to-end as a merged PR
playbooks.description: Take an issue and ship a merged PR. Loop: read repo, code, test, open PR, address review, merge.
steps: Plan the change and test surface
Make edits + run tests until green
Open the PR and respond to review
playbooks.prompt:
Take this GitHub issue and ship it end-to-end as a merged PR — read the repo, plan, code, test, open the PR, respond to review, merge.

Inputs:
- Issue URL or pasted text: [paste]
- Repo path: [path or URL]
- Branch base (default main): [base]
- Test commands: [paste]
- Lint commands: [paste]
- Reviewer to request: [GH handle]
- Hard stop after N failed CI runs: [default 2]

Phase 1 — Understand.
- Read the issue plus linked context (PRD, screenshots, related issues, prior PRs)
- Walk the repo to identify in-scope files and the test surface covering them
- Restate the change: user-visible behavior, surface area, tests that should exist after
- If ambiguous, post a clarifying comment on the issue and STOP. Don't guess.

Phase 2 — Branch and plan.
- `git checkout -b fix/<issue-id>-<slug>` from {base}
- Write a 5-10 line plan as the PR description draft. Stick to it.

Phase 3 — Code in passes.
- Smallest possible change that fixes the issue
- Add or extend tests FIRST when the change has behavioral impact
- Commit small: each commit is a "thought" the reviewer can follow

Phase 4 — Local green.
- Run lint; fix what it complains about
- Run tests for the affected module first, then full suite
- If tests fail, root-cause from the trace — never silence them. Max 2 CI retries before escalating.

Phase 5 — Open the PR.
- Title: `<area>: <one-line summary>`
- Body: What broke / Why / The fix / How I tested / Risks
- Link the issue, request the named reviewer
- Push via `gh pr create`

Phase 6 — Review loop.
- Watch via `gh pr view --comments`
- For each comment: read, decide, ask if you disagree — never silently disagree
- Apply as NEW commits (don't force-push during review)
- On approval: `gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch`

Feedback signal (log for the next loop):
- Did the reviewer accept on first pass? Log pushback themes.
- Did CI go green on first try? Track flaky-test patterns.
- Append every "thing I should have caught earlier" to CLAUDE.md.

Quality bar:
- NEVER skip CI to ship faster. NEVER force-push during review.
- NEVER claim tests pass unless you watched them go green THIS session.
- If the change touches auth, payments, or migrations: stop and ask before merging — even if CI is green.
- After merge, watch the deploy for 15 min for regressions before declaring done.

playbooks.name: Run an on-call alert loop with runbook update
playbooks.description: Run an alert end-to-end. Get a diagnosis, fix or escalation, postmortem, and runbook updates that compound.
steps: Propose fix or escalate by authority
playbooks.prompt:
You're on rotation. An alert just fired. Run the loop: diagnose, fix or page, postmortem, update runbook.

Inputs:
- Alert payload (PagerDuty / Opsgenie / Slack — paste the full thing): [paste]
- Service that's degraded: [name + repo + dashboard URL]
- Existing runbook (if any): [path or URL]
- My authority level: [read-only / can-run-safe-commands / can-deploy-fix — default read-only]
- Escalation contact: [name + how to reach]

Phase 1 — Acknowledge and frame.
- Acknowledge in channel: "investigating <alert>, working hypothesis in 5 min"
- Restate what's broken in one sentence — user-visible symptom, not the metric name
- Pull dashboards (latency, error rate, throughput, recent deploys) into context

Phase 2 — Diagnose.
- Check recent changes first: deploys, config flips, feature-flag changes last 24h
- Compare current values to same time last week — normal blip or real shift?
- Run the runbook's diagnostic steps if one exists
- Form a hypothesis with confidence (high/med/low) and the evidence
- DO NOT GUESS. If you can't get to medium confidence, escalate.

Phase 3 — Act by authority level.
- Read-only: post hypothesis + proposed remediation, page the human
- Can-run-safe-commands: only commands listed as safe in the runbook; observe; loop
- Can-deploy-fix: open PR, get approver, deploy, watch 30 min before declaring resolved
- NEVER deploy a hotfix to auth, payments, or migration code without a human

Phase 4 — Resolve and postmortem.
- Resolve ONLY after the metric has been stable for 15 min
- Postmortem sections:
  - Headline (user-visible impact, duration, scope)
  - Timeline (alerted → first action → mitigation → resolution, with timestamps)
  - Root cause (technical cause, NOT "the engineer who deployed it")
  - What worked / what didn't (which diagnostic steps helped, which wasted time)
  - Action items (each: owner, deadline, ticket link)

Phase 5 — Update the runbook (the loop closes here).
- If the diagnosis steps you used aren't in the runbook, add them
- If the runbook had bad info, fix it (and explain why in the commit)
- Open a PR against the runbook with your edits — even small ones

Feedback signal (compounds across incidents):
- Diagnostic steps that were the fast path → promote to the top of the runbook
- Dead-end steps → demote or delete
- Alert false-positive rate: if 3+ in a week, propose tuning the threshold

Quality bar:
- Never "resolve" without verifying the metric is actually stable
- Never declare root cause without evidence (log line, query, graph)
- Blameless postmortem — focus on system + process, not the person

playbooks.name: Scrape Google Maps and ship personalized cold outreach
playbooks.description: Scrape Google Maps for a niche+city, enrich, and ship outreach. Get a vetted list and a 3-touch sequence per lead.
playbooks.prompt:
Build a local-business lead-gen pipeline end-to-end: scrape Google Maps for a niche+city, enrich emails, verify, and write personalized outreach.

Inputs:
- Niche / category (be specific): [e.g. "independent dental practices", "yoga studios with <10 staff"]
- Target cities / areas: [list]
- My offer + one-liner: [paste]
- My credibility / proof point: [paste]
- Scraper tool: [Apify Google Maps / Outscraper / SerpAPI / scrap.io]
- Enrichment stack: [Hunter / Apollo / Snov / Clay]
- Verifier: [EmailListVerify / NeverBounce / ZeroBounce]
- Sending stack: [Instantly / Smartlead / Lemlist]
- Daily volume per inbox: [default 30]
- Tone: [warm-and-direct / playful / industry-peer]

Phase 1 — Scope and scrape.
- Confirm niche + cities. Estimate list size before scraping.
- Wait for my approval.
- Run the Google Maps scraper for {category} + {city}. Capture: name, address, phone, website, hours, rating, review count, photo URLs.
- Filter obvious chains (>3 locations indexed) unless I asked for chains.

Phase 2 — Enrich.
- For businesses with a website but no email, crawl contact / about / footer for visible emails
- For still-missing, try Hunter/Apollo lookup
- Drop rows missing both email AND phone — not actionable

Phase 3 — Verify.
- Run every email through deliverability
- Tag: green (safe) / yellow (catch-all or risky) / red (bounce)
- Drop reds; queue yellows for manual review

Phase 4 — Personalize per lead.
- Find ONE specific hook from their Google Maps presence:
  - A recent review (positive or negative) you can reference
  - A specific service or specialty they advertise
  - A photo subject that says something about the business
- If you cannot find a real hook, mark "skip" — don't fake personalization

Phase 5 — Write the sequence.
- Email 1 (<=80 words): subject <=6 words lowercase, open with hook, one credible proof, one low-friction CTA
- Email 2 (+3 days, <=60 words): new angle or proof, not "just bumping"
- Email 3 (+7 days, <=40 words): honest breakup, leaves door open

Phase 6 — Export.
- CSV ready to import: email, first_name, business_name, hook, subject1, body1, subject2, body2, subject3, body3
- Summary row at top: scraped / enriched / verified green / personalized / skipped

Feedback signal (after campaign sends):
- Reply rate per niche × city — feed back into next list's targeting
- Which hook types landed (review / specialty / photo) — bias future personalization
- Which inboxes flagged for spam — rotate them out

Quality bar:
- NEVER send anything from this prompt — outputs only
- NEVER scrape behind a login (no LinkedIn cookies, no Apollo session)
- Respect robots.txt for any site crawl
- US: CAN-SPAM physical address + unsubscribe in every email
- EU/UK: drop the row unless there's a clear B2B legitimate-interest basis
- Flag cities where local laws ban unsolicited B2B email (e.g. Canada CASL)

playbooks.name: Mine competitor reviews and pitch a fix
playbooks.description: Mine reviews for pain points. Get an audit PDF per prospect and a tailored email pitching the fix as a service.
playbooks.prompt:
For each prospect, mine their reviews for pain points and produce an audit PDF + a tailored cold email pitching the fix as a service.

Inputs:
- Sector: [e.g. local dental practices, boutique gyms, plumbers]
- Target prospects (5-20 names + Google/Yelp URLs): [list]
- Review sources to scan: [Google / Yelp / Trustpilot / Facebook / industry sites]
- My offer / what I'd fix: [paste — "missed-call recovery", "review reply automation", "appointment-booking bot"]
- Tone: [data-driven consultant / friendly local agency / etc.]

Phase 1 — Scrape.
- For each prospect, pull last 100 reviews per source (or all, whichever is fewer)
- Capture: rating, date, snippet, owner response if any
- Drop reviews with no text (rating-only)
- Show me the volume table before going further

Phase 2 — Cluster per prospect.
- Tag each review with one theme:
  - Wait time / scheduling
  - Communication (calls not returned, no follow-up)
  - Pricing surprises
  - Quality of service
  - Staff attitude
  - Physical space / cleanliness
  - Booking experience
- Count by theme. Average rating per theme.

Phase 3 — Produce the audit PDF per prospect (3-4 pages).
- Page 1: 1-sentence verdict + stats (avg rating, review count, response rate, top 3 themes)
- Page 2: top 3 themes with 2-3 verbatim quotes each
- Page 3: cost-of-ignore estimate using sector benchmarks if available
- Page 4: the fix and the cost of ignore vs address

Save as `audit-<prospect-slug>.pdf`.

Phase 4 — Pitch email per prospect.
- Subject (<=6 words, lowercase): tease the specific theme — "missed calls hurting reviews?"
- Body (<=120 words): one verbatim review, the pattern across their reviews, what the fix would do, attach the audit PDF, soft CTA (15-min walkthrough)
- Sign-off matching tone
- NEVER use shame language ("your reviews are terrible") — neutral observation

Phase 5 — Output.
- PDFs in workspace
- CSV: prospect | email | subject | body | top theme | rating
- "Fastest reply path" ranking: prospects whose complaints map cleanest to my fix

Feedback signal:
- Reply rate by complaint theme — which themes resonate for outreach
- Audit-PDF view tracking — who opened it
- Closed-won themes — bias next round to the highest-converting complaint pattern

Quality bar:
- Every quote is verbatim from a real review (cite source + date)
- NEVER invent reviews. If a prospect has too few, skip them.
- Don't pitch on theme A if their actual complaints are about theme B
- Respect review-site ToS: cite, link back, don't republish in bulk

playbooks.name: Turn a podcast episode into a multi-platform content pack
playbooks.description: Turn a podcast episode into a content pack. Get show notes, audiograms, a LinkedIn post, a thread, and a newsletter.
playbooks.prompt:
Turn this podcast episode into a multi-platform content pack.

Inputs:
- Episode audio URL or path: [paste]
- Episode title + show context: [paste]
- Host + guest names: [paste]
- Target audience: [who listens + what they want]
- Brand voice / tone: [paste or link]
- Primary CTA across platforms (optional): [subscribe / book guest / join community]

Phase 1 — Transcribe + chapter.
- Generate or pull the full transcript with speaker labels and timestamps
- Identify natural chapter breaks (topic shifts >=2 min)
- Tag the 5-8 strongest moments — quotable insight, contrarian take, story beat, surprising stat
- List timestamps before drafting anything

Phase 2 — Produce deliverables in this order:

1) Show notes (the host's MVP deliverable)
- 1-paragraph episode summary
- Bulleted chapter list with timestamps + 1-line per chapter
- Guest links (site, social, anything they plugged)
- 3-5 "quotes worth pulling" with timestamps

2) Audiogram briefs (5 clips, 30-90 sec each)
- For each: timestamp range, headline caption, recommended visual (waveform color, background image vibe)
- Tag platform-fit: YouTube Shorts / Reels / TikTok / LinkedIn / X

3) LinkedIn long-form post (200-350 words)
- Narrative open referencing one specific moment + timestamp
- One sharp takeaway
- Link to full episode at the bottom

4) X / Twitter thread (5-7 tweets)
- Hook tweet works standalone — no "listen to the pod" filler
- Each tweet: one concrete claim or quote
- Final tweet: episode link

5) Newsletter draft (400-600 words)
- Standalone — makes sense to someone who never listened
- Structure: anecdote -> the conversation's central tension -> the resolution -> one takeaway
- End with the episode link

Feedback signal (after publishing):
- Per platform: which audiogram drove the most plays back to the full episode — bias next batch's clip selection
- Which guest type drives the most newsletter signups — feeds future booking choices
- Show notes traffic week over week — surface the chapter format that lands

Quality bar:
- Every quote is verbatim — copy the speaker's words, not your paraphrase
- Attribute every quote to the speaker by name + timestamp
- Strip cross-talk and filler ("like", "you know") in pull quotes; keep in show notes
- Flag any contentious moment — let the host decide whether to amplify
- Never invent a moment that wasn't in the transcript

playbooks.name: Run an SEO content-decay refresh loop
playbooks.description: Find decaying posts and ship refreshes. Get a ranked list, refresh briefs, and refreshed copy with a 30-day re-measurement.
steps: Read top SERP competitors per post
Write a refresh brief + new copy
playbooks.prompt:
Run a content-decay refresh round on my site.

Inputs:
- Site: [URL]
- Analytics source: [GSC + GA4 / Ahrefs / Semrush / Plausible]
- Time window: [last 90 days vs prior 90]
- Decay threshold: [default >20% MoM traffic drop OR rank drop >5 positions]
- Top N to action this round: [default 10]
- Brand voice notes: [paste or link]

Phase 1 — Pull decay signals.
For every URL, compute:
- Organic traffic delta (% MoM)
- Average position delta
- CTR delta
- Engagement delta (avg time or scroll depth)
Surface URLs breaching the threshold. Sort by lost traffic in absolute terms.

Phase 2 — Diagnose per post.
For the top {N}:
- Why decaying:
  - Outdated info (stat from 2 years ago, defunct product, broken external link)
  - SERP shifted (competitor wrote deeper version; AI Overview eats the answer)
  - Intent shifted (people now want X, post is about Y)
  - Technical (slow page load, broken layout, robots/canonical issue)
- Pull current top-5 SERP results — read them. Note what they have that ours doesn't.

Phase 3 — Brief the refresh per post.
- Verdict: refresh / consolidate / sunset (with 301)
- For refresh: specific changes
  - Update which stats/sources
  - Add which sections (with H2/H3)
  - Remove which dated language
  - New angle or contrarian take if SERP demands it
- Effort (S / M / L)

Phase 4 — Write the refresh.
- Rewrite with the brief's changes
- Keep the URL (preserves backlinks)
- Update the post date + add a "last updated" line at top
- Verify every fact / stat / quote — cite or remove
- Output as a markdown block ready to paste into the CMS

Phase 5 — Schedule re-measurement (closes the loop).
- For each refreshed post, schedule a 30-day check: did traffic recover? rank improve?
- Output a calendar block for my project tracker

Feedback signal (after 30 days):
- Which decay drivers recovered ("updating stats lifted traffic 40%") — bias next round's diagnosis
- Which didn't recover — those might need sunset, not refresh
- Average lift per refresh — calibrates ROI vs net-new content

Quality bar:
- Never rewrite for the sake of "fresh date" — only with a real reason
- Never delete a post with backlinks without a thoughtful 301 plan
- Strip AI-slop: "delve", "unlock", "navigate the complexities"
- If a post has <100 monthly visits, flag for sunset

playbooks.name: Audit a newsletter and build the sponsorship rate card
playbooks.description: Audit a newsletter and build the sponsorship rate card. Get a media kit, rate card, and 3 sponsor pitches ready to send.
steps: Build a tiered sponsorship rate card
Draft 3 pitch emails to target sponsors
playbooks.prompt:
Audit my newsletter and build the sponsorship rate card + pitch path.

Inputs:
- Newsletter platform: [beehiiv / Substack / ConvertKit / Ghost — and how to pull stats]
- Total subscribers + 90-day growth: [paste]
- Avg open rate, click rate, unsubscribe rate (last 90 days): [paste]
- Top 10 posts by engagement (titles + open % + click %): [paste]
- My audience description (1-2 sentences — role, industry, intent): [paste]
- Closest 2-3 competitor newsletters running sponsorships: [list]
- Target sponsor types (SaaS / service / book / event / etc.): [paste]

Phase 1 — Audit the surface.
- Subscriber tier (under 1k / 1-10k / 10-100k / 100k+) and typical CPM at that tier
- Engagement quality (open % vs Substack/beehiiv benchmark by tier)
- Topic concentration — which themes consistently overperform
- Subscriber segments you can credibly slice (job title, industry, geography) given platform data
- Verdict: is the list MONETIZABLE today, or do you need 3-6 more months of growth first?

Phase 2 — Build the rate card.
- Per-placement pricing: dedicated send / classified slot / primary slot / "presented by" full sponsor
- Rate logic: blend CPM + flat minimums + scarcity (one sponsor per issue)
- Bundle options (4-pack, 12-pack with discount)
- Add-ons (social cross-post, podcast read, custom landing page)
- Realistic per-issue revenue range at current size

Phase 3 — Draft 3 pitch emails to target sponsor types.
- Each <=120 words
- Open with a specific reason THIS sponsor fits this audience (not "great deal")
- One credible proof (engagement stat, segment they care about, comparable case)
- Clear rates + next step (book a 15-min slot or send the media kit)
- Sign-off matching my voice

Phase 4 — Output.
- Rate card as a 1-page PDF
- Media kit (2 pages) with audience profile, engagement stats, sample issue
- The 3 pitch emails as drafts
- A "do this before pitching" checklist (sponsor page on site, logo wall, etc.)

Feedback signal (after 30 days of pitching):
- Reply rate per sponsor type — which segments are warmest
- Pricing pushback patterns — recalibrate rate card if a tier consistently gets discounted
- Sponsor performance once placed (clicks, signups) — feed into the next pitch's case-study line

Quality bar:
- Never inflate subscriber count or open rates — sponsors verify; one bust kills the reputation
- Never promise audience overlap you can't measure (no "mostly CTOs" without survey data)
- Be honest if the list isn't monetizable yet — recommend a growth plan instead
- Don't use "we" if it's a solo newsletter — sponsors hate fake teams

playbooks.name: Mine closed deals to refine your ICP
playbooks.description: Mine last quarter's closed deals to refine your ICP. Get patterns by segment and updated scoring rules for next quarter.
playbooks.prompt:
Mine my last quarter's closed deals to tighten my ICP for the next quarter.

Inputs:
- CRM source: [Salesforce / HubSpot / Pipedrive / Close — how to access]
- Quarter to analyze: [Q3 2026 / etc.]
- Current ICP: [paste — title + company size + industry + use case]
- Closed-won, closed-lost, in-progress counts: [paste totals]
- Sales / CSM notes (call summaries, deal notes): [paste or link]

Phase 1 — Pull and classify.
- For every closed deal: firmographics (size, industry, region), behavioral (lead source, touches), buying committee (titles), velocity (days to close), ACV, expansion potential
- Classify each: closed-won-good-fit / closed-won-bad-fit (will churn) / closed-lost-good-fit (should have won) / closed-lost-bad-fit (correctly disqualified)

Phase 2 — Pattern analysis.
For each bucket:
- Firmographic / behavioral signals that predict it
- Velocity profile (fast wins vs slow grinds)
- ACV profile
- Top objections

Findings as: "X% of closed-won-good-fit had {signal}; only Y% of closed-lost-bad-fit did" — concrete and measurable.

Phase 3 — Update the ICP.
- What's IN that wasn't (new sub-segment performing well)
- What's OUT (segment losing or winning bad-fit deals)
- New must-have qualifiers
- New disqualifiers

Show me the updated ICP as a diff. Wait for approval.

Phase 4 — Translate to scoring rules.
- Lead-scoring per signal: +X or -X points
- Stage gates: "do not advance to demo without {signal verified}"
- BDR talk-track changes: which discovery questions to ask first

Phase 5 — Output.
- ICP update memo (1-2 pages) as `icp-q<X>-update.pdf`
- CSV of scoring-rule changes ready to load into CRM
- A "kill list" of in-progress deals that no longer match — recommend tactful disqualification

Feedback signal (after next quarter):
- Did closed-won rate go up for new-ICP leads?
- Did time-to-close shorten?
- Did churn drop in the closed-won cohort?
- Loop the result back into the ICP for the following quarter

Quality bar:
- Every claim cites specific deals (IDs or anonymized names)
- NEVER fabricate a pattern from one deal — minimum 3 examples
- If sample sizes are too small for a segment, say so — don't force a conclusion
- This is sales analysis, NOT a layoff list — frame for targeting, not blame

playbooks.name: Write this month's investor update
playbooks.description: Write this month's investor update from raw KPIs. Get a polished memo + email + an ask list with specific intros.
playbooks.prompt:
Write this month's investor update.

Inputs:
- Last month's update (for delta + tone reference): [paste or link]
- This month's KPIs: [paste — revenue, MRR/ARR, growth, churn, runway, headcount, key launches]
- Wins this month (3-5 bullets): [paste]
- Misses this month (be honest — 2-3): [paste]
- Asks I have for investors (intros, hires, advice): [paste]
- Tone: [transparent-founder / sharp-operator / chatty]

Step 1 — Structure the memo.
Sections, in order:
1. TL;DR (3 sentences max — the single most important thing)
2. Numbers table (this month vs last vs plan, with deltas)
3. Wins (3-5, each with a concrete outcome — not "we launched X" but "X drove $Y in revenue")
4. Misses (2-3, with what you're doing about each — never just "we'll do better")
5. What I'm focused on next month (3 priorities, in outcome language)
6. Asks (specific intros by company or role; not "intros welcome")

Step 2 — Write it.
- TL;DR first. Investors skim — front-load.
- Numbers table: metric, this-month, last-month, % delta, plan target. Flag anything off plan with a 1-line explanation.
- Wins: one paragraph each, with a metric you can defend
- Misses: name it, cause as you understand it today, the experiment to fix it. Owners + timelines.
- Asks: list each ask with the WHY ("we need a head of growth because conversion is stuck at X")

Step 3 — Output.
- Polished memo (.pdf and .md) to my workspace
- Same content as an email body with subject: "<Company> — <Month> update: <one-line theme>"
- A "what to leave out next time" note for me (anything that felt too in-the-weeds)

Feedback signal (closes loop month over month):
- Reply rate from investors — if it drops, you're being too long or too generic
- Asks that get answered — which framing of asks gets actual intros? Bias next month's wording.
- Which sections investors quote back in 1:1s — those are the parts that landed

Quality bar:
- NEVER hide a miss to "manage perception" — investors find out and lose trust
- Never invent metrics or growth rates — round only to plausible precision
- No "we're seeing momentum" filler — quote a number or cut it
- Keep total length under 800 words — every line should earn its place

playbooks.name: Cluster customer interviews and feed shipped fixes back
playbooks.description: Cluster customer interviews and feed shipped fixes back. Get a discovery report and a ranked product backlog.
steps: Loop back last cohort's shipped items
playbooks.prompt:
Cluster this cohort of customer interviews, surface the highest-leverage themes, and prepare next sprint's backlog.

Inputs:
- Interview transcripts (5-20): [paste files or paths]
- Customer attributes per interviewee (segment, ACV, tenure): [CSV]
- Last cohort's shipped items (so we can measure adoption): [list]
- My product / company in 1 line: [paste]

Phase 1 — Read every transcript end-to-end.
Do not skim. Note your reading order so the analysis isn't biased by the loudest customer first.

Phase 2 — Per-interview extraction.
For each transcript, extract:
- 1-line "what they're trying to do"
- 3-5 jobs-to-be-done mentioned (in their words)
- Frictions encountered with current solution (theirs OR ours)
- A wish: what would they want to be magically possible?
- Would-they-pay-for-it answer if tested
- Direct verbatim quotes with timestamps for the most quotable lines

Phase 3 — Cluster across cohort.
- Theme each friction / wish across interviewees
- Frequency (how many mentioned)
- Revenue impact (sum of ACV)
- Score = frequency × revenue + sentiment intensity tag (mild / strong / blocker)

Phase 4 — Prioritize.
- Top 5 themes: name, 3 verbatim quotes, customers affected, revenue at stake, recommendation (ship / investigate / decline + why)
- Bottom themes: what to explicitly NOT work on, with reasoning

Phase 5 — Loop back last cohort's shipped items (closes the loop).
- For each item shipped last round: did interviewees mention it? Did they use it? Did it close the friction?
- Verdict per shipped item: hit / partial / miss

Phase 6 — Output.
- Discovery report (3-5 pages) as `discovery-<date>.pdf`
- Prioritized backlog CSV: theme | priority | suggested experiment | owner | rough effort
- A "what to ask next cohort" list to test hypotheses we couldn't validate this round

Feedback signal:
- Adoption rate of shipped items per theme — if low, the fix missed the real friction
- Which interview style / question elicited the strongest signal — refine the discovery script
- Drop-off in friction mentions over cohorts — measures whether you're closing problems for good

Quality bar:
- Every theme cites at least 3 customer quotes (not just one loud one)
- Never speak FOR customers — use their words verbatim
- If a customer asked for X but the JTBD is Y, surface BOTH
- If a theme is huge but only 1 customer mentioned it, flag "outlier — investigate" not "P0"

playbooks.name: Run an NPS detractor save loop
playbooks.description: Triage detractors, diagnose, and run a save play. Get a save script per detractor and a 30-day re-survey schedule.
steps: Draft save plays per high-value detractor
playbooks.prompt:
Run a detractor save round end-to-end: triage, diagnose root cause, draft tailored save plays, and schedule re-surveys.

Inputs:
- NPS data export (last 30 days, score + free-text + customer_id + ACV): [paste]
- CRM source for context (interactions, tickets, usage): [how to access]
- CSM team + workload: [paste]
- Known save plays (discount / exec sponsorship / new feature preview / training): [list]

Phase 1 — Triage detractors.
- Every score 0-6 from the last 30 days
- Drop responses with no free-text (can't act on no signal)
- For each: pull account context (ACV, tenure, recent tickets, last login)
- Flag high-ACV as P0; mid-ACV as P1; low-ACV as P2

Phase 2 — Diagnose per detractor.
For each:
- Extract the single most actionable phrase from their free-text
- Tag root cause: product-gap / pricing / support / onboarding / sales-promise-mismatch / champion-left / out-of-our-control
- Identify history pattern (recent ticket, billing event, executive change at their company)

Phase 3 — Cluster across all detractors.
- Theme frequency
- Revenue at stake per theme
- Top 3 themes → product / sales / CS leadership need to see these

Phase 4 — Draft save plays per detractor (P0 + P1).
For each:
- Suggested CSM (load-balanced by workload)
- Save play to lead with (most likely to resonate given the root cause)
- 100-word script: validate feedback, name the specific issue, propose action, ask for 15 min next week
- Backup play if the first is declined
- Realistic P(save): high / med / low — be honest

Phase 5 — Schedule re-survey (closes the loop).
- 30-day re-survey task for each save attempt
- 60-day check for "did the underlying issue actually get fixed?"

Phase 6 — Output.
- Save-play CSV: customer | score | theme | CSM | play | script | re-survey date
- Weekly digest for product / sales / CS leadership: themes + revenue at stake + recommended ownership
- "Do not contact" list for detractors who asked for no follow-up

Feedback signal (after 30 days):
- Save rate per theme — which are saveable, which aren't
- Save rate per CSM — promote what's working
- Themes that recur quarter over quarter — surface to product as systemic

Quality bar:
- Never frame a save call as "we want to keep your business" — lead with their problem
- Never over-promise — if you can't fix the root cause, say so and earn trust
- Respect "do not contact" responses immediately
- If a detractor's issue is genuinely out of our control, accept gracefully — don't drag it out

playbooks.name: Run a weekly review on calendar, journal, and todos
playbooks.description: Run a weekly review with calendar, journal, and todos. Get patterns, 3 priorities for next week, and a slipped log.
steps: Log what slipped for next loop
playbooks.prompt:
Run my weekly review. Read what actually happened, identify patterns, and set up next week.

Inputs:
- Calendar for the past 7 days: [link or paste]
- Journal entries / daily notes for the past 7 days: [paste or path]
- Todo list (open + completed): [paste or link]
- Last week's planned 3 priorities (so we can score): [paste]
- Energy notes (when I focus best): [paste]

Phase 1 — Read what happened.
- Per day: calendar blocks, journal sentiment / energy / wins / friction, todos closed vs slipped
- Simple stats: meeting hours, deep-work hours, todos completed / opened ratio

Phase 2 — Score last week's 3 priorities.
For each: hit / partial / miss. One sentence why.
- If miss: bad planning, bad execution, or wrong priority?

Phase 3 — Patterns.
- Energy peaks and valleys
- Calendar shape: did the structure match the priorities? Or did meetings eat focus blocks?
- One recurring friction (a task that kept slipping, a person blocking, a tool that wasted time)
- One surprise win (something that worked you didn't plan for)

Phase 4 — Next week's plan.
- 3 priorities in outcome language ("ship X", not "work on X")
- A time-blocked skeleton: protect deep-work blocks around fixed meetings
- One thing to STOP doing this week
- One thing to START doing this week

Phase 5 — Log what slipped (closes the loop).
- Append to `slipped.md` the tasks that didn't close
- Pattern check: are the same tasks slipping 3+ weeks running? Kill them or break them down.

Feedback signal:
- Priority hit rate over 4 weeks — if <50%, over-planning or under-protecting time
- Recurring friction themes — surface to a "kill list" for the month
- Energy patterns refined each week — schedule deep work in your peak window

Quality bar:
- Total output <300 words — tight plan, not a journal
- Be honest about misses — don't sugarcoat
- Don't add new ideas as priorities if last week's didn't ship
- If I missed all 3 priorities, ASK before just rolling them over — something's wrong upstream

playbooks.name: Run an annual review from a year of journals
playbooks.description: Read 12 months of journals and run an annual review. Get patterns, 3 themes for next year, and a quarterly check-in schedule.
playbooks.prompt:
Run my annual review using a year of journals, calendar, and notes.

Inputs:
- 12 months of journal entries / daily notes: [path or paste]
- Calendar for the year (or summary): [link or paste]
- Last year's themes / goals (if any): [paste]
- Closest people in my life this year: [list]
- Areas of life to score (work / health / relationships / craft / money / etc.): [paste]

Phase 1 — Read the year.
- Read every journal entry in chronological order. Note your reading order so you don't anchor on recent months.
- For each month, jot a one-line summary: dominant theme + energy + turning point if any
- Pull the 10-20 longest entries — usually the ones that matter most

Phase 2 — Surface patterns.
- 3-5 biggest wins, with concrete outcomes (not "I grew" but "I shipped X")
- 3-5 biggest losses or misses — what they cost, what you learned (honest, not punishing)
- Recurring frictions that NEVER got resolved — systemic issues to attack next year
- Surprises: anything that mattered more than expected; anything you expected to matter that didn't
- Per area of life: hit / partial / miss for the year

Phase 3 — Compare to last year's themes.
- For each theme last year: did it land? Evidence?
- Which themes you kept showing up for vs which faded
- Which themes were ill-defined and need a sharper next-year version

Phase 4 — Set next year's themes (3, not 10).
- Each theme: name, why this year, what success looks like in concrete terms (a metric, an artifact, a relationship change), what you'll say NO to
- One thing to STOP
- One thing to START

Phase 5 — Calendar block the year.
- Block major projects, retreats, family/relationship time
- Schedule a quarterly check-in: re-read this review + your weekly slipped log

Phase 6 — Output.
- Polished annual review PDF (5-8 pages) as `annual-review-<year>.pdf`
- 1-page summary for sharing with a coach / partner / close friend if I want
- Calendar import file (.ics) for blocked time

Feedback signal (next year, closes the multi-year loop):
- Did the 3 themes still feel right at the quarterly check-in?
- Patterns that recur 2+ years — those are identity-level, not goal-level
- Misses that recur 2+ years — kill them or radically restructure

Quality bar:
- Don't sugarcoat — but don't punish either. Diagnostic, not punitive.
- Use my actual words from the journal wherever possible — your paraphrase loses the texture
- If a theme feels forced ("I should care about networking"), say so — fake themes are worse than no themes
- Keep digestible — if I won't re-read it in 3 months, it's too long

playbooks.name: Keep your close relationships warm
playbooks.description: Spot relationships decaying and re-engage tastefully. Get a scored list, drafted messages, and follow-up dates.
playbooks.prompt:
Audit my close relationships and keep the important ones warm.

Inputs:
- Contact list with last-interaction date (CSV from phone / email / Notion / personal CRM): [paste or path]
- Tier rubric (define your own — examples below): [paste or use defaults]
   - Tier 1: closest family + 5 closest friends — touch at least monthly
   - Tier 2: close friends + key professional ties — touch at least quarterly
   - Tier 3: extended network — touch at least twice a year
- Recent journal entries mentioning any of these people (last 3 months): [paste or path]
- My current bandwidth: [how much time / week can I actually give this?]

Phase 1 — Tier and score.
- Tag every contact with a tier
- Flag anyone past their tier's threshold
- Sort by decay risk — how long past the threshold AND how important

Phase 2 — Surface context per decaying relationship.
For each flagged contact:
- Last interaction: when, what about
- Anything in my journal that mentioned them recently
- Any life event you can find (birthday this month, recent move, milestone — only if I gave you data)
- The most natural reason to reach out

Phase 3 — Draft a tasteful re-engagement per contact.
- Tone: how I'd actually text or email them — not LinkedIn "let's reconnect"
- Reference something specific (last conversation, shared memory, life event)
- A low-friction next step (a coffee, a call, a "no need to reply just thinking of you")
- Length matches the relationship — Tier 1 short and warm, Tier 3 longer "here's what I've been up to"

Phase 4 — Schedule.
- Spread the outreach over the week so I'm not blasting 30 in a day
- Tag any contacts I should call rather than text/email
- Add a follow-up date on my calendar so I don't drop the thread

Phase 5 — Output.
- Markdown table: contact | tier | days since last touch | context | drafted message | suggested channel | scheduled date
- A "do not reach out this week" list (people in conflict, recent loss, asked for space)

Feedback signal (closes loop month over month):
- Reply rate by tier — are you actually reconnecting with Tier 1?
- Patterns in which messages got the longest replies — those are the warmth-builders
- Relationships that stayed dormant despite multiple touches — accept it, drop from active list

Quality bar:
- NEVER batch-send identical messages — every one is 1:1
- NEVER reference something they shared in confidence
- Tier 1 outreach is never asking for something — it's just showing up
- If a relationship is genuinely over (mutual fade, life apart), respect it
- Don't add new contacts to active tiers without explicit input — relationships are earned in

playbooks.name: Plan a family meal week from pantry + budget
playbooks.description: Plan 7 days of meals from your pantry + budget. Get a grocery list and a kid-friendly schedule.
steps: Generate grocery list grouped by section
playbooks.prompt:
Plan a family meal week from the pantry + budget + dietary constraints.

Inputs:
- Household: who's eating (ages, preferences, allergies): [paste]
- Pantry inventory (snap a photo or list staples + perishables): [paste]
- Dietary constraints (allergies, religious, preference): [paste]
- Weekly grocery budget: [amount]
- Nights with hard time constraints (kids' activity, late work): [paste]
- Cuisines we love + would like more of: [paste]
- Leftover tolerance: [love 'em / once is enough]

Phase 1 — Inventory + plan shape.
- Group pantry: USE THIS WEEK (perishables) vs anything else
