- Decide cuisine mix for the 7 days (don't make the same culture 3 nights in a row)
- Identify 1-2 nights for fast / one-pot meals based on time constraints
- Identify 1 night for a "stretch" recipe — a fun project

Phase 2 — Draft the 7-day plan.
For each night:
- Recipe name + cuisine
- 5-min summary of how to make it
- Pantry items it uses (mark which)
- New ingredients needed (drives the grocery list)
- Active cook time
- Kid-friendly flag

Phase 3 — Build the grocery list.
- Group by store section (produce, dairy, dry, frozen, meat/fish)
- Specific quantities (not "onions" but "3 yellow onions")
- Estimate cost per item using rough current prices
- Total estimate vs budget — if over, suggest swaps

Phase 4 — Output.
- 1-page meal plan as PDF for the fridge
- Grocery list as a markdown checklist
- A "what to prep on Sunday" list (wash-and-chop that makes weeknights faster)

Feedback signal (next week):
- Which recipes got eaten happily vs pushed around the plate — promote winners
- Which pantry items got used vs piled up — stop buying the unused ones
- Did actual grocery cost match estimate? Tune the price list.

Quality bar:
- Never propose a recipe nobody will actually eat
- Respect allergies absolutely — even trace contamination warnings
- Default to whole-food, scratch-cook unless I said otherwise
- If budget is tight, lead with cheaper proteins (eggs, beans, ground meat); skip steak-night
- Keep total active cook time under 45 min for any weeknight unless I asked for the project meal

playbooks.name: Optimize an Airbnb listing and set re-measurement
playbooks.description: Optimize an Airbnb listing end-to-end. Get title + photos + price + message templates with a 30-day re-measurement.
playbooks.prompt:
Optimize an Airbnb listing end-to-end and set up the re-measurement loop.

Inputs:
- Listing URL or property name: [paste]
- 90 days of booking + revenue + occupancy data: [paste or CSV]
- 90 days of reviews (titles + full text): [paste or path]
- Competitor listings in the area (3-5 comparable): [URLs]
- Current pricing strategy (flat / dynamic / seasonal): [paste]
- Current message templates (inquiry / pre-arrival / check-out / review): [paste]
- Constraints (min stay, gap day, owner-blocked dates): [paste]

Phase 1 — Diagnose performance.
- Occupancy vs comps (above / at / below market)
- Average daily rate vs comps
- Total revenue vs comps (occupancy × ADR)
- Review score + 2-3 themes from reviews — both wins and gripes
- Conversion rate (views to bookings) if available

Phase 2 — Optimize the listing.
- Title: rewrite for the strongest single hook (proximity to X, the unique feature, the trip type)
- Photos: list 5-10 photo upgrades (cover photo, missing room, lighting, staging)
- Description: rewrite using wins from reviews — let guests' words sell the place
- House rules: surface anything causing review hits (cleanliness fee surprise, parking confusion)
- Amenities: any I'm under-tagging that comps are tagging

Phase 3 — Pricing.
- Recommended dynamic curve for next 90 days, calibrated to weekday / weekend / seasonal events
- Minimum stay rules to optimize occupancy without leaving money on the table
- Gap-day discount logic for awkward one-night gaps

Phase 4 — Rewrite the message templates.
- Inquiry response: <=120 words, warm + concrete (proximity / parking / wifi / check-in)
- Pre-arrival: 48h before — practical (entry, parking, neighborhood)
- Check-out: simple list, no guilt-trippy "please leave a 5-star review"
- Post-stay review request: 24h after — a specific compliment to the guest, soft review ask

Phase 5 — Schedule re-measurement (closes the loop).
- 30 days from now: re-check occupancy, ADR, review score, conversion
- 60 days: full re-audit on the same axes

Phase 6 — Output.
- An action list ranked by ROI (changes that take an hour and lift bookings 10%+ first)
- Rewritten title + description + house rules + amenity list
- 4 message templates ready to paste into Airbnb
- A 1-page summary PDF for my co-host or cleaner

Feedback signal:
- After 30 days: which changes moved the metric you targeted?
- Patterns in new reviews — did the gripes go away?
- Did pricing changes lift revenue, or just shift bookings around?

Quality bar:
- NEVER fabricate amenities (no "ocean view" if you can see a parking lot)
- NEVER write fake-friendly templates — guests can smell scripts
- Respect platform rules (no off-platform contact ask in templates)
- If reviews are dropping for a structural reason (the bed, wall thinness), name it — cosmetic fixes won't save it

playbooks.name: Draft a novel chapter with continuity
playbooks.description: Draft a novel chapter without breaking continuity. Get beats, prose at your voice, and a continuity diff vs the bible.
steps: Read the bible + last chapter end-to-end
Diff new facts back into the bible
playbooks.prompt:
Draft the next chapter of my novel without breaking continuity.

Inputs:
- Continuity bible (characters, world rules, established facts, timeline): [path]
- Prior chapter(s) — at minimum the last full chapter: [paste or path]
- My outline for THIS chapter (a paragraph is fine): [paste]
- The book's POV (1st / 3rd limited / 3rd omniscient) + tense: [paste]
- 2-3 prose samples that capture my voice: [paste]
- Target word count: [e.g. 3000-4000 words]
- Off-limits (a scene I'm not writing, a reveal not yet earned): [paste]

Phase 1 — Read the bible + last chapter end-to-end.
- Note every character on stage at the end of the previous chapter — they need to either be moved off or accounted for
- Note any time-of-day / location continuity needed for the opening line
- Note any open emotional or plot thread this chapter should close, advance, or deliberately leave hanging

Phase 2 — Beat the chapter.
- Open beat: where + when + who (continue from prior chapter, not jump cold)
- 3-6 middle beats: what changes scene to scene? What's the protagonist trying / failing / learning?
- Close beat: ends on a turn — a reveal, a decision, a cliffhanger, or a still moment that sets up the next chapter
- Show me the beats. Wait for approval before drafting prose.

Phase 3 — Draft the prose.
- POV + tense locked from the bible
- Voice matches the prose samples — sentence rhythm, vocabulary, comma habit
- Dialogue carries weight — no chit-chat that doesn't reveal character or move plot
- Scene description in service of mood, not inventory
- Hit the target word count within ±15%

Phase 4 — Continuity check.
- For every fact you used about the world, character, or timeline: verify against the bible
- Surface any place you had to invent — name the new fact and ask whether to add to the bible
- Flag any phrase that drifted from the voice samples

Phase 5 — Output.
- Drafted chapter (.docx + .md) to my workspace
- A diff against the bible: new facts the chapter introduces
- A note on what threads this chapter advanced and what's still open for the next one

Feedback signal:
- After I edit: which lines I cut tell you what's drifting from the voice
- Continuity issues caught at edit — bake into the bible so they don't recur
- Pacing: too long / short relative to beat count? Tune ratios for next time.

Quality bar:
- NEVER invent a character, place, or rule that contradicts the bible
- NEVER advance a thread the outline said to leave alone
- Show, don't tell — replace "she was angry" with the action that proves it
- Strip first-draft tics: weak verbs ("was/were"), filter verbs ("she felt", "she heard")
- Don't ship a chapter that ends on a wet noodle — every chapter end is a small hook

playbooks.name: Build a course / cohort program end-to-end
playbooks.description: Build a course / cohort program end-to-end. Get modules, quizzes, drip schedule, sales page, and a fully-drafted Module 1.
steps: Write the sales page + launch sequence
playbooks.prompt:
Build a course / cohort program end-to-end.

Inputs:
- Topic + the single transformation it delivers ("learn to ship a SaaS landing page" not "marketing"): [paste]
- Target student (level + goal + pain): [paste]
- Format: [self-paced async / live cohort / hybrid] + length [4 weeks / 6 weeks / etc.]
- My credibility (why I can teach this): [paste]
- Tools I'll use (Maven / Skool / Teachable / Kajabi / Discord + email): [paste]
- Existing material I have (blog posts, talks, notes): [path or list]
- Price target: [amount]

Phase 1 — Lock the transformation.
- Restate the transformation in one sentence (student goes from X to Y in Z weeks)
- The single artifact the student will produce by the end (a deployed thing, a finished work, a portfolio piece)
- The 3-5 specific outcomes a graduate will demonstrate

Wait for me to confirm. The transformation drives every module.

Phase 2 — Module outline.
- 6-10 modules, each with: title, 1-line learning objective, the homework artifact the student ships
- Sequence so each module's homework feeds the next
- Identify the 1-2 modules where students typically drop off and make those extra concrete

Phase 3 — Per-module content.
For each module:
- 3-5 lessons (each 5-15 min if video, or 800-1200 words if written)
- A quiz or self-check at the end (5 questions max, calibrated to "did you understand the load-bearing concept")
- A homework brief with: goal, steps, a real example, a rubric for "good enough to move on"
- Optional stretch challenge for advanced students

Phase 4 — Drip + community.
- Drip schedule (when each module unlocks for self-paced / what's covered in each live session for cohort)
- Community rhythm: weekly office hour question, peer-review channel, accountability buddies
- Mid-course check-in to catch drop-off risk

Phase 5 — Launch + pricing.
- Sales page outline (hero + problem + solution + curriculum + outcomes + price + FAQ)
- Email sequence for waitlist → launch (5 emails)
- Pricing logic + cohort cap reasoning

Phase 6 — Output.
- Full course outline as a single PDF
- Module 1 fully written as a proof-of-concept (lessons + homework + quiz)
- Sales page draft
- The waitlist email sequence

Feedback signal (after cohort 1, closes the loop):
- Drop-off curve — which module loses students. Restructure THAT module.
- Homework completion rate per module — low completion needs easier wins or clearer rubric
- NPS at the end + "what would you tell a friend" quotes — those become next cohort's sales page

Quality bar:
- Never promise outcomes you can't deliver — under-promise, over-deliver
- Every module has one clear takeaway — if you can't name it, the module isn't ready
- Avoid filler ("welcome video", "what we'll cover") — students paid for transformation, not throat-clearing
- If the course works async, don't fake live urgency — different students buy different formats

playbooks.name: Distill reusable skills from your recent agent runs
playbooks.description: Mine recent agent runs and distill reusable Skills. Get new skill files with verification steps and pitfalls.
steps: Extract patterns from wins and failures
Write skill files with pitfalls + verification
playbooks.prompt:
Look at my recent agent runs and distill reusable skills from them so I don't have to re-explain every time.

Inputs:
- Recent task history (last 7-30 days of agent runs / chats / completed work): [paste path or summary]
- Current skill directory: [path]
- Skill format I use: [Anthropic Skills SKILL.md / .claude/skills / custom]
- Max new skills to propose this round: [default 5]

Phase 1 — Read the history.
- Skim every completed task
- Tag each: one-off / pattern (might recur) / system change (worth a skill)
- Drop the one-offs

Phase 2 — Pattern extraction.
For "pattern" tasks:
- Goal in one sentence
- Inputs
- Steps that actually worked (what shipped value, not what was planned)
- What went wrong? What had to be re-asked or re-done?
- The canonical "good run" of this task

Cluster patterns. If 3+ tasks share the same shape, that's a skill candidate.

Phase 3 — Score candidates.
For each:
- Frequency: how often will this recur?
- Stakes: cost of getting it wrong?
- Drift: how often does the right approach change? (high-drift skills age fast)
- ROI: time saved per future invocation

Show me the top {N} candidates ranked. Wait for confirmation.

Phase 4 — Write the skill files.
For each approved candidate:
- Title + 1-line purpose
- When to use (and when NOT to)
- Required inputs (named, with types)
- Step-by-step procedure
- Verification steps (how to know the run succeeded)
- Pitfalls (specific failure modes from history + workaround)
- Example invocation
- Update history at bottom (date + what changed)

Save each as a separate file in the skill directory.

Phase 5 — Update the index (closes the loop — the agent becomes smarter for next time).
- Add new skills to the registry
- Re-sort the index by frequency-of-use if available

Feedback signal:
- After a month: which new skills got invoked, which gathered dust?
- Skills that got invoked but produced bad runs — root-cause and patch the skill
- Patterns the agent keeps re-asking about despite a skill existing — the skill is hidden or routing is broken

Quality bar:
- Never create a skill from a single example — minimum 3 instances to call it a pattern
- Each skill has explicit verification steps — no "trust me"
- Pitfalls section is mandatory — no skill ships without documented failure modes
- If two skills overlap, merge them or call out the difference clearly
- Skills drift — every skill has a "last reviewed" date; flag anything >90 days for re-review

playbooks.name: Plan a trip with the expensive research done first
playbooks.description: Plan a trip end-to-end with visa + vaccine + advisory research done first. Get a day-by-day itinerary, packing list, and budget.
steps: Do the visa / vaccine / advisory research first
playbooks.prompt:
Plan this trip end-to-end with the "being wrong is expensive" research done.

Inputs:
- Destination(s) + dates: [paste]
- Travelers (count, ages, mobility / dietary / medical considerations): [paste]
- Trip style (lazy / adventure / cultural / business+leisure / etc.): [paste]
- Budget (total, or per-person per-day): [paste]
- Passports / citizenships in the group: [paste]
- Non-negotiables (must-see, must-eat, must-do): [paste]
- Pace preference (1 thing/day / packed / mix): [paste]

Phase 1 — The "expensive to get wrong" research.
- Visa requirements per traveler for each destination (entry stamp, e-visa, visa-on-arrival, pre-application)
- Vaccine + health requirements (yellow fever cert, required vaccines, recommended)
- Travel advisories for the dates (gov advisory level, recent unrest, weather hazards, monsoon / hurricane / wildfire season)
- Travel insurance recommendation tier + 2-3 specific policies fitting the trip
- Currency + payment landscape (cash heavy? cards widely accepted? specific apps locally dominant?)
- SIM / eSIM options + cost
- Power adapter type

If anything is a blocker (visa not obtainable in time, vaccine needs weeks to take effect), flag it loudly NOW.

Phase 2 — Day-by-day itinerary.
For each day:
- City + neighborhood you'll be in
- Morning / afternoon / evening blocks
- 1-2 anchor activities per block (don't over-pack)
- Travel time between activities (realistic — include the 20 min to find an Uber, not just the drive)
- Food: 1 specific recommendation per meal, with cuisine + price tier + walking time
- A buffer block (90 min minimum) for downtime / weather contingency
- Logistical notes (book the museum slot 48h ahead, the restaurant requires a reservation, this market is closed Mondays)

Phase 3 — Logistics + budget.
- Lodging: shortlist 3 per city with neighborhood logic, price, why-this-pick
- Inter-city transport: flights / trains / ferries with realistic timings
- Estimated budget per day per category (lodging / food / activities / transport / shopping buffer)
- Total trip cost vs budget — if over, suggest cuts

Phase 4 — Packing + prep checklist.
- Documents (printed copies, photos in cloud)
- Clothing for the climate at the dates + 1-2 things the climate isn't obvious about
- Health kit specific to destinations (mosquito repellent, altitude meds, etc.)
- Cash strategy

Phase 5 — Output.
- Polished itinerary PDF (printable + shareable)
- 1-page "essentials at a glance" (addresses, confirmation numbers, emergency contacts in destination)
- Pre-departure checklist with dates by which each item should be done (visa, insurance, etc.)
- Offline-accessible Google Maps list of every venue mentioned

Feedback signal (mid-trip, closes loop for next trip):
- Which blocks ran long vs short — recalibrate the rest of the trip
- Which restaurants / activities exceeded expectations — bias next city's picks toward the same source
- Anything the research missed — capture for the next trip's planning prompt

Quality bar:
- NEVER assume visa rules from prior trips — they change. Verify against the destination's current government site.
- NEVER recommend an activity without checking it's actually operating in the season I'm visiting
- Cite real, current sources for the health / safety advisories — link them
- If anything in the trip is high-risk for one of the travelers (mobility, allergy, condition), name it and recommend a swap
- Flag every place you had to guess (lodging price during a specific event, restaurant availability) so I can verify before booking

playbooks.name: Mine likers of a viral LinkedIn post for outreach
playbooks.description: Mine likers/commenters of a viral post. Get a scored list and DMs tied to the original post's hook.
steps: Find a hook tied to the post
playbooks.prompt:
Mine the people who engaged with a viral LinkedIn post and run a tight outreach round.

Inputs:
- LinkedIn post URL: [paste]
- My ICP filter (job title + company size + industry): [paste]
- My offer + 1-line value prop: [paste]
- Tooling: [Leadspicker / PhantomBuster / Apify LinkedIn engagement scraper]
- Max leads this round: [default 50]
- Send channel: [LinkedIn DM / email / both]

Phase 1 — Pull engagement.
- Use the scraper to pull every liker + commenter on the post (cap 500)
- For each: name, role, company, location, headline, engagement type (like / comment text)
- Show me the count before going further

Phase 2 — Score for ICP fit (0-3).
- 3 = perfect match; 2 = close; 1 = adjacent (expanded buyer / influencer); 0 = noise
- Drop 0s. Show me the distribution and let me reject any 1s I want to skip.

Phase 3 — Write the outreach.
For each remaining lead:
- Open by referencing the SPECIFIC viral post (NOT "I saw you engage with content recently")
- For commenters: reference what they said in 1 sentence
- For likers: reference the post's main argument and a related question they probably care about
- Connect their context to my offer in one sentence
- Low-friction CTA: a question or a 15-min ask
- <=400 chars for LinkedIn DM; <=80 words for email

Phase 4 — If email is on:
- Find a verified email via Hunter/Apollo
- Write a parallel email with the same hook, email-appropriate length

Phase 5 — Output.
- Table: Name | Company | ICP Score | Engagement | Hook | DM | Email | Notes
- A send order grouped by score (3s first)
- A reply-triage cheatsheet: if reply says X, tag Y, next action Z

Feedback signal:
- Reply rate by ICP score — calibrates next threshold
- Reply rate by engagement type (commenter vs liker) — which to prioritize
- Which hooks landed — hook-template bank gets a winner update each round

Quality bar:
- NEVER scrape using a logged-in LinkedIn session you'd risk getting banned for
- NEVER mass-send identical DMs — each references something specific
- Respect LinkedIn's daily DM limits — flag if my volume would trip them
- If the post is about a sensitive topic (layoffs, personal loss), default to declining and tell me why

playbooks.name: Build personalized chatbot demos per prospect
playbooks.description: Build a tailored chatbot demo per prospect. Get a live demo URL, the cold email, and a follow-up plan.
steps: Write the cold email with the demo link
playbooks.prompt:
Build a tailored chatbot demo for each prospect and pitch them with the live demo URL. The demo should look like it was built FOR them.

Inputs:
- Prospect list (name + website URL + sector): [paste 5-20 rows]
- My chatbot platform: [Voiceflow / Botpress / Chatbase / Stack AI / custom]
- Hosting domain: [e.g. demo.myagency.com/<slug>]
- Pricing: [setup fee + retainer]
- Tone: [warm + competent local agency / sharp consultant / etc.]

Phase 1 — Scope per prospect.
- Crawl each prospect's website: services, hours, FAQ, contact form, common questions
- Identify the SINGLE highest-value bot use case:
  - Dentist → appointment booking + insurance question deflection
  - Plumber → emergency dispatch routing + quote intake
  - Restaurant → reservation + dietary FAQ
- Show me your picks before building. Wait for confirmation.

Phase 2 — Build the demo.
- Take brand colors and logo from their site (if visible)
- Configure with 5-10 of their actual FAQ questions and answers
- Wire the high-value intent (booking) to a fake-but-realistic flow
- Embed at a personalized URL: demo.myagency.com/<prospect-slug>
- Test every intent end-to-end before declaring it ready

Phase 3 — Cold email per prospect.
- Subject (<=6 words): "<prospect-name>, built you a demo"
- Body (<=120 words):
  - "I built a demo of an AI assistant for your <type of business>"
  - One specific thing it handles ("books appointments without calling the front desk")
  - Live link: <demo URL>
  - "If it's useful, 15 min to talk through what it'd take to deploy?"
- Sign-off + signature

Phase 4 — Follow-up plan.
- T+3 days: "did you get a chance to try the demo? happy to walk you through it"
- T+7 days: case study from a similar business + a specific metric
- T+14 days: honest breakup, leave the demo URL live for 30 more days

Phase 5 — Output.
- Each demo deployed and tested
- CSV: prospect | sector | demo URL | email subject | email body | follow-up 1 | follow-up 2 | breakup
- Demo retention check: alert me which demos got >0 sessions in the first 72h — those are hot leads

Feedback signal:
- Demo open rate (subject A/B), session rate, demo-to-call conversion
- Which sectors close at what price point — feed back into next prospect list

Quality bar:
- NEVER fabricate hours, prices, or services — only what's on the public site
- NEVER claim "AI knows everything about your business" — set realistic expectations
- Mark the demo with a small "demo built by <my agency>" footer
- If a site blocks iframes, deliver as a hosted page link

playbooks.name: Run local SEO domination for a small business
playbooks.description: Audit local SEO and ship the wins. Get a GMB plan, citation gaps, schema, and a review-response system.
steps: Ship schema markup for the site
playbooks.prompt:
Run a local-SEO domination round for an SMB.

Inputs:
- Business name + address + phone + website: [paste]
- Service area or primary location: [paste]
- 3-5 top local competitors: [paste with URLs]
- Industry: [paste]
- Current local rank for top 3 queries: [paste or "unknown"]
- Existing GMB profile URL: [paste]

Phase 1 — Audit.
- GMB completeness: categories, services, attributes, hours, photos, posts, Q&A
- NAP (Name/Address/Phone) consistency across top 10 citation sources (Yelp, BBB, Yellow Pages, industry-specific)
- Review profile: count, recent volume, response rate, sentiment
- Google Maps rank for top 5 queries from 3-5 grid points around the service area
- Schema markup on the website (LocalBusiness, Service, Review, FAQ)
- Mobile page speed (Google's #1 local ranking factor)

Phase 2 — GMB optimization plan.
- Primary category + 4 secondary
- Services matched to what competitors are ranking for
- 10 GMB Posts for the next 30 days (offers, events, products) with image briefs
- 20 Q&As to seed (with answers — ranking signal)
- Photo upload schedule (2-3/week with what to shoot)

Phase 3 — Citation gaps.
- Sources where competitors are listed and you aren't
- Industry-specific citations (e.g., dentists → Healthgrades, plumbers → Angi)
- A NAP standardization sheet so the next 50 citations match

Phase 4 — Review-response system.
- Templates for 5-star (thank, name a specific thing, soft CTA to return)
- Templates for negative (acknowledge, offer to make it right offline, never argue publicly)
- Outreach to get 10 new reviews this month (specific past customers + the ask script)

Phase 5 — Output.
- Audit PDF
- 30-day GMB plan
- Citation submission checklist (sorted by traffic)
- Review templates + outreach scripts
- Schema markup code ready to drop into the site

Feedback signal:
- Local rank delta on target queries (grid view monthly)
- GMB call / direction clicks delta
- Review count + average rating trajectory

Quality bar:
- NEVER buy reviews — Google detects and de-ranks
- NEVER use a virtual office address — GMB requires real service-area or staffed location
- Schema must validate (Google Rich Results Test)
- Don't keyword-stuff GMB business name — that's a violation

playbooks.name: Re-score the cold-call list on yesterday's dispositions
playbooks.description: Re-score the call list using yesterday's dispositions. Get a connect-tuned dial order and a talk-track A/B.
playbooks.prompt:
Use yesterday's cold-call dispositions to reorder today's call list for the highest connect rate.

Inputs:
- Yesterday's call log (CSV: lead_id, name, company, time_called, disposition): [paste]
- Today's available list (CSV: lead_id, name, company, phone, time_zone, ICP score): [paste]
- Dial windows today: [e.g. 9-11am, 1-3pm local time]
- Disposition codes I use: [CONNECT_INTERESTED / CONNECT_NOT_NOW / VOICEMAIL / NO_ANSWER / WRONG_NUMBER / DNC]
- Talk-track variants tested yesterday: [paste]

Phase 1 — Yesterday's analysis.
- Connect rate by hour of day in their time zone
- Connect rate by ICP score
- Top 3 patterns from CONNECT_INTERESTED calls (what did they say first? top objection?)
- Patterns from CONNECT_NOT_NOW — real "not nows" or polite blowoffs?

Phase 2 — Re-score today's list.
- Predicted connect probability from yesterday's hour-of-day data + their time zone
- ICP score (re-use if available)
- Dial priority = connect_prob × ICP_fit
- Reorder by dial priority within each dial window

Phase 3 — Talk-track A/B.
- Variant A: yesterday's best-performing opener (carry forward)
- Variant B: a hypothesis based on what objection killed deals yesterday
- Split 50/50

Phase 4 — Output.
- CSV: time_window | lead | phone | dial_priority | talk_track_variant
- 3-bullet summary for the team
- A "do not dial today" list (DNCs, dead numbers from yesterday, leads on snooze)

Feedback signal (end of today):
- Did dial priority correlate with connect rate? (validates the model)
- Which talk-track variant won? Promote to default.
- Which window had highest connect per ICP segment? Pin for tomorrow.

Quality bar:
- Never queue a DNC lead — re-check the scrub
- Never auto-dial outside permitted hours by jurisdiction
- If yesterday's sample is <20 calls, don't pretend to find a pattern — say so
- Tag any lead with 3 consecutive NO_ANSWER as "rest" for 2 weeks

playbooks.name: Turn a sales call recording into a CRM update
playbooks.description: Turn a sales call into a CRM update + next-step tasks + follow-up email. Get a clean stage move and ready-to-paste notes.
playbooks.prompt:
Turn a sales call recording into a CRM update + a next-step task list + a follow-up email.

Inputs:
- Call recording or Gong/Fathom/Otter transcript: [paste]
- Deal/account ID + opportunity: [paste]
- Buying committee from CRM (titles + names): [paste]
- Our methodology (MEDDIC / SPICED / CHAMP): [paste]
- Tone for follow-up email: [paste]

Phase 1 — Read and structure.
- Identify speakers; reconcile against the buying committee
- Extract: pains discussed, objections raised, decisions made, commitments by either side, timing signals
- Surface explicit and implicit blockers (champion missing, exec sponsor undisclosed)

Phase 2 — Update the CRM record.
- Suggested stage move (advance/hold/regress with one-sentence reason)
- Updates per MEDDIC field (or your methodology): metrics, economic buyer, decision criteria, decision process, identify pain, champion
- Risks: flag anything that lowers close probability
- Suggested next stage gate

Phase 3 — Next-step list.
- Tasks for me (action, owner, deadline, why)
- Tasks for the prospect (we send the proposal by X, you send IT review by Y)
- Internal asks (need legal review, need SE for demo)

Phase 4 — Follow-up email.
- Subject (<=8 words): reference the specific commitment from the call
- Body (<=200 words): recap, action items with owners + dates, one open question that earns a reply
- Attach anything they asked for
- Send-or-schedule recommendation

Phase 5 — Output.
- CRM diff (markdown) ready to paste into the deal
- Task list (CSV) ready to import
- Email draft (markdown)
- A 1-paragraph internal note for sales manager / RevOps

Feedback signal:
- Did the stage move match what actually happened?
- Which methodology slots were consistently empty after first call — refine the discovery script
- Email reply rate per follow-up template — promote the winning structure

Quality bar:
- Never invent commitments or pains that weren't said
- Cite timestamps for any direct quote
- Mark anything "low confidence — verify" if the call was muddy
- Never auto-send the follow-up — drafts only

playbooks.name: Optimize an Amazon listing end-to-end
playbooks.description: Optimize an Amazon listing with keyword research + review mining. Get title, bullets, A+ brief, and backend keywords.
playbooks.prompt:
Optimize my Amazon listing end-to-end with keyword research and review mining.

Inputs:
- My ASIN + 3-5 competitor ASINs in the same niche: [paste]
- Target marketplace: [US / UK / DE / JP / etc.]
- Brand voice notes: [paste]
- Current listing performance (sessions / conversion / revenue if available): [paste]
- Constraints: [trademarked terms to use, brand registry status, A+ access yes/no]

Phase 1 — Keyword research.
- Pull top search terms from Helium 10 / Jungle Scout / Brand Analytics for the niche
- Intent tiers: head (high volume, hard rank), torso (mid), long-tail (specific buyers)
- Cross-reference with competitor titles — what keywords are they ranking on?
- Output a ranked keyword list with monthly search volume and competition score

Phase 2 — Review mining for voice + objections.
- Pull last 500 reviews across my ASIN + competitors
- Cluster positive reviews by what buyers loved (use their exact phrases)
- Cluster negative reviews by what disappointed buyers
- Identify the top 3 "objections to overcome" my listing must address

Phase 3 — Write the listing.
- Title: front-load with the highest-volume relevant keyword. Pattern: [Brand] + [Product] + [Key Feature] + [Use Case] + [Variant] within Amazon's character limit
- 5 bullets: lead each with a benefit IN ALL CAPS THEN a sentence. First bullet handles the #1 objection. Last bullet handles brand/warranty trust.
- A+ content brief: 5-7 modules (hero with overlay, 3-feature comparison, FAQ, brand story, social proof, related products)
- Backend search terms: 250-byte limit, no duplicates, no competitor brand names

Phase 4 — Output.
- Title (counted)
- 5 bullets ready to paste
- A+ content module brief (text + image directions per module)
- Backend keywords (formatted to byte count)
- A before/after diff showing the key changes

Feedback signal (after 30 days):
- Session-to-purchase conversion delta
- Search-term performance: which keywords now have impressions / clicks
- Review themes — did the new bullets address the objections?

Quality bar:
- NEVER use prohibited terms (Amazon's flagged words: performance claims, medical claims, etc.)
- NEVER copy competitor brand names into title or backend
- Every claim has a supporting feature in the listing — no marketing-only fluff
- A+ content must work for buyers on mobile — short text, big images

playbooks.name: Generate Shopify product descriptions in bulk
playbooks.description: Generate SEO product descriptions for a Shopify catalog. Get titles, descriptions, meta, tags, and alt text per SKU.
playbooks.prompt:
Generate product descriptions for a batch of Shopify SKUs.

Inputs:
- Shopify catalog export (CSV with SKU, current title, current description, category, key attributes): [paste]
- Brand voice + tone notes: [paste or link]
- Target audience: [paste]
- SEO keyword strategy (head terms per category): [paste]
- Batch size this run: [default 50 SKUs]

Phase 1 — Audit the batch.
- For each SKU: identify what's missing (no description, generic copy, no meta, no alt text)
- Categorize by template (apparel / home / electronics / etc.)
- Flag any SKU with insufficient data — needs human input first

Phase 2 — Per-SKU generate.
For each:
- Title (<=70 chars): brand + product + key attribute + variant
- Product description (200-350 words):
  - Lead with the transformation (what the buyer gets, not what the product is)
  - 3 feature/benefit blocks (concrete)
  - Specs section (bullet list, scannable)
  - Closing line that earns the add-to-cart click
- SEO meta description (<=155 chars)
- 5 image alt-text strings tied to specific product shots
- 5-7 relevant tags

Phase 3 — Voice consistency check.
- Sample 5 random outputs back-to-back — do they sound like the same brand?
- Strip AI-slop: "elevate", "discover", "introducing", "unleash", "transform your"

Phase 4 — Output.
- Updated CSV ready to import to Shopify
- A "needs human input" CSV for the flagged SKUs
- Sample preview (3 randomly chosen SKUs) for spot-checking

Feedback signal:
- Which categories saw the highest conversion lift post-update
- Which AI phrasings buyers complained about in reviews — bake into the ban list
- Top-converting product pages — which structure did they share?

Quality bar:
- NEVER invent specs or materials — only what's in the input data
- Match Shopify SEO best practices (length, structure)
- One unique angle per product — don't pattern-match identical openers across the catalog
- If the input data is too sparse for a product, flag it — don't fill with fluff

playbooks.name: Launch a print-on-demand niche
playbooks.description: Pick a POD niche and launch 10 designs. Get a niche brief, design briefs, listings, and a 30-day publishing plan.
steps: Brief 10 designs in the chosen niche
playbooks.prompt:
Launch a print-on-demand niche end-to-end.

Inputs:
- POD platform: [Printify / Printful / Redbubble / TeePublic / Merch by Amazon]
- Storefront: [Shopify / Etsy / Amazon / direct on POD platform]
- My skills + interests (be honest): [paste]
- Budget for design tools + ads: [budget — $0 is OK]
- Time per week: [hours]

Phase 1 — Niche brief. Wait for approval before designing.

Propose 3 niche options. For each:
- Specific niche in one sentence ("nursing-specialty humor for night-shift ER nurses" NOT "nurse t-shirts")
- Why it has demand: cite 3-5 existing TeePublic/Redbubble/Etsy listings with seller name + sales rank / review count
- Why it's not over-saturated: estimated seller count + design freshness
- Smallest viable v1: 10 designs in one product format
- Realistic price + commission per sale

Recommend one. Explain why. Wait for confirmation.

Phase 2 — Design briefs (10 designs).
For each:
- Concept in one sentence (the joke / sentiment / visual hook)
- Layout (text-only / text+illustration / visual-only)
- Color palette (specific hex codes)
- Typography direction (sans / serif / handwritten — name the font family)
- Reference style ("Sarah Lawrence Press meets Smitten Kitchen") — pick artists / brands the designer would know
- Variant suggestions (mug / sticker / poster)

Phase 3 — Listings.
For each design:
- Title pattern (front-loaded keyword + niche tag + emotion + variant)
- Tag list (Etsy: 13 tags max, mix head + long-tail)
- Description (300 words): hook, who it's for, what's printed where, gift-giving angle, care instructions
- Pinterest pin caption + 5 hashtags

Phase 4 — Output.
- Niche brief PDF
- 10 design briefs (markdown)
- 10 listings ready to paste
- A 30-day publishing schedule (don't dump all 10 at once — Etsy/POD favors steady cadence)

Feedback signal (after 30 days):
- Per-design sales — which earned out the design time
- Search terms that led to clicks — bias future title patterns
- Refund rate or complaint themes — adjust quality / fulfillment partner

playbooks.name: Move a trading idea from hypothesis to paper
playbooks.description: Move a trading idea from hypothesis to paper. Get a defensible backtest, paper-trade plan, and scale-or-kill verdict.
steps: Translate idea to a testable signal
playbooks.prompt:
Take this trading idea from hypothesis to a defensible paper-trade decision. Be brutally honest — most ideas should die at backtest.

Inputs:
- The idea in plain English: [paste — what signal, what asset class, what's the edge thesis]
- Asset universe: [e.g. S&P 500 stocks / liquid futures / top 50 crypto by mcap]
- Data source: [polygon / yfinance / Tiingo / Alpaca / etc.]
- Backtest period: [e.g. 2018-01-01 to 2025-12-31]
- Initial capital + per-trade size: [paste]
- Frictions to assume: [commission / spread / slippage / borrow cost for shorts]
- Risk limits: [max drawdown / max single-position size / sector caps]

Phase 1 — Translate to a testable signal.
- Define the signal mathematically (don't accept fuzziness)
- Define entry rule and exit rule
- Define universe filter (liquidity, market cap, sector exclusions)
- Define position-sizing (equal-weight / vol-targeted / Kelly fraction)
- Show me the rules before running the backtest. Wait for confirmation.

Phase 2 — Backtest with realistic frictions.
- Walk-forward, no look-ahead
- Include: commission, spread, slippage, borrow cost for shorts, dividend handling
- Compute: total return, CAGR, Sharpe, Sortino, max drawdown, max DD duration, win rate, profit factor, turnover, average holding period
- Per-year breakdown
- Stress windows: 2018 Q4, 2020 March, 2022, any custom

Phase 3 — Defend against false-positives.
- Out-of-sample: hold out the last 20% of the period and test only there
- Walk-forward optimization: if you tuned any parameter, show sensitivity
- Look-ahead audit: prove every input was available at decision time historically
- Survivorship bias: point-in-time universe membership vs current
- Multiple-comparison check: how many variants did you try? Adjust for it.

Phase 4 — Paper-trade plan.
If backtest survives Phase 3:
- Paper-trade for a defined window (3 months minimum, or 30 trades, whichever is later)
- Track real prices, real slippage estimates, real fills
- Predefine kill conditions early (drawdown > X%, signal coverage < Y trades)

Phase 5 — Verdict.
After paper, compare to backtest:
- Did Sharpe survive? (fell more than 30% = real warning)
- Did slippage assumptions hold?
- Did the signal fire as often as expected?
- Verdict: scale to live small / continue paper / kill

Output:
- Backtest report as `signal-<name>-backtest.pdf` with charts and per-year table
- Signal-rules file (`signal-<name>.md`) with exact entry/exit/sizing logic
- Paper-trade tracking sheet
- Verdict in 3 sentences with the supporting metric

Feedback signal:
- Per signal: backtest Sharpe vs paper Sharpe gap — calibrates your backtest-to-live model
- Patterns in killed signals — bake into future Phase 1 filters

Quality bar:
- This is research, NOT financial advice
- If backtest looks too good (Sharpe >2.0 on equities), assume broken and audit harder
- NEVER look at the test set during parameter tuning
- Position sizing must be reproducible and bounded — no "use your judgment" rules
- If realistic frictions kill the edge, kill the idea — do not weaken the frictions

- A short kickoff call invite (15 min) — the cheap conversion path

- Proposal as a markdown block ready to paste
- A short cover note (<=60 words) for platforms that need it
- A 2-step follow-up plan (+3 days, +7 days)
- A red-flag list to share with me before I hit Send

Feedback signal:
- Win rate by platform + job type — focus your time
- Win rate by package selection (basic / recommended / premium) — calibrate pricing tiers
- Patterns in losses — was it pricing, fit, slow response, or no portfolio match?

Quality bar:
- NEVER inflate experience or claim work you didn't do
- NEVER use the same boilerplate across postings — each proposal is 1:1
- Respect platform ToS (no off-platform contact ask before win on platforms that forbid it)
- If the budget is clearly too low for quality work, say so — propose a smaller scope at your rate

playbooks.name: Produce a children's picture book end-to-end
playbooks.description: Produce a children's picture book end-to-end. Get a story, page-by-page art briefs, and storefront copy.
playbooks.prompt:
Produce a children's picture book end-to-end.

Inputs:
- Age range: [3-5 / 6-8]
- Theme or moral: [e.g. sharing, resilience, bedtime, identity]
- Tone: [calm-bedtime / silly-energetic / quietly-magical]
- Length: [8 / 12 / 16 / 24 pages]
- Visual style: [watercolor / flat-vector / paper-cut / pencil-sketch / 3D]
- Storefront: [Amazon KDP / Etsy / 小红书 PDF / Gumroad / Shopify]
- Language: [English / 中文 / bilingual]
- Cultural specificity wanted: [paste]

Phase 1 — Story arc.
- Protagonist (name, age, defining trait — must be relatable to the age range)
- Setting (concrete, sensory)
- Inciting moment (small but real to a child)
- 3-act structure: setup → challenge → resolution
- Page-by-page beat list (text per page + emotional arc)
- A repeated phrase / rhythm a child can predict (huge for re-readability)

Show me the arc. Wait for me to approve before writing prose.

Phase 2 — Write the text.
- Age-appropriate vocabulary (no condescending baby talk; age 6-8 can handle real words)
- Read-aloud rhythm — every page should pass the "say it out loud" test
- Max word count per page (younger ages: 30-50 words; older: 60-100)
- Show emotion through action, not labels ("Maya stomped" not "Maya was angry")

Phase 3 — Page-by-page art briefs.
For each page:
- Scene description (composition, characters' poses, expressions)
- Color palette (specific to the page's mood)
- Camera distance (wide / mid / close-up — vary across pages)
- Recurring visual element (a pet, a comfort object, a background gag — kids love spotting these)
- Reference style (artists / books / films the artist would recognize)

Phase 4 — Cover + storefront.
- Cover art brief (the hook image)
- Title pattern (3-7 words, alliterative or rhyming if possible)
- Back-cover blurb (50-80 words — to parents, mentioning the gift / moral / age)
- Storefront listing: title, tags, description (parents read these, not kids)

Phase 5 — Output.
- Story manuscript (markdown)
- Art-direction PDF (page-by-page briefs)
- Cover brief + back-cover blurb
- Storefront listing ready to paste
- A 30-day promotion plan (3 social hooks for launch)

Feedback signal (after launch):
- Reviews mentioning re-readability — that means the rhythm worked
- Comments from parents on the moral landing — bias next book toward the same effect
- Sales by storefront — focus next launch's effort there

Quality bar:
- NEVER include scary content beyond the age range's tolerance
- NEVER moralize at the reader — show the moral through the story
- Verify cultural references (food, names, customs) with someone from that culture if it's not yours
- Respect children's actual cognitive level — they're smarter than condescending books assume

playbooks.name: Build a seed / Series A pitch deck
playbooks.description: Build a fundable pitch deck. Get a Sequoia-style structure, a sharp 'why now', and a slide-by-slide pressure test.
playbooks.prompt:
Build a fundable seed / Series A pitch deck.

Inputs:
- Stage: [seed / Series A / Series B]
- Company one-liner: [paste]
- Traction snapshot (revenue, growth rate, key metric): [paste]
- Target VC list (5-10 funds): [paste]
- Existing deck or memo (if any): [paste]
- "Why now" answer: [a SPECIFIC 2024-26 technology or market enabler, NOT a macro trend]

Phase 1 — Lock the narrative. Wait for my approval before slides.
- One-sentence "what we do" (passes the "explain to your mom" test)
- One-sentence "why now" tied to a specific enabler
- The single most defensible traction claim (number + delta + duration)
- The 3-bullet ask (round size, use of funds, milestone you'll hit)

Phase 2 — Draft slides (Sequoia structure adapted to my stage).
1. Title (company + one-liner + your name)
2. Problem (one image, one number)
3. Solution (one screenshot + the angle that makes it inevitable)
4. Why now (specific enabler from Phase 1)
5. Market (TAM/SAM/SOM with sourced numbers — not "$1T market")
6. Competition (positioning grid with axes that segment the market)
7. Product (3 screenshots: onboarding, magic moment, retention)
8. Traction (ARR chart, cohort if compelling)
9. Business model (price × volume math at scale)
10. Team (LinkedIn + relevant "why us" credential per founder)
11. Financials (Series A+: revenue + burn + runway + plan)
12. The ask (round size + lead/follow + use of funds + 18-month plan)

Phase 3 — Pressure-test.
For each slide, answer in one line: what question does this slide raise? What's the counter on the next slide? Fix any slide that raises an unanswered question.

Phase 4 — Output.
- .pdf for sending
- .pptx / .key editable
- Shareable Notion / Google Drive link
- A 1-page memo version for first-touch outreach

Feedback signal:
- After each meeting: which slide did they linger on? Which raised an unanswered question?
- Q&A volume per slide — surface the slides that consistently raise the same question
- Which slides got cut by the partner you trusted most — that's the truth

Quality bar:
- NEVER round up TAM by an order of magnitude — sourceable or off the slide
- NEVER include a logo wall unless logos are paying customers
- Team slide is not a resume — it's "why YOU are the team that wins"
- One idea per slide; if you need 2 bullets to explain, the slide is wrong

playbooks.name: Run the investor outreach process
playbooks.description: Run a tranched VC outreach process. Get a 50-fund target list, warm-intro mapping, and templated outreach + tracker.
playbooks.prompt:
Run a tranched investor outreach process for my round.

Inputs:
- Stage of round: [seed / Series A]
- Round size + expected check size per investor: [paste]
- Existing investor list (if any): [paste or CRM link]
- Industry / thesis fit (for filtering): [paste]
- Timeline (when do I want to close?): [paste]
- Existing intros I have: [paste]

Phase 1 — Build the 50-60 fund target list.
- Filter by stage they lead, sector thesis, check size, recent investment activity (last 90 days)
- For each fund: lead partner name, sector focus, most relevant 3 portfolio companies, last public talk / blog / podcast
- Mark cold vs warm (warm = mutual connection, common angel, public engagement)
- Drop funds whose thesis clearly excludes you

Phase 2 — Build the warm-intro map.
- For each warm fund: 2-3 intro paths, scored "would they vouch with conviction?" (1-3)
- For cold funds I really want: identify a "wedge" — a partner whose latest investment is most similar
- Output: CSV ranked by P(meeting) × fit

Phase 3 — Tranche the outreach.
- Tranche 1 (5-10 funds): friendliest warm intros — they meet first, give feedback, sharpen the pitch
- Tranche 2 (20-25 funds): main push — fire 7-10 days after Tranche 1 feedback
- Tranche 3 (rest): cold + lower-priority — fire only if Tranches 1-2 haven't closed
NEVER blast all 50 at once. The market talks. Sharpen between tranches.

Phase 4 — Templates.
- Warm-intro request to the connector (60 words, makes their forward easy)
- Cold outreach (80 words, references a specific portfolio investment + your "why now")
- Forward-ready deck link + memo
- The "no thanks" reply (gracious, leaves the door open)

Phase 5 — Tracking.
- CSV: fund | partner | tranche | intro path | last touch | response | next step | meeting date | outcome
- Updated daily during a live round

Feedback signal:
- Conversion rate per tranche — Tranche 1 conversion calibrates Tranche 2 narrative
- Drop-off reasons ("too early", "no thesis fit", "come back at $X ARR") — refine the list
- Time-to-meeting after intro — slow paths indicate weak relationship

Quality bar:
- NEVER outreach a fund whose thesis you can't articulate in one sentence
- NEVER skip the "thank you for the intro" reply to the connector
- Personalize Tranches 1 + 2; templatize only Tranche 3
- If you're getting "too early" 3+ times in a row, stop — the round may not be ready

playbooks.name: Model SAFE vs priced round dilution
playbooks.description: Model SAFE conversion + priced round dilution. Get a cap table, scenarios, and a minimum-acceptable-terms sheet.
steps: Convert SAFEs at the next round
Apply the new round + ESOP top-up
Run base / bigger / smaller / down-round scenarios
playbooks.prompt:
Model SAFE vs priced round dilution. Get a cap table I can change inputs in.

Inputs:
- Current cap table (post-money simple — founders + ESOP + prior investors): [paste]
- Stack of existing SAFEs (cap, discount, MFN clauses): [list each one separately]
- Proposed next round size + valuation: [paste]
- Target ESOP top-up at the round: [paste %]
- Investors leading vs following + check sizes: [paste]

Phase 1 — Model the current stack.
- Compute current ownership for: founders, ESOP available, employees holding, each angel / SAFE holder
- Surface the most-dilutive SAFEs (lowest cap, biggest check)
- Flag any unusual provisions (full ratchet, MFN, side letter)

Phase 2 — Convert SAFEs at next round.
For each SAFE:
- Applied valuation (cap vs discount vs price, whichever is lowest for the SAFE holder)
- Shares issued
- Net ownership after conversion

Phase 3 — Apply the new round.
- Pre-money calculation INCLUDING converted SAFEs
- Top up ESOP per target — MODEL BOTH pre-money and post-money ESOP top-ups (the difference is a real negotiation lever)
- New share issuance for new investors
- Final post-money ownership table

Phase 4 — Scenarios (side-by-side columns).
- Base case
- 25% bigger round
- 25% smaller round
- Down round (10% lower than the last cap)
- Bridge SAFE before round (extra $1M)
For each: founder ownership after, ESOP available, dilution per founder

Phase 5 — Output.
- Cap table .xlsx WITH FORMULAS (so I can change inputs)
- 1-page scenario comparison PDF
- A "minimum acceptable terms" sheet I can take into term sheet negotiation
- A list of red flags in the stack (full ratchets, MFN clauses, pro-rata stacking)

Feedback signal:
- After the round closes: which assumption was wrong? (commonly: ESOP top-up timing)
- Track post-round dilution against the model — surface drift for the next round
- If certain SAFEs surprised you on conversion, document for future SAFEs

Quality bar:
- NEVER skip MFN / ratchet provisions when modeling — they silently change the math
- NEVER assume "standard" SAFE terms without reading each one
- This is modeling, NOT legal advice — your lawyer signs off on actual terms
- Pre-money vs post-money ESOP top-up is a real negotiation lever — show both

playbooks.name: Set up a fundraise data room
playbooks.description: Set up a fundraise data room with the right gating. Get a folder structure, missing-artifact list, and a diligence Q&A pre-answered.
playbooks.prompt:
Set up a fundraise data room for a live round.

Inputs:
- Stage of round: [seed / Series A / Series B]
- Existing data room (if any): [link]
- Sensitive items I want gated: [list]
- Investors who'll get access + tier (lead vs follow): [paste]

Phase 1 — Build the structure (standard 8 folders).
1. Corporate (incorporation, cap table, board minutes, prior SAFEs / notes)
2. Financial (P&L, balance sheet, cash flow, MRR/ARR walk, customer concentration)
3. Product (product spec, roadmap, screenshots, security architecture)
4. Customer (customer list, NRR/GRR, contract values, top-10 logos)
5. Team (org chart, key hires, founder bios, equity grants)
6. Legal (MSA template, DPA template, redlined customer contracts, IP assignment)
7. Pipeline (sales pipeline, marketing funnel, growth experiments)
8. Strategic (positioning, competitive analysis, roadmap, "why now")

Phase 2 — Generate the missing artifacts per folder.
- Cap table: clean version (no informal notes)
- Customer list: logos + start dates (anonymize the smallest if needed)
- Pipeline: 90-day forward snapshot
- Key hires planned: role + comp + timeline

Phase 3 — Gate appropriately.
- Lead tier: full access (watermarked + NDA)
- Follow tier: numbers + summary, not the raw customer list
- Pre-NDA: just the public stuff (deck + one-line metrics)

Phase 4 — QA pass.
- Find every assertion in the pitch deck. Is it sourced in the data room?
- Find every number in the deck. Is the supporting query / file in the data room?
- Any inconsistency between deck and data room → fix immediately

Phase 5 — Output.
- Folder structure deployed (Notion / Google Drive / Docsend with watermarking)
- A "what's where" index PDF investors get at intro
- An audit log of who accessed what (for follow-up calibration)
- A diligence Q&A doc — the 30 questions investors always ask, pre-answered

Feedback signal:
- Which questions investors ask repeatedly that aren't in the diligence Q&A — add them
- Which docs investors actually open (Docsend tells you) — promote those
- Which gaps stalled diligence — backfill before the next round

Quality bar:
- NEVER include customer contracts with active redlines
- NEVER share unredacted customer info with follow-only investors
- Watermark every PDF with the recipient's email — leaks happen
- Keep a SINGLE source of truth; never have two versions of the cap table

playbooks.name: Build the quarterly board deck
playbooks.description: Build a quarterly board deck with KPIs + benchmarks + asks. Get numbers + narrative + pre-board 1:1 prep.
steps: Pull KPIs vs plan + last Q + benchmark
playbooks.prompt:
Build this quarter's board deck.

Inputs:
- Board members + their information preferences: [paste]
- Last quarter's deck (so we can diff): [link]
- This quarter's KPIs (ARR / NRR / burn / runway / pipeline / hiring): [paste]
- Bessemer / OpenView benchmark quartile I'm tracking against: [paste]
- Strategic asks for this meeting: [paste]
- Time slot: [60 / 90 / 120 min]

Phase 1 — Numbers section (7-10 slides).
- Headline KPIs vs plan + last quarter (traffic-light colors sparingly)
- ARR growth + monthly walk
- NRR + GRR with cohort detail
- Burn multiple (net new ARR / cash burned) — flag if >1.5x
- CAC payback period
- Cash position + runway at current burn vs target burn
- Pipeline by stage with conversion rates
- Headcount + planned hires

Per KPI: this Q vs last Q vs plan, plus a benchmark line against Bessemer / OpenView quartile.

Phase 2 — Narrative section (3-5 slides).
- What's working (one win with a defensible number)
- What's not working (be specific — and what you're doing about it)
- The one strategic question for the board (NOT "any feedback?")
- Pre-decided proposals for board approval (option pool top-up, exec hire, large customer concession)

Phase 3 — Appendix.
- Detailed financials for deep-divers
- Customer logos + biggest deals shipped this Q
- Product roadmap detail
- Any specific board member's pet topic

Phase 4 — Pre-meeting prep.
- Send the deck 48h before
- 1:1 calls with each board member 24-48h ahead to surface friction
- Adjust any slide likely to draw a board-member grandstand

Phase 5 — Output.
- Deck (.pdf + editable)
- Pre-read summary (1 page — what we'll cover, what we need from you)
- Action-item template for the meeting
- Post-meeting recap template (action items go out <=24h)

Feedback signal:
- Which slides drove the most board discussion — promote those
- Action items completed by next board meeting
- Board member 1:1 feedback vs surprises in the room — minimize the gap

Quality bar:
- NEVER bury bad news in the appendix — surface it on the headline slide
- NEVER ask "any questions?" without specific questions ready
- A 90-min board meeting is 30 min content + 60 min discussion — don't fill all 90 with slides
- Investors hate surprises — surface drift WEEKS before the meeting, not in the deck

playbooks.name: Run the quarterly operating cadence
playbooks.description: Stand up a quarterly operating cadence (David Sacks-style). Get a calendar, ritual templates, and an end-of-quarter review.
playbooks.prompt:
Stand up the quarterly operating cadence for the company.

Inputs:
- Company size + functional teams: [paste]
- Current rituals (if any): [paste]
- Fiscal quarter dates: [paste]
- Last quarter's plan + actuals: [paste or link]

Phase 1 — Lay out the quarter's spine.
- Month 1: Plan finalization + kickoff
- Month 2: Mid-quarter check + course correction
- Month 3: Wrap + next quarter prep + board meeting

Phase 2 — Schedule the core rituals.
- Monday: exec team weekly + functional standups
- Bi-weekly: 1:1s between exec team
- Monthly: investor update (last business day)
- Monthly: all-hands
- Quarterly: board meeting (week 11)
- Quarterly: QBR with top customers (week 12)
- Quarterly: roadmap review (week 10 — gates next quarter's plan)
- Quarterly: hiring review (week 11)

Phase 3 — Define artifacts per ritual.
- Weekly exec: 1-page status dashboard
- Investor update: 5-section template (headline / KPIs / wins / misses / asks)
- All-hands: 30-min deck (CEO update + a guest team's deep dive)
- Board meeting: see board-deck playbook
- QBR: customer-facing 1-pager (usage + outcomes + asks)
- Roadmap review: trade-off matrix (ship / won't / defer)
- Hiring review: open reqs / candidates / decisions needed

Phase 4 — Tooling.
- Calendar invites for the full quarter (do it once, not weekly)
- Document templates linked in the calendar invite
- A status dashboard that auto-pulls from CRM / financial system / GitHub if possible

Phase 5 — Output.
- Quarterly cadence calendar (PDF for the team)
- A template library (8 templates) in one Notion folder
- A "Cadence v1" doc the whole team reads at the start of the quarter
- An end-of-quarter 3-question review: what worked, what didn't, what changes

Feedback signal (closes loop quarter over quarter):
- Rituals you skipped — those were either wrong or wrong frequency
- Attendance + participation patterns — engagement signals fit
- Decisions made in rituals vs side conversations — too many side conversations means rituals aren't load-bearing

Quality bar:
- NEVER schedule a recurring meeting without a written agenda template
- NEVER let a ritual run past its allotted time — that's a structure failure
- Kill any ritual that runs 3 quarters without producing a decision
- One person owns each ritual — they don't run it, but they're accountable for it happening

playbooks.name: Set company OKRs + V2MOM
playbooks.description: Set company OKRs + V2MOM. Get a 1-page V2MOM, cascading OKRs, and a confidence + dependency map.
playbooks.prompt:
Set the company OKRs + V2MOM for the cycle.

Inputs:
- Scope (quarter or year): [paste]
- Company vision (1 sentence): [paste]
- Last cycle's OKRs + outcomes: [paste]
- Functional team count + leads: [paste]
- The single biggest strategic bet for this cycle: [paste]

Phase 1 — Draft the V2MOM (Benioff style).
- Vision: where we're going (1 sentence)
- Values: 3-5 we'll trade off for
- Methods: 3-5 ways we'll get there
- Obstacles: what could prevent it
- Measurements: how we'll know we got there

Show me the V2MOM. Wait for confirmation before drafting OKRs.

Phase 2 — Draft 3-5 company OKRs.
Each:
- Objective (qualitative, ambitious, 1 sentence, no metric)
- 3-5 Key Results (quantitative, time-bound, measurable, ambitious — "50%" not "increase")
- Owner (single person on the exec team)
- The single experiment / project that drives each KR

Constraints:
- NEVER more than 5 company OKRs — that's how strategy dies
- Every team's OKRs roll up to a company OKR
- Sum of team OKRs across teams should NOT add to 100% — overlap means coordination

Phase 3 — Cascade to teams.
- Each team writes 2-3 OKRs rolling up to a company OKR
- Sales / Marketing / Eng / Product / CS / Ops / People
- Review the cascade as a group — kill anything that doesn't connect

Phase 4 — Confidence + dependency map.
- Each KR: confidence score (1-10) at start of cycle
- Dependencies between teams' KRs — surface them on a map
- The 3 KRs the company NEEDS to hit vs the 3 nice-to-have stretch

Phase 5 — Output.
- V2MOM as a 1-page doc (company-wide)
- OKR doc (Notion / sheet) with all teams rolling up
- A dashboard query / pull for tracking each KR
- A weekly OKR check (15 min in the exec meeting) and a mid-cycle reset moment

Feedback signal (closes loop cycle over cycle):
- KRs hit vs missed — patterns in misses (over-planned? wrong owners? dependency stuck?)
- KRs nobody looked at — those weren't load-bearing
- Confidence score at start vs actual outcome — calibrates planning realism

Quality bar:
- KRs that aren't measurable aren't KRs — rewrite or cut
- Don't pile KRs to fill the cycle — quality over quantity
- One owner per KR — "everyone" = no one
- Aspirational ≠ ambiguous — "double revenue" is clear; "drive innovation" is fluff

playbooks.name: Build an executive role scorecard with extreme referencing
playbooks.description: Hire an executive with rigor. Get a scorecard, structured interview loop, and a backchannel reference plan.
steps: Design the interview loop + working session
playbooks.prompt:
Run a rigorous executive hire end-to-end.

Inputs:
- Role I'm hiring (VP Sales / VP Engineering / Head of CS / etc.): [paste]
- Stage: [pre-revenue / $1-5M ARR / $5-20M / $20M+]
- Current team + culture notes: [paste]
- Salary band + equity range I'm willing to pay: [paste]
- Timeline to fill: [paste]

Phase 1 — Build the role scorecard.
- Mission (1 sentence): why this role exists this year
- Outcomes (3-5, time-bound, measurable): what they'll achieve in 12 months
- Competencies (5-8): what they need to do the job
- Cultural fit dimensions (3-5): how they need to operate at our stage
- Anti-patterns: what disqualifies (won't roll sleeves up, comes from too-big company, etc.)

Phase 2 — Source the longlist.
- Map the talent market: relevant talent communities + 5 closest comparable companies + 3 levels of network
- For each prospect: last 3 roles, public artifacts (talks, posts), outcome at each stop
- Score against scorecard — top 30-50 enter top of funnel

Phase 3 — Interview design.
- Loop: founder screen → working session → 4-person panel → ref calls → CEO close
- Each interviewer owns 2 scorecard dimensions — never overlap
- Working session: a real problem at the company, time-boxed, evaluated against scorecard

Phase 4 — Extreme referencing.
- 10-12 references per finalist, not just on their list
- Backchannel through: prior reports (most signal), prior peers, prior managers
- Question bank: "What would make you not rehire them?", "When did they fail and what did they do?", "What would their team say if anonymous?"
- The true bar: would I bet $5M of company runway on this person?

Phase 5 — Output.
- Role scorecard (1-page Notion doc)
- Longlist + score CSV
- Interview kit (loop, scorecard mapping, working-session prompt)
- Reference call doc per finalist
- Offer + onboarding plan (link to 30/60/90 playbook)

Feedback signal:
- At 6 months: did the hire hit scorecard outcomes?
- Patterns in misses (over-indexed on competency, under-indexed on culture, etc.)
- Reference signals that predicted vs missed — calibrate the question bank

Quality bar:
- NEVER hire on resume alone — scorecard or no hire
- NEVER skip backchannel references — they reveal what listed refs hide
- "Move fast" doesn't mean skip diligence — exec mishires cost 4-12 months
- A "B+ that culture-fits" beats an "A that doesn't" at startup stage

playbooks.name: Plan the hiring sequence by ARR
playbooks.description: Plan the exec + senior hiring sequence by ARR milestones. Get a hiring map tied to revenue plan with comp benchmarks.
steps: Map exec roles to ARR triggers
Output a hiring plan tied to revenue
playbooks.prompt:
Plan the exec + senior hiring sequence tied to my ARR trajectory.

Inputs:
- Current ARR + 12-month plan: [paste]
- Current team (with titles + tenure): [paste]
- Industry: [paste — comp benchmarks vary]
- Cash position + runway: [paste]
- Fundraising plan (timing + size): [paste]

Phase 1 — ARR trigger map (Jason Lemkin defaults).
- VP Marketing: ~$0.2M ARR
- VP Sales: $1-1.5M ARR
- VP Customer Success: $2M ARR
- VP Product: $3-4M ARR
- VP Engineering: $5-6M ARR
- CFO: $10M ARR
- COO: $20M ARR

For each, output: ARR trigger / role / when (month) / why now.

Phase 2 — Calibrate to my stage.
- For each role: is it under-hired vs over-hired given my growth rate?
- For roles I should hire NEXT: scorecard reqs (link to executive-role-scorecard)
- Roles I should DELAY: which of my current team can stretch?

Phase 3 — Comp benchmarks.
For each near-term hire:
- Salary band (Pave + Levels.fyi market data)
- Equity grant (% of company by stage)
- Acceleration clauses (single vs double trigger)
- Performance review cadence + refresh grants

Phase 4 — Cash + runway impact.
- Burn-rate impact per hire (fully loaded)
- Runway extension required to ship a hire
- Fundraise dependencies (do we need to close round X before hiring role Y?)

Phase 5 — Output.
- Hiring plan PDF (1-page Gantt of who/when/why/cost)
- Per-role scorecard stubs (link out to executive-role-scorecard for the deep dive)
- A "readiness checklist" per role: signals that say "now is the right time" + signals that say "wait"
- A comp benchmark sheet

Feedback signal:
- After each exec hire: did the ARR trigger justify the cost?
- Roles where my team stretched successfully — promote that pattern
- Hires that came too early — costly lesson, capture in the plan

Quality bar:
- NEVER hire an exec to "build the function" before you've done the function yourself
- NEVER over-hire on title in exchange for raw output ("VP" titles inflate fast at startups)
- This is planning, NOT a commitment — markets shift, plans shift
- Bias toward stretch + builder hires over executive-from-big-co at <$10M ARR

playbooks.name: Write a 30/60/90 onboarding plan for an exec hire
playbooks.description: Write a 30/60/90 plan for a new exec. Get learn / contribute / lead phases with specific deliverables.
steps: Output the plan as a shared doc
playbooks.prompt:
Write a 30/60/90 onboarding plan for a new exec hire.

Inputs:
- Role + hire's name: [paste]
- Their first day + first major board / customer meeting: [paste]
- 12-month outcomes from the scorecard: [paste]
- Current team + cultural notes: [paste]
- Stretch goals the hire said they want to drive: [paste]

Phase 1 — Mission + outcomes (1-page header).
- Mission: why this role exists (1 sentence)
- Top 3 12-month outcomes the hire owns
- Top 3 things the hire is NOT responsible for in year one (kill scope creep)
- Boundaries / handoffs with peers

Phase 2 — Days 0-30: LEARN.
- People to 1:1 (named): direct reports + peers + key cross-functional + 5 customers + 2 board members
- Reading: company history (founding story, strategic memos), roadmap, last 3 board decks, OKRs
- Access (technical): tools, dashboards, repos, customer data
- Tangible deliverable at day 30: a "what I learned" memo to the CEO + a "what I'd change in 90 days" note (the latter for context-setting, not committing)

Phase 3 — Days 31-60: CONTRIBUTE.
- One small, scoped project that delivers value in their function (not a strategic bet)
- First public artifact (board update, all-hands talk, customer call, hire decision)
- Cross-functional working relationships established (named: who do they have monthly 1:1s with?)
- Tangible deliverable at day 60: a written plan for days 61-180 (their plan, not yours)

Phase 4 — Days 61-90: LEAD.
- One real strategic decision they own (with CEO as escalation, not co-owner)
- Hiring or restructure proposals if needed
- Their function's input into the next OKR cycle
- Tangible deliverable at day 90: a self-assessment + a CEO assessment, side by side

Phase 5 — CEO check-in cadence.
- Weekly 1:1 for first 90 days
- Bi-weekly after
- Quarterly: explicit "is this working?" conversation with named criteria

Phase 6 — Output.
- The 30/60/90 plan as a 2-page Notion doc, shared with the hire + their manager
- A calendar template auto-populating the check-ins
- A "success metrics by day 90" checklist for the post-90 review

Feedback signal:
- Patterns in what gets done by day 30 vs day 60 vs day 90 — calibrates pace
- Which onboarding meetings produced signal vs which were performative
- Where the plan was too rigid / too vague — feeds the next plan

Quality bar:
- NEVER expect strategic bets in day 0-30 — that's setup for failure
- NEVER skip the bi-directional CEO assessment at day 90
- Be specific about boundaries — vague mission = scope creep
- If the hire is failing the plan, raise it at week 6, not week 12

playbooks.name: Redesign pricing around a value metric
playbooks.description: Redesign pricing around a value metric. Get tiers, packaging, a pricing page, and a price-test plan.
playbooks.prompt:
Redesign pricing around a value metric (Patrick Campbell / ProfitWell style).

Inputs:
- Product + current pricing model: [paste]
- Top 3 customer use cases / personas: [paste]
- Current ACV distribution + churn by tier: [paste]
- Closest 3 competitors' pricing: [paste]
- Constraints (existing contract terms, grandfathering policy): [paste]

Phase 1 — Pick the value metric.
- Map options: seats, API calls, GMV, projects, records, msgs, MAUs, storage
- Score each: does it scale WITH customer value? Is it predictable? Is it gameable?
- Recommend ONE primary value metric. Explain the trade-offs of the runners-up.

Show me the metric + reasoning. Wait for me to approve.

Phase 2 — Tier design (good / better / best).
- 3 tiers (not 5+ — choice paralysis)
- Anchor: top tier 3-4x the middle (anchors against "I'll never need that")
- Feature gating: middle tier gets 80% of features; top tier gets the team / governance / SLA layer
- Value-metric thresholds per tier
- "Most popular" badge on the middle tier (it works)
- An "Enterprise / Talk to us" CTA for the top tier (preserves negotiation room)

Phase 3 — Pricing page.
- Headline: outcome-based ("scale to X without Y")
- 3-column layout, annual default (with monthly toggle)
- Each plan: 1-sentence positioning + 3-5 bullets + the value metric line + CTA
- FAQ: 5 questions ("can I switch plans?", "do you offer a trial?", "what counts as a [value metric]?")
- Social proof: 3-5 logos + 1 testimonial

Phase 4 — Price-test plan.
- A/B: control = current, variant = new pricing
- Run 30 days minimum or N conversions, whichever later
- Track: signups, trial-to-paid, ACV, churn at 30/60/90
- Kill rules: if conversions drop >X%, revert

Phase 5 — Communicate to existing customers.
- Grandfathering policy (clear, time-bound)
- Email sequence (3 emails): change preview → final notice → "what to do" recap
- One-pager FAQ to give to support
- Renewal flow: existing customers either grandfather or migrate at renewal

Phase 6 — Output.
- New pricing page (markdown for the dev to build)
- Tier comparison PDF (for sales)
- Customer comms email sequence
- A/B test rig spec + kill rules

Feedback signal:
- Tier mix shift (are people picking the middle? top?)
- ACV delta vs control
- Churn at 30 / 60 / 90 — pricing changes show churn signal at month 2
- Sales push-back themes — surface objections to refine messaging

Quality bar:
- NEVER hide pricing — every "talk to sales" without a starting number scares devs
- NEVER ship pricing without a kill rule
- Communicate price changes to existing customers BEFORE prospects see them
- Don't fix pricing while also redesigning packaging — change one variable at a time

playbooks.name: Run a reverse-trial conversion experiment
playbooks.description: Test reverse trial vs opt-in trial. Get an experiment plan, upgrade nudge sequence, and a 30-day measurement.
steps: Identify the Pro-only feature that drives upgrade
playbooks.prompt:
Run a reverse-trial conversion test (Notion / Canva / Airtable pattern).

Inputs:
- Current trial / freemium setup: [paste]
- Current trial-to-paid conversion rate: [paste]
- Top 5 Pro-only features (with usage data if you have it): [paste]
- Activation event (the moment users get value): [paste]
- Sample size + traffic per day to the trial: [paste]

Phase 1 — Design the mechanic.
- Reverse trial: 14 days full Pro access from signup, NO card required, auto-downgrade to free at day 15
- Confirm activation event flows in days 1-7
- Define which Pro features are visible during the trial period
- Define the friction-free downgrade ("you're now on Free; here's what changes")

Phase 2 — Identify the upgrade hook.
- For each Pro-only feature: usage frequency during trial × feature stickiness × difficulty to replace
- Pick the SINGLE feature most likely to drive upgrade
- Plan the in-product nudge that appears exactly when the user hits that feature

Phase 3 — Build the upgrade nudge sequence.
- In-product: feature-specific modal on day 10 + day 14
- Email day 12: "your trial ends in 2 days; here's what you'll lose"
- Email day 15: "you're on Free; here's how to come back"
- Email day 22: "Pro-only feature you used X times — want it back?"

Phase 4 — A/B against current trial.
- Split: 50/50 over 30 days minimum
- Track: trial-to-paid conversion, ACV by cohort, churn at 30 / 60 / 90, NPS at trial end
- Kill rule: if conversion drops >20%, revert immediately

Phase 5 — Read out at 30 days.
- Headline metric: trial-to-paid conversion vs control
- Mix: are users converting because of the SINGLE feature you bet on, or something else?
- Churn signal: do reverse-trial converters churn faster (lower commitment)?
- Verdict: ship / kill / iterate

Phase 6 — Output.
- Experiment doc (hypothesis + arms + metrics + kill rules)
- The upgrade nudge sequence (in-product copy + email copy)
- A 30-day readout template
- A scaling plan if the test wins

Feedback signal (closes the loop):
- Per cohort: trial-to-paid + retention at 90 days
- Which Pro feature actually drove conversion vs which you bet on
- Time-to-conversion distribution — surface the bandit's sweet spot

Quality bar:
- NEVER ship "free Pro forever" by accident — confirm the auto-downgrade fires
- NEVER claim the test won at day 7 — wait for the full window
- Cohort the analysis by acquisition channel — some channels convert differently
- If the test loses, surface why before throwing it away — sometimes the hook was wrong, not the mechanic

playbooks.name: Run a willingness-to-pay study
playbooks.description: Run a willingness-to-pay study (van Westendorp + Gabor-Granger). Get a price recommendation segmented by persona.
playbooks.prompt:
Run a willingness-to-pay study to set defensible pricing.

Inputs:
- Product description + value prop: [paste]
- Closest 3 alternative tools customers compare against: [paste]
- Persona segments to test: [paste — e.g. solo creators / SMB teams / enterprise]
- Existing customer list (for current users) + prospect list (for non-users): [paste]
- Target sample size (200+ for stat-sig): [paste]

Phase 1 — Persona segmentation.
- Define 2-3 personas with distinct contexts (use case, team size, prior tool, budget authority)
- For each: estimate population size + how to recruit (email list, X/LinkedIn DMs, panel provider)

Phase 2 — Design the instrument.
Van Westendorp 4 questions:
1. At what price would the product be SO EXPENSIVE you would not consider buying it?
2. At what price would it be SO CHEAP you would question its quality?
3. At what price would it be expensive but still consider it?
4. At what price would it be a bargain?

Gabor-Granger (sequential):
- Present prices in random order; ask "would you buy at $X?" Yes/No
- Use to estimate demand curve

Plus:
- "What's the most important reason this would be worth $X?" (open text)
- Persona-qualifier questions (size, role, current solution, budget)

Phase 3 — Sample 200+ respondents.
- Run the survey via Typeform / SurveyMonkey
- Recruit via channels matched to personas (no LinkedIn for solo creators, no Reddit for enterprise)
- Incentive: $5-10 gift card or product credit
- QA: filter for speeders (<2 min completion), straight-liners

Phase 4 — Analyze.
- Van Westendorp: plot the 4 curves; identify Optimal Price Point (OPP), Indifference Price (IPP), Point of Marginal Cheapness (PMC), Point of Marginal Expensiveness (PME)
- Gabor-Granger: estimate price-elastic demand per persona
- Segment by persona — surface meaningful WTP differences
- Cross-tabulate by current solution (price-anchored against the alternative)

Phase 5 — Price recommendation.
- Recommended price points per persona
- Confidence interval (this is research, not law)
- Implications for packaging (where to draw tier lines)
- The single test you should run to confirm in-market

Phase 6 — Output.
- Survey results raw + cleaned (.csv)
- Van Westendorp + Gabor-Granger charts (PDF)
- A 3-page recommendation memo
- Discussion guide for the 5 qualitative follow-up calls

Feedback signal (closes loop for the next study):
- Discrepancy between WTP and actual conversion at the recommended price — calibrates response bias
- Which personas were under- vs over-sampled
- New segments that emerged in the open-text responses

Quality bar:
- NEVER set price ON the WTP point — use it as a SIGNAL, not gospel
- NEVER skip current-solution anchoring — context shifts WTP by 30%+
- Cite sample size + confidence range whenever you cite a WTP number
- Stated preference ≠ revealed preference — pair with an in-market A/B before locking

playbooks.name: Run an Obviously Awesome positioning workshop
playbooks.description: Run April Dunford's 10-step positioning workshop. Get a positioning statement that drives messaging, sales, and website.
playbooks.prompt:
Run the Obviously Awesome positioning workshop (April Dunford's 10 steps).

Inputs:
- Product + current positioning (if any): [paste]
- 3-5 best customers + why they bought: [paste]
- Top 5 customer interview quotes about what we replaced: [paste]
- Closest 3 competitors / alternatives: [paste]
- Founder gut feel on the category: [paste]

Phase 1 — Competitive alternatives.
- What would customers use if we didn't exist? (NOT just direct competitors — spreadsheets, agencies, doing-nothing all count)
- Cluster alternatives by type
- For each, note: why customers reject it, what they're optimizing for instead

Phase 2 — Unique attributes.
- What capabilities does our product have that customers care about?
- Filter: must be true AND differentiated AND defensible
- Drop anything customers don't actually mention in interviews
- Output: 5-10 attributes

Phase 3 — Map attributes to value.
- For each attribute: what's the customer benefit? (translate features to value)
- Cluster benefits into themes (typically 2-3 themes)
- Identify the SINGLE highest-leverage theme

Phase 4 — Best-fit customer.
- Describe the customer for whom our value is most valuable
- Persona attributes that predict fit (industry, team size, current tool, trigger event)
- Anti-persona: who is this NOT for (saying no sharpens the yes)

Phase 5 — Market category.
- Pick the market frame that makes your differentiation matter
- Three options: existing category, sub-category, new category — score each on credibility + market readiness
- Recommend ONE category with one paragraph of why

Phase 6 — Trends (the "why now").
- 2-3 macro / market / tech trends that make your positioning resonate now
- Tie each to your differentiation

Phase 7 — Positioning statement (1 paragraph).
- For [best-fit customer]
- Who has [trigger / problem]
- [Product] is a [market category]
- That unlike [alternative]
- Delivers [highest-leverage benefit theme]
- Because [unique attribute that makes it credible]

Phase 8 — Messaging cascade.
