- Homepage H1 (one sentence, based on the positioning)
- 3 supporting messages (one per feature theme)
- One-line pitch for sales
- One-line pitch for fundraising

Phase 9 — Output.
- A 2-page positioning doc (statement + workshop outputs)
- Homepage copy draft tied to the positioning
- Sales deck refresh outline
- A "what changes" memo (so the team knows what's different)

Feedback signal:
- Customer interviews 90 days post-launch — does the positioning land?
- Sales meeting outcomes — does the new pitch shorten sales cycles?
- Inbound lead quality — better-fit leads = the positioning works

Quality bar:
- NEVER position around features — position around value
- NEVER claim a category you can't credibly own
- The positioning statement is NOT the website headline — it's the input to the headline
- Re-run the workshop annually OR when the market shifts (new competitor, new buyer)

playbooks.name: Define the North Star Metric + input tree
playbooks.description: Define a North Star Metric + its input tree. Get a one-pager that drives OKRs and dashboards.
playbooks.prompt:
Define the company's North Star Metric (NSM) + its input tree.

Inputs:
- Business model (subscription / usage / marketplace / transactional): [paste]
- Current top-level metrics (ARR, GMV, sessions, etc.): [paste]
- Last 6 months of revenue + customer behavior data: [paste]
- Strategic 2-year goal: [paste]

Phase 1 — Pick the NSM candidate.
The NSM is a SINGLE customer-behavior metric that leads revenue. Examples:
- Spotify: time spent listening
- Airbnb: nights booked
- Slack: messages sent in connected teams
- Figma: weekly active editors

Score candidates against:
- Does it lead revenue? (a customer doing more of THIS predicts more revenue)
- Is it customer-behavior, not company output? (not "ARR" itself)
- Is it measurable WEEKLY, not quarterly?
- Will it survive a strategic pivot?

Recommend ONE candidate with reasoning. Wait for me to confirm.

Phase 2 — Validate it leads revenue.
- For the last 12 months: plot the NSM trend vs revenue
- If they correlate, what's the lag? (NSM should lead revenue by 1-3 months)
- Cohort: do customers with high NSM values retain better?
- If correlation is weak, reconsider the NSM choice

Phase 3 — Decompose into 3-5 input metrics.
The classic decomposition: Breadth (how many) × Depth (how much per) × Frequency (how often) × Efficiency (per unit cost)
Output: a tree with the NSM at the root, 3-5 inputs in the next layer, sub-inputs below.

Phase 4 — Map inputs to team ownership.
- Each input metric has one owner (a team or function)
- Each team's OKRs should ladder into their NSM input
- Surface dependencies (where two teams share an input)

Phase 5 — Build the dashboard.
- Single screen showing: NSM weekly + 4-week MA + last quarter
- Inputs: same view per metric
- Cohort filters: by acquisition channel, by tier, by tenure

Phase 6 — Output.
- 1-page NSM doc (Lenny / Amplitude style)
- The input tree diagram
- A team-ownership map
- Dashboard spec (for the data team to build)
- A "review the NSM annually" reminder + criteria for changing it

Feedback signal:
- Per quarter: did movement in NSM predict revenue? (validates the choice)
- Inputs that decoupled from the NSM — surface and re-decompose
- Inputs nobody worked on — surface ownership gaps

Quality bar:
- The NSM is ONE metric — not "the top 5 KPIs"
- NEVER pick a metric you can't measure weekly
- NEVER pick a vanity metric (signups, downloads) — pick a value-creating behavior
- The NSM should survive the next pivot — if not, you have a feature metric, not a strategy metric

playbooks.name: Launch a Customer Advisory Board
playbooks.description: Launch and run a Customer Advisory Board. Get a charter, member selection, agenda template, and a roadmap-input loop.
playbooks.prompt:
Launch and run a Customer Advisory Board (CAB) for strategic input.

Inputs:
- Stage + ARR: [paste]
- Top 30 customers (with ACV, tenure, industry): [paste]
- Strategic questions I want CAB input on this year: [paste]
- Time commitment I can sustain (2-3 meetings/year is realistic): [paste]

Phase 1 — Write the CAB charter.
- Purpose (NOT "feedback" — be specific: roadmap input, strategic direction, market signal)
- Term length (12-24 months)
- Member commitments (attend N meetings, complete pre-reads, share NPS-like input)
- What CAB members get (early access, exec relationships, peer network, brand benefit)
- What the company does NOT promise (feature commitments, exclusive deals)

Phase 2 — Pick 8-12 members.
Mix:
- 4-5 enterprise (high ACV, governance buyers)
- 3-4 mid-market (operational buyers)
- 1-2 power users (champions, not buyers — heard differently)
- Diverse industries (so no one industry dominates the input)

Per member: name, title, company, ACV, tenure, what they bring (operator vs strategist vs technical voice)

Phase 3 — Meeting cadence + agenda.
- 2 in-person meetings/year (1 at your office or HQ, 1 at industry event) + 2 virtual quarterlies
- Agenda per meeting:
  - State of the company (CEO, 15 min)
  - Strategic question 1 + open discussion (60 min)
  - Strategic question 2 + open discussion (60 min)
  - Open round (each member: top-of-mind, 5 min each)
  - Next steps + commitments
- Pre-read sent 7 days ahead

Phase 4 — Capture inputs into the roadmap.
- Real-time scribe during the meeting (not the CEO)
- 48h post-meeting: a "what we heard, what we're committing to" memo back to members
- 30-day check-in: status on the commitments made
- Surface CAB inputs in the next quarter's roadmap review with explicit attribution

Phase 5 — Run a 90-day follow-through.
- Per commitment: owner + deadline + outcome
- 90-day public update to CAB on what shipped (and what didn't and why)
- Annual NPS-style survey of CAB members themselves ("is this CAB worth your time?")

Phase 6 — Output.
- CAB charter PDF (sent to invitees before they say yes)
- Member roster + roles
- Meeting agendas (4 per year, pre-built)
- A roadmap-input log linking CAB sessions to shipped features
- A "thank you" gift cadence (small, thoughtful, recurring)

Feedback signal:
- CAB-attributed roadmap items: did they outperform other roadmap items?
- Member attendance + engagement — surface decay
- The 1 strategic question per meeting that produced the BEST debate — calibrate future agendas

Quality bar:
- NEVER use the CAB as a sales channel — that breaks trust fast
- NEVER over-promise on inputs — be honest about what you can/can't ship
- Skipping the follow-through memo is the single biggest reason CABs die
- The CEO attends every meeting — delegating signals it's not strategic

playbooks.name: Run a case-study + reference customer pipeline
playbooks.description: Run a case-study + reference customer pipeline. Get a tiered advocacy program from logo to CAB.
playbooks.prompt:
Run a case-study + reference customer pipeline as a tiered advocacy program.

Inputs:
- Current proof assets (logos, quotes, case studies): [paste or link]
- Customer list with NRR, ACV, tenure, NPS, usage: [paste]
- Sales team's most-requested case study types: [paste]
- Brand voice + production capacity (in-house vs agency): [paste]

Phase 1 — Audit current proof.
- What proof do we have? (logos / quotes / 1-page case / long-form / video / quantified ROI)
- What's MISSING for the top 3 buyer personas?
- Which assets are stale (>12 months old) and need a refresh?
- Which logos have permission to use vs which we use without permission (risky)?

Phase 2 — Build the advocacy ladder.
Tier 1: logo permission (low ask, big value)
Tier 2: pull-quote with name + title
Tier 3: 1-page case study with metric
Tier 4: long-form case study + customer interview
Tier 5: live reference call (1:1, scheduled by sales)
Tier 6: CAB member / on-stage speaker / co-marketing

Each tier graduates from the previous. Don't ask for tier 4 from a customer who hasn't done tier 1-3 first.

Phase 3 — Identify candidates per tier.
Score every customer:
- Outcome strength: do they have a defensible metric? (NPS, ROI, time saved, growth)
- Vocal quality: do they speak well about us in any forum? (review sites, Slack, LinkedIn)
- Buyer match: do they map to a top-3 buyer persona we need proof for?
- Legal risk: are they in a regulated industry (banks, healthcare) that limits public refs?

Output: a ranked list per tier with the next ask per customer.

Phase 4 — Production line.
For tier 3-4 case studies:
- 60-min interview with the buyer (recorded, transcribed)
- 60-min follow-up with the user (recorded, transcribed)
- Draft within 7 days; customer review within 14 days; publish within 30 days
- Promote across: website, sales deck, sales emails, social, conference

Phase 5 — Track reference health.
- Per reference: last touched, current state (active / dormant / churning), open asks
- Refresh every 12 months OR after major customer outcome change
- Watch for churn signals — pull references BEFORE they leave

Phase 6 — Output.
- Advocacy ladder spreadsheet (per customer: current tier + next ask)
- Case study production template (interview guide, draft outline, approval flow)
- Reference health dashboard
- A "thank you" cadence (concrete: swag, exec lunch, in-person at the conference)

Feedback signal:
- Conversion rate per tier ask — calibrate the request copy
- Sales cycle impact: deals with case studies vs without
- Customer churn rate among active references vs general — surface the "ref → churn" signal

Quality bar:
- NEVER use a customer logo without explicit written permission
- NEVER ship a case study without customer sign-off on every number and quote
- Tier 5 (live reference) is rare — protect references from over-asking
- If a customer says no, ask why — sometimes the answer reveals a churn signal

playbooks.name: Run founder-led sales to repeatable revenue
playbooks.description: Run founder-led sales toward repeatable revenue. Get an ICP doc, discovery script, demo flow, and the first AE-ready playbook.
steps: Run the first 50 sales calls personally
Write the ICP + discovery + demo flow
Codify the sales playbook for the first AE
playbooks.prompt:
Run founder-led sales toward a repeatable motion ($0-$5M ARR, Meka Asonye / First Round pattern).

Inputs:
- Product + current ACV range: [paste]
- Closed-won deals to date (with story per deal: who, why, how long): [paste]
- Closed-lost deals (with reason): [paste]
- My current weekly outbound + inbound volume: [paste]
- My current top-of-funnel: [paste]

Phase 1 — Diagnose existing wins.
- For each closed-won: what was the trigger (Why did they buy? Why now?), what did they replace, who championed it inside, who held the budget, what was the sales cycle, what was the discount
- Cluster the patterns
- Surface the "looks-like" ICP from the wins (not your imagined ICP)

Phase 2 — Diagnose existing losses.
- For each closed-lost: why did they say no? (Price? Fit? Timing? Competitor? Internal politics?)
- Cluster by reason
- The reason that recurs most = the next sales-cycle blocker to address

Phase 3 — Write the ICP doc.
- Industry, company size, role of buyer, role of user, current solution
- Trigger events (hiring spike, funding round, public price change at incumbent)
- Disqualifiers (do not pursue if they have X)
- Score model: 0-5 fit per dimension

Phase 4 — Write the discovery script.
- 30-min discovery call structure
- Opening (90 sec — set context)
- Pain qualification (10 min — using a MEDDIC / SPICED frame)
- Solution narrative (5 min — NOT a feature dump)
- Next-step proposal (3 min — concrete, time-bound)
- Q&A (10 min — but front-load value before they ask)

Phase 5 — Demo flow.
- Pre-demo: confirm what they want to see (NOT a "tour")
- Open with the magic moment + the customer outcome (15 sec)
- Walk through 3-4 specific user stories tied to the pain they raised in discovery
- Save Q&A for the end
- Always end with the next step explicitly named

Phase 6 — Output (playbook for the first AE).
- ICP doc (1-page)
- Discovery script (printable)
- Demo flow with screenshots
- Objection-handling card (top 10 objections from the loss data + responses)
- Proposal + SOW template
- Sales cycle map (stage gates with required artifacts)
- Quota model (realistic, calibrated against your conversion data)

Feedback signal (closes the loop):
- AE win rate vs founder win rate — track the gap (it's normal, not a failure)
- Stage where deals stall — promote interventions
- Objections that appear with new ICP segments — refine the doc

Quality bar:
- NEVER hire an AE before you can answer "what's the script that won 10 deals in a row?"
- NEVER hand off without sitting in on the first 10 calls together
- The discovery script is a guide, not a script — train the AE to listen first
- If the AE pushes back on the playbook, that's signal — they're seeing what you missed

playbooks.name: Define PQLs and the sales handoff
playbooks.description: Define product-qualified leads and the sales handoff. Get a multi-step PQL definition + dashboard + outreach trigger.
playbooks.prompt:
Define product-qualified leads (PQLs) and the sales handoff (Slack / Atlassian model).

Inputs:
- Current product usage signals you can measure: [paste]
- Closed-won deals' usage profiles BEFORE buying: [paste]
- Sales team's current handoff (MQL definitions, lead routing): [paste]
- Target ACV for sales-touched deals: [paste]

Phase 1 — Map signals.
- List every measurable usage signal (events, frequency, breadth)
- For each: how strongly does it correlate with paid conversion in your data?
- Drop signals with weak correlation
- Keep 3-6 strong signals

Phase 2 — Define the PQL threshold (multi-step).
Example Slack model: 2+ channels created AND 1+ teammate invited AND first conversation completed AND 2,000+ messages sent.
For your product:
- Combine 3-5 signals into a SINGLE definition (all must be true)
- Validate against closed-won data: what % of converted accounts hit this? what % of free accounts that hit this convert?
- Iterate the threshold until both numbers look strong

Phase 3 — Design the handoff.
- Trigger: account crosses the PQL threshold
- Action: Slack alert to assigned AE + auto-create CRM opportunity at "PQL" stage
- AE response: contact within 24h with a specific message ("noticed your team scaled from X to Y last week — want to talk through how others handled the next step?")
- NEVER send a generic "ready to upgrade?" — the PQL is contextual, the outreach must be too

Phase 4 — Build the dashboard.
- PQL count per week
- PQL → opportunity conversion
- Opportunity → close conversion
- Time from PQL to close (vs MQL-sourced)
- ACV by source (PQL vs MQL)

Phase 5 — Read out at 90 days.
- PQL conversion vs MQL: it should be 3-5x
- Sales feedback: are PQLs better conversations than MQLs?
- The threshold may need to tighten OR loosen — calibrate

Phase 6 — Output.
- PQL definition document (the rule + the validating data)
- Handoff workflow (Slack alert + CRM auto-create + AE response template)
- Dashboard spec (for the data team)
- A "what counts as a PQL" 1-pager for the sales team

Feedback signal (closes the loop):
- PQL-to-close conversion rate quarter over quarter — sharpen the threshold
- Which signal in the definition is doing the most work — focus instrumentation
- New product behaviors that correlate strongly with conversion — promote to PQL

Quality bar:
- NEVER let "PQL" mean "free user who clicked pricing" — that's not a PQL
- NEVER skip the validation against closed-won data — PQLs without validation are MQLs renamed
- The PQL definition will change every 2-3 quarters as the product evolves — review it
- If sales says "PQLs are bad leads", listen — the threshold is wrong, not the strategy

playbooks.name: Run the Superhuman PMF engine
playbooks.description: Run Superhuman's PMF engine. Get a 4-question survey, the very-disappointed cohort analysis, and a roadmap split.
playbooks.prompt:
Run Rahul Vohra's Superhuman PMF engine (he lifted Superhuman from 22% to 58% in under a year).

Inputs:
- Active users (used the product 2+ times in last 14 days): [paste count + sample]
- Existing PMF measurement (if any): [paste]
- Current top complaints + delighters surfaced via support: [paste]
- Current roadmap: [paste]

Phase 1 — Identify the active-user cohort.
- Filter to users who used the product 2+ times in last 14 days (Vohra's threshold)
- Drop users <14 days tenure (they don't know yet)
- Verify the cohort represents your target customer (not just everyone)

Phase 2 — Send the 4-question survey.
1. How would you feel if you could no longer use [product]?
   - Very disappointed / Somewhat disappointed / Not disappointed / N/A I no longer use [product]
2. What type of people do you think would most benefit from [product]? (1 sentence)
3. What's the main benefit you get from [product]? (1 sentence)
4. How can we improve [product] for you? (open text)

Distribution: in-product modal + email to non-modal-shown users. Target 100+ responses.

Phase 3 — Calculate PMF + analyze.
- PMF score = % "very disappointed" / (very + somewhat + not disappointed)
- Score >40% = strong PMF; 20-40% = developing; <20% = weak
- Segment the "very disappointed" cohort: who are they? What benefit do they cite?
- Read the "somewhat disappointed" open text: what's the SINGLE biggest blocker?

Phase 4 — Split the roadmap 50/50.
- 50% of next-quarter roadmap: double down on what the "very disappointed" cohort loves
- 50%: remove the top blocker cited by "somewhat disappointed"
- The remaining 0%: anything else (yes, this is uncomfortable)

Phase 5 — Re-survey monthly.
- Same 4 questions, same cohort definition
- Track PMF score trend: are you climbing toward 40%?
- Track the "very disappointed" cohort growth: is it expanding to new personas?
- If PMF stalls for 2 months, the diagnosis is wrong — re-read the open text

Phase 6 — Output.
- Survey instrument (ready to deploy)
- Cohort analysis dashboard
- Monthly PMF score with trend chart
- A roadmap doc that explicitly maps every feature to "double down" or "unblock"
- The "very disappointed" persona doc (used for marketing + sales targeting)

Feedback signal (closes the loop):
- Month-over-month PMF score trend — the engine working = climbing
- "Very disappointed" cohort growth — new personas joining = expansion territory
- "Somewhat disappointed" blockers that recur — that's the systemic friction

Quality bar:
- NEVER conflate PMF score with NPS — they measure different things
- NEVER survey users who haven't tried the product enough to have an opinion
- The "very disappointed" cohort IS your ICP — use their language in marketing
- If you ignore the open text, you've wasted the survey

playbooks.name: Audit activation in 3 moments (setup, aha, habit)
playbooks.description: Audit activation as setup / aha / habit (Reforge framework). Get a step-by-step diagnosis with the largest-drop fix.
steps: Define each of the 3 moments concretely
playbooks.prompt:
Audit activation as 3 moments (Setup → Aha → Habit) — the Reforge framework that lifted Attention Insight from 47% → 69% activation.

Inputs:
- Current activation rate (define your existing metric): [paste]
- Onboarding flow screenshots or recording: [paste or path]
- Product analytics access (Mixpanel / Amplitude / PostHog / etc.): [paste how to access]
- Top 5 customer interview quotes about onboarding: [paste]

Phase 1 — Define each moment concretely.

Setup moment: the user completes the minimum configuration needed for the product to function
- For Slack: workspace created + 1 channel + 1 teammate
- For Notion: workspace created + 1 page
- For your product: ?

Aha moment: the user experiences the SINGLE highest-leverage outcome the product delivers
- For Loom: first share + recipient watches
- For Calendly: first meeting booked through the link
- For your product: ?

Habit moment: the user performs the aha moment at the frequency that predicts retention
- For Slack: 2,000+ messages in connected teams
- For Notion: 3+ pages created per week over 3 weeks
- For your product: ?

Pick the 3 moments. Wait for me to confirm.

Phase 2 — Measure drop-off at each.
- % of signups completing Setup
- % of Setup-completers hitting Aha
- % of Aha-hitters reaching Habit
- Each step is its own funnel

Phase 3 — Diagnose the largest-drop moment.
- For the worst step: where exactly do users drop?
- Pair with customer interview quotes for context
- Identify the SINGLE friction (a missing instruction, a confusing UI, a permission gate, a slow API call)
- Validate: would removing this friction lift the step's conversion by 10+ pp?

Phase 4 — Ship the fix.
- Smallest possible change that addresses the friction
- A/B against the current flow (50/50, 30 days)
- Kill rule: if it doesn't move the step's conversion by 5 pp+, revert

Phase 5 — Re-measure and loop.
- After 30 days: read out and decide ship/iterate/kill
- Move to the next-largest drop and repeat
- Weekly: 15-min activation review with the team

Phase 6 — Output.
- The 3-moments definition doc
- Funnel dashboard (one screen, all 3 moments visible)
- Top 3 hypotheses + experiments queued
- A weekly review template

Feedback signal (closes the loop):
- Per moment: conversion delta after each fix
- Which fixes moved the metric vs which didn't — surface the patterns
- New friction that emerges after fixing one (sometimes the bottleneck just moves)

Quality bar:
- NEVER count signups as activation — that's an acquisition metric
- NEVER define the Aha moment without customer interviews — your guess is usually wrong
- Habit metric must be defined at the FREQUENCY that retains — not just "uses the product"
- If activation lifts but retention doesn't, your Aha definition is wrong

playbooks.name: Run a Product Hunt launch playbook
playbooks.description: Run a Product Hunt launch end-to-end. Get a 4-week prep plan, day-of script, and supporter outreach templates.
playbooks.prompt:
Run a Product Hunt launch end-to-end (4-week prep + day-of script + follow-through).

Inputs:
- Product + one-liner: [paste]
- Launch date target: [paste]
- Existing supporter network on PH (likers from prior launches, hunter friends): [paste]
- Founder's PH account history + karma: [paste]
- Asset capacity (designer? video?): [paste]

Phase 1 — Pick date + category.
- Avoid Mondays (low traffic) and Fridays (PH-employee distraction)
- Tuesdays or Wednesdays optimal
- Avoid major news events / holidays that suck attention
- Category choice matters: AI category needs ~800-1,200 upvotes for #1; non-AI ~500-700
- Output: launch date + 4 backup dates

Phase 2 — Assemble supporters (4 weeks out).
- Goal: 400+ committed supporters with PH accounts
- Source 1: scrape your previous launches' upvoters and message via PH inbox
- Source 2: your X / LinkedIn audience that mentioned PH
- Source 3: 10 hunter-friend asks (they comment + nudge their network)
- Track in a sheet: name, account, last-checked-active, committed?, posted?, commented?

Phase 3 — Build assets to PH spec.
- Gallery images: 1270x760 pixels, 4-7 images (hero + features + social proof + team + roadmap)
- Tagline: <=60 characters, outcome-driven (NOT "Powered by AI")
- Description: 260 chars max, hook + 3 features + CTA
- Maker comment: drafted in advance, 200-400 words, shows the human story
- First-comment thread script: 10 angles to seed (hunter friends post these)

Phase 4 — Day-of (hour-by-hour, PT time).
- 00:01 PT: post goes live
- 00:01-00:15: founder posts the maker comment + 3 hunter friends comment
- 00:15-08:00: every hour, respond to every comment within 30 min; rotate posts across X, LinkedIn, Reddit, niche Slack/Discord
- 08:00-20:00: peak voting window — maintain comment cadence, drive supporters via DM blast
- 20:00 PT: final push email to supporters who haven't voted

Phase 5 — Post-launch follow-through.
- Thank-you post on X / LinkedIn with the result + lessons
- Email everyone who signed up during the launch (within 48h) with a personal note
- Convert engagement to email list / waitlist / paying customer — design the funnel BEFORE you launch
- A "what went well / what didn't" memo for the next launch

Phase 6 — Output.
- 4-week prep timeline (Notion doc)
- Supporter outreach template + tracking sheet
- Asset checklist with PH specs
- Day-of script with hour-by-hour actions
- Post-launch follow-up plan

Feedback signal (closes the loop for next launch):
- Ranking outcome vs target
- Comment volume + sentiment vs control launches
- Conversion of PH visitors to signups + paid — that's the real metric, not upvotes

Quality bar:
- NEVER pay for votes — PH detects and de-ranks
- NEVER schedule a launch on a Friday or holiday
- The maker comment is NOT a feature dump — it's a story about why this exists
- Day-of: respond to every comment within 30 min, even the critical ones — the engagement signal matters

playbooks.name: Run a programmatic SEO sprint
playbooks.description: Run a programmatic SEO sprint. Get a templated landing-page matrix, schema, internal-link map, and quality gate.
playbooks.prompt:
Run a programmatic SEO sprint (Zapier / Calendly / Webflow pattern — Zapier 6.3M monthly visits, Calendly 1.1M).

Inputs:
- Product + ICP: [paste]
- Existing site domain authority (DA / DR): [paste]
- Existing top-ranking pages (so we don't cannibalize): [paste]
- Data source for unique content (your DB, public API, your integrations list): [paste]
- Capacity to hand-tune (humans + days): [paste]

Phase 1 — Pick the 2-dimension matrix.
Examples:
- {App A} × {App B} (integration pages — Zapier)
- {Tool} × {Use case} (Calendly: scheduling × CRM)
- {City} × {Job role} (talent marketplaces)
- {Industry} × {Software type} (vertical SaaS)

Score candidates:
- Total page count (matrix size): aim for 100-10,000, not 1,000,000 (Google penalizes thin)
- Search volume: every cell needs SOMEONE searching; ideally most cells have monthly volume >10
- Intent: commercial > informational > navigational
- Existing competition: low-DA pages ranking on this matrix = opportunity

Recommend ONE matrix. Wait for me to confirm.

Phase 2 — Validate search volume + intent.
- Pull volume per cell from Ahrefs / Semrush / KWFinder
- Sample 50 cells; look at the current SERP — what dominates? Can we credibly compete?
- Identify cells where intent is COMMERCIAL (closer to purchase) and prioritize

Phase 3 — Build the template + unique content slots.
- Template structure: H1, hero (intro paragraph with both keywords), use-case examples, screenshots, CTA, FAQ, schema markup (FAQPage + Product + BreadcrumbList)
- Unique content per cell: pulled from your data source (e.g., for {App A} × {App B} integration: actual fields synced, popular use cases, customer count if available)
- DO NOT use the same paragraph across cells — Google will downgrade

Phase 4 — Generate + hand-tune top 50.
- Generate the full matrix programmatically
- Hand-tune the TOP 50 cells (by search volume × intent): better intro, custom screenshots, real-customer quotes
- These 50 carry the quality signal that lifts the rest of the matrix

Phase 5 — Internal link map.
- Every page links to: 5 related cells (same dimension A or B), the pillar page, and the relevant product page
- Pillar page links out to top 100 cells
- Each cell page has 2-3 incoming internal links minimum

Phase 6 — Quality gate before publishing.
- Lighthouse score >85 mobile
- Schema validates (Rich Results Test)
- No cell has <300 unique words
- Robots.txt + sitemap.xml updated

Phase 7 — Output.
- Matrix spec + template
- Generated pages staged for publish
- Internal link map (CSV)
- A 90-day measurement plan (organic clicks per cell, conversion to signup, pages indexed)

Feedback signal:
- Per cell type: organic traffic growth + ranking
- Conversion rate by cell to product signup
- Cells Google chose NOT to index (these are the thin ones — improve or delete)

Quality bar:
- NEVER publish 10,000 pages with thin content — Google de-ranks the WHOLE site
- NEVER duplicate paragraphs across cells — that's the death signal
- A 100-cell matrix that ranks beats a 10,000-cell matrix that doesn't
- Disclose AI-generated content if your audience cares (devs, journalists do)

playbooks.name: Run a build-in-public launch sequence
playbooks.description: Run a build-in-public launch sequence (Pieter Levels / Marc Lou). Get a daily posting plan, revenue-screenshot cadence, and an audience-to-revenue funnel.
steps: Plan the launch with the audience
playbooks.prompt:
Run a build-in-public launch sequence (Pieter Levels $3M ARR / Marc Lou $4K/day pattern).

Inputs:
- Existing X / LinkedIn / IH audience size + engagement rate: [paste]
- Product + launch date: [paste]
- Existing revenue (if any): [paste]
- Comfort level with public transparency (revenue, churn, mistakes): [paste]
- Founder's voice samples (what's already worked): [paste]

Phase 1 — Audit current audience + funnel.
- Audience size per platform + engagement rate
- Bio CTA (what's it driving to?)
- Existing funnel: posts → profile visits → product signups → revenue
- Surface the conversion gap

Phase 2 — Set the daily posting cadence.
- X: 2-3 posts/day (a build update + a lesson + an engagement post)
- LinkedIn: 1 post/day (longer-form, founder narrative)
- Indie Hackers: 2-3 posts/week (community-focused, more transparent)
- Each post matched to the platform's norms (X tight, LinkedIn narrative, IH peer-to-peer)

Phase 3 — Build the metric-screenshot rhythm.
- Weekly: Stripe MRR screenshot with one lesson
- Monthly: full revenue + churn + cost transparency
- Each milestone: shipping screenshot ($1k MRR, $10k, $100k, etc.)
- Failures shared candidly — fails build trust faster than wins

Phase 4 — Plan the launch with the audience.
- 30 days out: tease the problem you're solving (NOT the product yet)
- 14 days out: tease the build with screenshots
- 7 days out: open a waitlist (or "DM me to be a beta tester")
- Launch day: drop the URL + price + first-customer offer
- Post-launch: daily revenue screenshots + lessons for 14 days

Phase 5 — Measure audience-to-revenue.
- Per-platform: clicks to product, signups, paid conversions
- Which post types convert (build updates? lessons? failures?)
- Average revenue per follower (RPF) — a real metric for indie founders

Phase 6 — Output.
- 30-day content calendar (per platform, per day)
- Screenshot rhythm calendar (what to share, when)
- Launch sequence checklist (30-day countdown)
- A spreadsheet tracking audience size + engagement + revenue weekly

Feedback signal (closes the loop):
- Post type that drove most clicks vs signups vs revenue — bias next month's mix
- Platform that converts best for your ICP — focus your time
- "Big number" milestones that compound (each milestone is a content asset)

Quality bar:
- NEVER fake the screenshots — the internet finds out
- NEVER post revenue screenshots if you're loss-leading (it confuses ICP)
- Engage with comments — passive build-in-public underperforms active engagement
- Be honest about what's not working — that's what builds trust (and the audience)

playbooks.name: Plan an open-source → commercial conversion
playbooks.description: Plan an OSS → commercial transition (dbt / PostHog / Plausible / n8n). Get a tier design, hosted offering spec, and OSS commit guarantees.
steps: Design the commercial wrapper (hosted / governance / SLA)
Spec OSS commits the company guarantees
playbooks.prompt:
Plan an open-source → commercial transition (dbt / PostHog / Plausible / n8n pattern).

Inputs:
- OSS project + GitHub stats (stars, contributors, deploys): [paste]
- Current community (Discord / Slack / Discourse size): [paste]
- Top 10 self-hosted users you know about: [paste]
- License (MIT? AGPL? Fair-code?): [paste]
- Founder principles (what stays free FOREVER): [paste]

Phase 1 — Audit OSS community + usage.
- Self-hosted deploy count (rough estimate from telemetry, npm/pip downloads, Docker pulls)
- Community engagement: Discord activity, GitHub issue velocity, PR cadence
- Top 5 use cases (ask the community in the Discord)
- Top 5 pain points self-hosters cite (these are your hosted-tier value props)

Phase 2 — Design the commercial wrapper.
Free (OSS, forever):
- Core functionality
- Single-instance, single-user / small-team usage
- Community-supported

Hosted (paid, value metric per the product):
- Zero-ops deployment
- Backups, monitoring, scaling
- Per usage tier (events, GMV, seats, whatever scales with value)

Team / Enterprise (paid, governance):
- SSO + SCIM
- Audit logs
- SLA + dedicated support
- Compliance (SOC2, HIPAA, GDPR controls)

Phase 3 — Spec OSS commits the company guarantees.
- Which features will ALWAYS be in OSS (no take-backs)
- Pace of OSS commits vs commercial features
- Public governance: who decides what goes where
- Public roadmap with commercial-vs-OSS labels

Phase 4 — Plan the launch + comms.
- The blog post: why we're doing this, what changes for users, what doesn't
- Community AMA in Discord — answer the hard questions live
- Migration story for current users (free hosted credit, white-glove migration for top users)
- Pricing-page launch with side-by-side OSS / Hosted / Enterprise

Phase 5 — Measure OSS → commercial conversion.
- Hosted-paid conversion rate from self-hosted users (target 1-3% in year one)
- Enterprise conversion from hosted-paid (target 5-10% by year two)
- Community sentiment: are commits accelerating or decelerating after launch?
- NPS in Discord pre vs post

Phase 6 — Output.
- Tier design doc + pricing
- OSS commit guarantee + governance doc
- Migration playbook for top self-hosted users
- Launch comms package (blog, Discord AMA, email to known self-hosters)

Feedback signal:
- Per quarter: hosted conversion + enterprise upgrade + community sentiment
- Backlash patterns — surface what looks like betrayal vs honest concern
- Features the community wants in OSS that you held back — re-evaluate

Quality bar:
- NEVER pull a feature from OSS into commercial — that breaks trust permanently
- NEVER ship a license change without 90-day community notice
- The OSS project must remain genuinely useful standalone — anything else is bait-and-switch
- Hire community-first: the community manager comes BEFORE the second sales rep

playbooks.name: Solve the marketplace cold-start problem (supply-first)
playbooks.description: Solve marketplace cold start by saturating supply first (Andrew Chen pattern). Get a city-by-city supply plan and demand trigger.
steps: Identify the supply concentration unit (city / niche / time)
Saturate one unit at a time
Define the supply density that unlocks demand
Open demand only after the threshold
playbooks.prompt:
Solve the marketplace cold-start problem by saturating supply first (Andrew Chen pattern — Airbnb / Uber / Tinder hard-side).

Inputs:
- Marketplace concept + take rate: [paste]
- Supply side (sellers / drivers / hosts / etc.) + demand side: [paste]
- Geographic or vertical concentration unit (city, niche, time-slot): [paste]
- Capital available for supply incentives: [paste]
- Competitive supply (where do they already sell?): [paste]

Phase 1 — Identify the concentration unit.
- For Airbnb: city (a host in NYC matters to NYC demand only)
- For Uber: city + time-of-day
- For a vertical talent marketplace: niche (frontend devs)
- For a creator marketplace: niche × creator-size tier

Recommend ONE concentration unit. Wait for me to confirm.

Phase 2 — Pick the first unit and saturate.
- Pick the unit where you have the strongest founder-network edge (NOT the biggest market)
- Define "saturated": e.g., Airbnb required 300 listings + 100 reviewed per city BEFORE opening demand
- For your unit: what's the equivalent threshold?

Phase 3 — Acquire supply.
- Tactic 1: poach from competitor marketplaces (personally email 100+ existing supply, offer "list with us free + send you a check minus reduced take rate")
- Tactic 2: white-glove onboarding (founder personally onboards first 50 supply — record what they ask)
- Tactic 3: anchor supply (recruit 3-5 high-status supply that draws others — celebrity hosts, top devs, signature restaurants)
- Tactic 4: subsidize early — pay supply directly to be present for the first 90 days

Phase 4 — Hold demand back.
- Resist the urge to acquire demand before supply is dense
- A poor first-demand experience kills brand
- Only open demand when supply density gives a 90%+ "find what you came for" rate

Phase 5 — Open demand (carefully).
- One channel only at first (e.g., one neighborhood, one Reddit community, one influencer)
- Measure: completion rate, NPS, return-visit rate
- Tune the supply mix based on demand feedback

Phase 6 — Iterate to the next unit.
- Once unit 1 is humming, replicate the supply-acquisition playbook in unit 2
- Don't open unit 3 until unit 2 has demand traction
- City-by-city beats nationwide-launch for the first 10 units

Phase 7 — Output.
- Concentration-unit choice + reasoning memo
- Supply density threshold per unit
- Supply acquisition playbook (4 tactics with scripts + budgets)
- 90-day plan for unit 1 with weekly milestones
- A "launch criteria" checklist for opening demand

Feedback signal:
- Supply density → demand completion rate curve — calibrates the threshold for next unit
- Supply churn per unit — surface why supply leaves
- Which acquisition tactic worked best per unit — bias the next unit's playbook

Quality bar:
- NEVER open demand before supply is saturated — first-impression damage compounds
- NEVER assume one supply playbook works in every unit — each unit has its own dynamics
- Subsidies expire — plan unit-economics that work without subsidy by month 12
- Order: supply, demand, supply, supply, supply (Andrew Chen's heuristic for hard-side marketplaces)

playbooks.name: Run a 5-day founder time audit + delegation log
playbooks.description: Run a 5-day founder time audit. Get a leverage map, a delegation log, and a 90-day re-audit plan.
steps: Log activity in 30-min blocks for 5 workdays
playbooks.prompt:
Run a 5-day founder time audit + delegation log (First Round pattern — re-audit at 90 days).

Inputs:
- Last week's calendar (or paste a screenshot): [paste]
- Last week's journal / Slack messages / commits: [paste or path]
- My current top 3 priorities: [paste]
- Team I could delegate to (with role + capacity): [paste]
- My self-perceived "energy zones" (high / low productivity times): [paste]

Phase 1 — Log 5 days in 30-min blocks.
- For each block: activity, who I was with, mode (deep work / shallow / meeting / reactive), energy level (high/med/low)
- Be honest — count Twitter scrolling and email refresh
- Don't skip the bathroom breaks and lunch — those have signal too

Phase 2 — Categorize by leverage tier.
Tier 1 (10x leverage — only-the-founder-can-do):
- Strategic decisions, hiring critical roles, top-customer relationships, public face
Tier 2 (3x — founder-best-equipped, but delegable later):
- Founder-led sales, fundraising prep, key product decisions
Tier 3 (1x — important but generic):
- Email management, scheduling, reporting, expenses
Tier 4 (<1x — reactive, eats time):
- Slack noise, low-stakes context-switching, reactive meetings

Total hours per tier. Surface where 60%+ of your week is going.

Phase 3 — Identify delegation candidates.
- Every Tier 3 / 4 activity: who could do this today? (name a person)
- If no one can do it today, what would they need to be ready in 30 days?
- Compute the cost: hiring vs delegating to an existing teammate vs automating

Phase 4 — Write the delegation log.
For each delegation:
- Activity, owner, transition plan (shadow → co-do → handoff)
- Approval needed before owner takes over (and how often that approval shrinks)
- Quality bar — what does "good" look like?
- The "I take back" condition (when do I re-own this?)

Phase 5 — Schedule the 90-day re-audit.
- Same 5-day log in 90 days
- Compare leverage-tier mix before vs after
- If Tier 3 / 4 still >40% of week, delegation isn't sticking — diagnose

Phase 6 — Output.
- 5-day log (filled in)
- Leverage tier pie chart
- Delegation log (Notion / sheet) with owners + transition plans
- A "stop list" — things I'll just stop doing (not delegate)
- 90-day re-audit calendar block

Feedback signal:
- Tier mix delta over 90 days — are you actually shifting?
- Delegations that snapped back to founder — why?
- Energy zone shifts — did peak hours move into Tier 1 work?

Quality bar:
- NEVER skip the embarrassing entries (scrolling, distraction) — they're the highest-ROI signal
- NEVER delegate without naming the quality bar — that's how delegation fails
- "Stop" beats "delegate" for low-ROI work — kill it entirely
- Founders systematically over-estimate the value of their reactive work — audit honestly

playbooks.name: Build a burn + runway scenario model
playbooks.description: Build a burn + runway model with burn multiple, scenarios, and a board-ready dashboard.
playbooks.prompt:
Build a burn + runway scenario model (Tomasz Tunguz / Theory pattern).

Inputs:
- Current cash + bank balance: [paste]
- Last 12 months P&L (revenue + costs by category): [paste]
- Current MRR / ARR + growth rate: [paste]
- Hiring plan for the next 12 months: [paste]
- Fundraise plan (timing + size + dilution target): [paste]

Phase 1 — Pull current state.
- Monthly revenue (recurring + one-time)
- Monthly costs by category: payroll (split eng / sales / G&A), infra, marketing, tools, other
- Monthly burn = costs - revenue
- Cash position + months of runway at current burn

Phase 2 — Compute base burn vs growth burn.
- Base burn: spend required to keep the lights on (payroll for existing team + infra + minimum marketing)
- Growth burn: incremental spend going into new acquisition + new hires
- Net new ARR added per quarter

Phase 3 — Calculate burn multiple.
- Burn multiple = net burn / net new ARR
- <1x = exceptional; 1-1.5x = good; 1.5-2x = OK; >2x = problem
- Track over the last 6 months — surface the trend

Phase 4 — Run scenarios.

Base case:
- Current trajectory + planned hires
- Months of runway at current burn growth

Aggressive growth:
- 50% more spend on growth (more sales, more marketing)
- Modeled revenue lift (be skeptical — most growth assumptions are too optimistic)
- Runway impact

Defensive:
- Hold spend flat for 6 months
- Reduced growth assumption
- Extended runway

Cuts (if needed):
- Where you'd cut 20% of monthly burn if you had to (named line items + dollar impact + revenue risk)

Phase 5 — Fundraise timing.
- Months of runway at each scenario
- Target: raise when you have 9+ months runway (NEVER let it dip below 6 unless you've committed term sheet)
- What metrics you need to hit BEFORE the raise (NRR, NDR, growth rate, ICP convergence)

Phase 6 — Output.
- Cash flow model .xlsx (with assumptions on a single sheet so I can vary them)
- 1-page board dashboard PDF (current burn, burn multiple, runway, scenario table)
- A "cut list" memo — where I'd cut and what the revenue risk is
- A fundraise timing memo

Feedback signal:
- Actual vs forecast burn per month — surface drift
- Burn multiple trend — improving or degrading?
- Which scenarios played out — refine assumptions for next model

Quality bar:
- NEVER model revenue growth that requires hiring you haven't made yet
- NEVER assume infra costs scale linearly with users — they don't (usually super-linear)
- Reserve 3-month buffer in the runway calculation — fundraises slip
- This is modeling, NOT a commitment — share with the board WITH the assumptions visible

playbooks.name: Run a 'why we lost' battlecard loop
playbooks.description: Run a weekly why-we-lost battlecard loop (Klue pattern). Get a 1-screen battlecard refreshed weekly with rep-usage tracking.
steps: Interview every closed-lost deal within 7 days
Track rep adoption + correlated win rate
playbooks.prompt:
Run a "why we lost" battlecard loop (Klue + Primary Intelligence pattern — weekly cadence, 1-screen format).

Inputs:
- Closed-lost deals from last 90 days: [paste with company + competitor + lost-reason if known]
- Top 3 competitors I lose to: [paste]
- Current battlecard format (if any): [paste]
- Sales team size + competitive deal volume per week: [paste]

Phase 1 — Interview every closed-lost deal within 7 days.
- Founder personally calls the buyer (NOT the rep) for a 20-min conversation
- Open: "I'm not trying to re-pitch — I want to understand what happened so we can be a better fit next time"
- Questions:
  - When did you first realize we weren't the right fit?
  - What did [competitor] do that we didn't?
  - What would have changed your decision?
  - Who else weighed in on the decision?
  - What's your honest take on our pitch?
- Take notes verbatim (NOT paraphrased)

Phase 2 — Pull 3 quotes/week into the battlecard.
Per competitor, surface:
- The 3 most recurring objections we lose on
- The 3 wedge angles competitors use against us
- The 3 things buyers WISH we did differently

Phase 3 — 1-screen battlecard per competitor.
Single screen format (don't fit a 30-page PDF — reps don't use those):
- Positioning (1 sentence on competitor + 1 sentence on us vs them)
- Top 3 traps (what they say about us — and the counter)
- Top 3 landmines (questions to ask that surface their weakness)
- Pricing reality (their actual price, not website)
- Best customer quote that lands the differentiation
- "Trigger to switch" (events at the buyer that signal we win)

Phase 4 — Track rep adoption.
- Embed the battlecard in the CRM at the deal stage where competitor is identified
- Track: which reps click the battlecard? Which use the talking points?
- Correlate rep usage with their win rate vs competitor — promote the winning patterns

Phase 5 — Weekly cadence.
- Friday 30-min: review last week's losses + 1 new quote per battlecard
- Update the 1-screen with the freshest material
- Notify sales of changes (Slack #competitive)

Phase 6 — Quarterly deep refresh.
- Re-research competitor pricing (their website lies)
- Customer interviews with 5 lost buyers + 5 won buyers
- Update the positioning paragraph if the market moved

Phase 7 — Output.
- 1-screen battlecard per top-3 competitor (Notion or PDF, fit on one screen)
- Closed-lost interview script + question bank
- Weekly refresh template
- Rep-usage dashboard
- Quarterly competitor pricing tracker

Feedback signal (closes the loop):
- Win rate vs competitor over time — improving = the battlecard is working
- Quote / objection frequency — surface emerging patterns
- Rep adoption rate — if low, the format is wrong (or the content is)

Quality bar:
- NEVER skip the 7-day interview window — memory fades fast
- NEVER put battlecard content in a 30-page PDF — it dies there
- The buyer's words matter MORE than the rep's interpretation — capture verbatim
- If a battlecard doesn't change for a month, the loop is broken — fix it

playbooks.name: Run a reason-segmented winback campaign
playbooks.description: Run a reason-segmented winback (Getir-style — outperformed benchmark without a discount). Get sequences branched by cancel reason.
playbooks.prompt:
Run a reason-segmented winback campaign for churned customers.

Inputs:
- Churned customer list (last 12 months, with cancel reason if captured): [paste]
- Current cancel-flow questions: [paste]
- Top product changes since they churned (features shipped, pricing changes, partner integrations): [paste]
- My sending email + signature: [paste]
- Brand voice: [paste]

Phase 1 — Map the cancel-reason taxonomy.
Standard buckets:
- Price-sensitive (cited cost / budget)
- Missing feature (cited specific feature gap)
- Competitor switch (named another tool)
- Inactive / lost-champion (no usage in last 60 days before cancel; champion left)
- Wrong fit (bought the wrong product for their need)
- Reason-unstated (no signal — typically the smallest sub-segment)

For each: count of churned customers in last 12 months + total ARR lost.

Phase 2 — Branch a 90-day sequence per reason.

Price-sensitive (3 emails over 30 days):
- Email 1 (day 0): "we shipped X" (the cost-impact feature) + a discount or annual deal
- Email 2 (day 14): ROI calculator showing their specific use case
- Email 3 (day 30): "would 6 months at half price help you re-evaluate?"

Missing feature (3 emails, triggered when the feature ships):
- Email 1 (day 0): "you asked for X. We shipped it. Here's how it works."
- Email 2 (day 14): "want to try it free for 30 days?"
- Email 3 (day 30): "interested? Here's a 1:1 walkthrough offer."

Competitor switch (3 emails over 60 days):
- Email 1 (day 30): "how's [competitor] working out? Honest take from us"
- Email 2 (day 60): head-to-head battle card on the specific gap they hit
- Email 3 (day 90): one-time migration offer

Inactive / lost-champion (3 emails over 30 days):
- Email 1 (day 0): "your champion [name if known] left — are you using [product] differently?"
- Email 2 (day 14): "if you need a re-onboarding, we'll do it free"
- Email 3 (day 30): clean break — "let us know if you ever come back"

Wrong fit (1 email — be honest):
- Day 0: "we weren't the right fit. Here's who we send people like you to."
- This builds reputation > revenue

Phase 3 — Send from a founder-from address.
- Personal email from founder (not @marketing or @noreply)
- Plain text, no images, no template feel
- Sign with name + role

Phase 4 — Read out at 90 days.
- Per reason: response rate + reactivation rate + ARR recovered
- Compare to no-action churn baseline
- Top-performing reason / email — promote to default winback

Phase 5 — Output.
- Reason-bucket dashboard (counts + ARR)
- 4-track email sequence (one per actionable reason)
- A "do not contact" list (customers who explicitly asked)
- A 90-day measurement template

Feedback signal (closes the loop):
- Reactivation rate per reason — calibrate which sequences are worth running
- Average revenue recovered per email — surface the highest-ROI track
- New reasons emerging in replies — add buckets

Quality bar:
- NEVER send to a customer who opted out of marketing — re-confirm before send
- NEVER fake personalization — the founder-from address must actually come from a real person
- Don't discount price-sensitive customers below what new customers pay — that breaks trust
- Sometimes the right answer is "we weren't the right fit, here's a better alternative" — those replies build long-term reputation

playbooks.name: Audit sleep and recovery from wearable data
playbooks.description: Audit 30 days of wearable data. Get a narrative of what's helping, what's hurting, and tonight's one action.
steps: Cluster what helps vs hurts recovery
playbooks.prompt:
Audit my last 30 days of sleep + recovery from wearable data.

Inputs:
- Source: [Oura / Whoop / Apple Watch / Garmin / Fitbit — export or paste]
- 30 days of nightly metrics (sleep stages, HRV, RHR, temperature deviation, sleep score): [paste or path]
- Daily context I tracked (workouts, alcohol, late meals, travel, caffeine): [paste]
- My current sleep goal (recovery / cognition / mood / training): [paste]
- Any sleep issues I'm tracking (waking at 3am, sleep onset, etc.): [paste]

Phase 1 — Compute baselines + drift.
- 30-day mean and SD for HRV, RHR, total sleep, REM %, deep %
- Last 7 days vs prior 23 — surface meaningful drift (>1 SD)
- Compare against age + sex norms (cite the source)

Phase 2 — Cluster what helps vs hurts.
- Cross-tab biometrics against my daily context (alcohol, late meals, hard workouts, etc.)
- Surface the 3 strongest signals helping recovery
- Surface the 3 strongest signals hurting it
- Distinguish correlation from causation — flag what needs an experiment

Phase 3 — Recommend the single biggest lever.
- One change I can make TONIGHT (not 5 — one)
- One experiment to run over the next 14 days (A/B-style: do X on odd days, skip on even)
- Explicit predictions: what biometric should move + by how much

Phase 4 — Output.
- 1-page audit PDF in my workspace
- A "tonight's action" line at the top
- 14-day experiment plan + the metric to watch
- A "what I'm NOT going to change" list (so I don't over-optimize)

Feedback signal (14-day re-check):
- Did the predicted metric move?
- Surprises (a signal you missed)
- Patterns to test next round

Quality bar:
- This is data interpretation, NOT medical advice — frame as such
- NEVER claim a clinical diagnosis from wearable data
- If you see consistent hypoxia / extreme HRV / new arrhythmia signals, recommend a doctor visit
- Don't over-fit on small differences — wearable accuracy has known limits

playbooks.name: Prep a symptom log and doctor's appointment
playbooks.description: Build a symptom timeline + question list for a doctor visit. Get a 1-page summary and a prioritized question stack.
playbooks.prompt:
Prep for a doctor's appointment with a symptom log + question list.

Inputs:
- Reason for the visit: [paste]
- Symptom log (free text — when, how bad, what helped, what hurt): [paste]
- Medications + supplements + dosages: [paste]
- Recent labs / vitals / imaging (paste or path): [paste]
- Family / personal history relevant to the visit: [paste]
- Appointment length (most are 15-20 min — plan accordingly): [paste]

Phase 1 — Build the symptom timeline.
- Sort symptoms chronologically with onset, severity (1-10), pattern (constant / episodic / worsening), triggers, things that helped
- Note any consistent time-of-day or correlation with food / stress / movement
- Flag any symptom that's NEW since last visit

Phase 2 — Cluster.
- Severity × frequency matrix — which symptoms get priority
- Group by likely system (cardiac / GI / neuro / etc.) to help the doctor
- Surface what you're NOT sure is related (let them connect the dots)

Phase 3 — Draft a 1-page handout to give the doctor.
- Top: reason for visit (1 sentence)
- Timeline: 5-8 bullets of the key events
- Current meds + supplements
- What I've tried already + what helped
- What I'm worried about (be honest — saves time)

Phase 4 — Write the question stack (ranked by priority).
- Top 3: questions you MUST get answered
- Next 3-5: nice-to-have
- For each: phrase it openly ("what could cause X?" not "is it Y?")
- Map each question to "tests / treatment / next steps" bucket

Phase 5 — Output.
- 1-page handout PDF
- Question list (print or phone-ready)
- A "what I'll do if they say X / Y / Z" decision tree

Feedback signal (after the appointment):
- Which questions got answered, which got deferred
- Any test or referral suggested — log to follow up
- New symptoms or angles the doctor surfaced — add to the next log

Quality bar:
- NEVER self-diagnose — describe symptoms, let the doctor diagnose
- Bring the handout printed AND on phone (some doctors prefer one)
- If you have a worst-fear question, ask it — most doctors prefer directness
- For chronic conditions, ask about the next 90-day plan, not just the next pill

playbooks.name: Run a CBT mood journal with weekly trends
playbooks.description: Run a daily CBT journal companion. Get cognitive-distortion catches, weekly mood trends, and one experiment per week.
playbooks.prompt:
Run a daily CBT-style mood journal as my reflective partner.

Inputs:
- Today's mood (1-10) + 2-line description of the day: [paste]
- A specific thought that's been sticky (worry, regret, self-criticism): [paste]
- Sleep last night + caffeine + exercise today: [paste]
- Current life context (job, relationship, health, money — what's loud right now): [paste — once, will persist for the journal]
- Any therapy or coaching I'm doing in parallel: [paste]

Phase 1 — Reflect, don't fix.
- Restate what I said back to me (validates the feeling first)
- Ask one open follow-up question to draw out detail
- DO NOT give advice in this phase

Phase 2 — Spot cognitive distortions (gentle Socratic).
For the sticky thought, identify any of these patterns:
- All-or-nothing
- Catastrophizing
- Mind-reading
- Personalization
- "Should" statements
- Discounting positives
- Emotional reasoning

If you spot one, name it as a possibility (NOT a verdict) and ask: "is there another way to read this?"

Phase 3 — Socratic reframe.
- Ask: what evidence supports the thought? What evidence contradicts it?
- Ask: what would I say to a friend in this exact situation?
- Help me draft a reframe — NOT a happier lie, a more accurate one
- The reframe is mine to accept or reject

Phase 4 — Weekly trend (Sundays).
- Mood graph for the week + average
- Recurring distortions
- The 1-2 themes that came up most often
- One experiment to try this week (small, concrete, reversible)

Phase 5 — Monthly check-in (1st of the month).
- PHQ-9 / GAD-7 short-form
- Trend over the last 3 months
- Whether to escalate to a therapist if not already in care

Phase 6 — Output.
- Daily entry saved as a markdown file (so I can search later)
- Weekly Sunday summary (mood + themes + experiment)
- Monthly trend PDF

Feedback signal:
- Mood trajectory over weeks (climbing / falling / volatile)
- Which experiments stuck vs which fizzled
- Distortion patterns that recur — those are the ones to bring to a therapist

Quality bar:
- This is a journal companion, NOT therapy. Frame as such.
- NEVER diagnose. If I describe symptoms of harm to self or others, immediately recommend professional help + crisis resources.
- Use my words, not yours — the reframe must feel like mine
- Be warm but not saccharine — the language matters

playbooks.name: Build a periodized strength training program
playbooks.description: Build a periodized strength program. Get a 4-12 week mesocycle with RPE targets, deloads, and weekly auto-adjust.
playbooks.prompt:
Build a periodized strength training program tailored to me.

Inputs:
- Goal: [strength / hypertrophy / power / fat loss with muscle / general]
- Current 1RMs (squat, bench, deadlift, OHP — if known) OR honest training maxes: [paste]
- Days per week I can train: [paste]
- Equipment available: [home / commercial gym / minimal]
- Methodology preference (if any): [5/3/1 / GZCL / GVT / Daniels / RPE-based / "you pick"]
- Recent injury history + movements to avoid: [paste]
- Cardio + sport context (running, climbing, etc.): [paste]

Phase 1 — Pick the methodology.
- Score 5/3/1, GZCL, Daniels GVT, RPE-based, classic linear against my goal + experience level
- Recommend ONE with reasoning (one paragraph)
- If I push back, propose a runner-up

Phase 2 — Generate the mesocycle (4-12 weeks).
- Weekly split (e.g., 4-day upper/lower)
- Per session: main lifts (sets × reps × % 1RM or RPE), accessory lifts, conditioning
- Progression scheme (linear / wave / RPE-adjusted)
- Deload week(s) inserted appropriately (typically week 4 or 6)
- A test week at the end (top set or rep test)

Phase 3 — Recovery + RPE feedback rules.
- Per session: log RPE on the top set
- If RPE is >1 higher than target for 2 sessions in a row: drop next session's load 5%
- If RPE is >1 lower for 2 sessions in a row: bump next session 5-10 lb
- HRV / sleep red flag (if I track): swap heavy day for technique work

Phase 4 — Movement quality + safety.
- Cues for the 4 main lifts (form points I should check on warmups)
- Warmup protocol
- Conditioning options that don't tank recovery

Phase 5 — Output.
- A printable per-week plan (PDF)
- A spreadsheet for logging (sets × reps × weight × RPE × notes)
- The auto-adjust rules in a 1-page reference
- A "what to do if I miss a session" cheat sheet

Feedback signal:
- Weekly: RPE drift vs plan — calibrate the next week's loads
- Monthly: are the top sets going up at the planned rate?
- Body comp / strength trajectory at the end of the mesocycle — confirms goal alignment

Quality bar:
- This is a training plan, NOT medical or PT advice
- NEVER prescribe past a movement I said I'd avoid
- If I report sharp pain (vs DOMS), advise stopping the lift and seeing a PT
- Defaults are conservative — I can always do more, but starting too aggressive injures

playbooks.name: Run a habit-tracker weekly retrospective
playbooks.description: Run a weekly habit retrospective. Get adherence patterns, slip triggers, and one experiment for the next week.
playbooks.prompt:
Run my weekly habit retrospective.

Inputs:
- Habits I'm tracking + the rule for each (e.g., "read 20 min before bed"): [paste]
- Last 7 days of check-ins (Y/N per habit per day): [paste]
- Notes I wrote about misses or wins: [paste]
- Last week's experiment + outcome (if any): [paste]

Phase 1 — Adherence math.
- Per habit: completion rate this week vs 4-week average
- The habit with the steepest decline — surface first
- The habit with the strongest streak — that's your anchor

Phase 2 — Spot slip triggers.
- Cluster misses by day-of-week + by surrounding context (late work day, travel, social, sick)
- Identify the ONE recurring trigger most predictive of misses
- Validate: do you have evidence over multiple weeks, or is it a hunch?

Phase 3 — Recommend one experiment.
- ONE small change for next week (anchor habit to existing routine, shift time, lower the bar)
- Make it concrete: "swap evening reading from after dinner to right after kids' bedtime"
- Predict: what completion rate will this lift the slipping habit to?

Phase 4 — Output.
- Adherence table (this week vs trend)
- Slip-trigger note
- Next week's experiment (one line)
- A "do nothing" list (habits that are working — don't tinker)

Feedback signal (closes the loop next week):
- Did the experiment lift the metric?
- Did fixing one habit hurt another? (energy budget is real)
- Recurring triggers across weeks — surface as systemic

Quality bar:
- Total output <250 words — this is a tight reflection, not an essay
- Be honest about slips — sugar-coating doesn't help
- Don't add a new habit on top of failure — fix what's slipping first
- If a habit slips 3 weeks in a row, propose killing it OR splitting it into something smaller

playbooks.name: Turn a textbook chapter into an Anki deck
playbooks.description: Turn a textbook chapter into an Anki deck. Get cloze + Q&A cards tagged by topic, ready to import as CSV.
playbooks.prompt:
Turn this textbook chapter into a high-quality Anki deck.

Inputs:
- Chapter text or PDF: [paste or path]
- Subject + course context: [e.g. USMLE Step 1 immunology, AP biology, organic chemistry 1]
- My current skill level (new / reviewing / mastery): [paste]
- Tag scheme to use (e.g. organ system, exam topic, week): [paste]
- Card budget for this chapter: [default 50-80 cards — quality over quantity]

Phase 1 — Identify load-bearing concepts.
- Read the chapter end-to-end
- Surface the 10-15 concepts you'd test on for understanding (not trivia)
- Surface the facts that students MUST memorize (definitions, named effects, numeric thresholds)
- Drop "nice to know" content — don't pad the deck

Phase 2 — Cloze cards for facts.
- One blank per card (NEVER multi-blank — bad for retention)
- The blank is the load-bearing word, not a function word
- Wrap context: "The {{c1::renin-angiotensin}} system regulates blood pressure via aldosterone."
- 20-30 cloze cards max per chapter

Phase 3 — Q&A cards for understanding.
- Q is an open question, not "what is X?" — instead "Why does X happen when Y?"
- A is concise (2-3 sentences max)
- Include one card per concept that connects to PRIOR chapters (spaced linking)
- 15-25 Q&A cards max

Phase 4 — Tag every card.
- Chapter / topic
- Type (cloze / qa / image-occlusion-if-applicable)
- Difficulty (basic / intermediate / advanced)
- A custom tag matching my scheme

Phase 5 — Output.
- CSV ready to import to Anki (tab-separated or CSV per Anki's format)
- A 1-line summary of what the deck covers (paste into Anki notes)
- A "skip these in your first pass" tag for the harder cards (build confidence first)

Feedback signal (after 30 days):
- Per card: how often did you flip "again" / "hard" / "good" / "easy"?
- Cards that consistently fail — rewrite or split
- Concepts where retention dies despite cards — surface; might need a different format (image occlusion, mnemonic)

Quality bar:
- NEVER write multi-blank cloze cards — they tank retention
- NEVER pad with trivia ("the textbook author was born in 1948")
- Cards should test understanding, NOT recall of textbook phrasing
- If you can answer the card without thinking about the concept, the card is wrong

playbooks.name: Plan a daily language-learning routine
playbooks.description: Plan a daily language-learning routine. Get vocab + listening + speaking + writing slots tuned to your CEFR level.
steps: Confirm target language + CEFR level + time budget
Allocate the 4 skills across the day
playbooks.prompt:
Plan today's language-learning routine.

Inputs:
- Target language + my CEFR level (A1 / A2 / B1 / B2 / C1 / C2): [paste]
- Daily time budget (30 min / 60 min / 90 min): [paste]
- Specific goal (travel / work / read a novel / pass an exam): [paste]
- Resources I have (Anki deck, textbook, podcasts, tutor, apps): [paste]
- This week's weak skill (listening / speaking / reading / writing): [paste]

Phase 1 — Allocate skills across the time budget.
For 60 min total (scale others proportionally):
- 15 min: vocabulary + grammar review (Anki + 1 new grammar point)
- 15 min: listening (a podcast, video, or song at +1 CEFR level)
- 15 min: output — speaking OR writing (active production)
- 15 min: reading (a graded reader, news, or excerpt at your level)

Adjust weighting toward this week's weak skill (give it +30%).

Phase 2 — Generate today's specific content.
For each slot:
- Vocab + grammar: 5-10 new words pulled from yesterday's input + 1 grammar pattern
- Listening: a specific recommendation (podcast episode, YouTube video) with timestamps
- Output:
  - Speaking: 3 prompts to roleplay with an AI tutor (in target language)
  - Writing: 1 prompt to write 100-200 words on, with self-check questions
- Reading: a specific text excerpt + 5 comprehension questions

Phase 3 — Weekly review schedule.
- Sunday: a 20-min review of the week's new vocab (sentence-level use, not just card flips)
- Monthly: a self-assessment against CEFR descriptors

Phase 4 — Output.
- Today's plan (1 page) with timing + resource links
- A "if I only have 20 minutes" fallback (minimum viable session)
- A vocab log to add to Anki tonight
- A "today I learned" line to log

Feedback signal (weekly):
- Which slot was most engaging — bias time toward it
- Which slot got skipped most — friction signal; redesign
- Weak-skill progress vs last week

Quality bar:
- Choose content at the right level — too easy is boring, too hard kills momentum
- Prioritize INPUT over output for A1-B1; flip toward output at B2+
- Don't drill conjugation tables for an hour — context beats drill
- If a session feels like a chore, the plan is wrong — adjust ratios

playbooks.name: Plan an adaptive test-prep study schedule
playbooks.description: Plan an adaptive test-prep schedule. Get a diagnostic-driven plan, targeted drills, and an A-week vs B-week structure.
steps: Take a diagnostic + score per topic
playbooks.prompt:
Plan my test-prep schedule, tuned to my weakest topics.

Inputs:
- Test: [LSAT / MCAT / SAT / GMAT / GRE / bar / step 1 / step 2 / etc.]
- Test date: [paste]
- My diagnostic score (overall + per section + per topic if available): [paste]
- Target score: [paste]
- Hours I can study per week (be honest): [paste]
- Resources I own (UWorld / Kaplan / Magoosh / OPL / books): [paste]
- Big constraints (work, family, travel): [paste]

Phase 1 — Diagnostic analysis.
- Score per section + per topic
- Identify the 3-5 weakest topics that block target score
- Identify the 3-5 strongest topics (don't over-study these)
- Compute the gap: target − current → translate to topic-level hours needed

Phase 2 — Weeks remaining + hours budget.
- Total weeks × hours/week = total budget
- Reserve 2 weeks for final review + 1 week for peaking taper
- Remaining weeks → topic study

Phase 3 — Allocate hours by weak topic.
- Per weak topic: target hours (more for weakest)
- Each topic block: theory (read / watch) + drill (timed questions) + review (re-do misses)
- Mix in cumulative practice tests every 2-3 weeks

Phase 4 — A-week vs B-week templates.

A-week (heavy practice):
- 3-4 days: topic drills (90 min each)
- 1 day: full-length practice test
- 1 day: review the test in detail
- 1 day: off

B-week (build foundations):
- 4-5 days: theory + new content + light drills
- 1 day: cumulative review
- 1 day: off

Alternate A/B weeks until 3 weeks before the test, then go A-heavy.

Phase 5 — Final 3 weeks (peaking).
- Week -3: 2 full-length tests + intensive review
- Week -2: 1 full-length test + targeted weak-topic drills
- Week -1: light review + sleep + logistics
- Test day: warmup with 3-5 easy problems, no new content

Phase 6 — Output.
- Full schedule (PDF, daily breakdown)
- Weekly check-in template
- Diagnostic re-take dates
- A "what to do if you miss a week" fallback

Feedback signal (every 2 weeks):
- Topic-level score on cumulative tests vs plan
- Hours actually studied vs planned
- Stamina / fatigue patterns — adjust intensity

Quality bar:
- Don't study what you're already good at to feel better — that wastes hours
- Spaced repetition beats massed practice — return to weak topics weekly, not in blocks
- Full-length tests under real conditions matter more than question count
- If burnout hits, take a 3-day break — better than a month of half-effort

playbooks.name: Rehearse mock interviews with feedback
playbooks.description: Rehearse a structured mock interview. Get role-tuned questions, STAR practice, and rubric-scored feedback.
playbooks.prompt:
Rehearse a mock interview as my practice partner.

Inputs:
- Role + level (e.g., senior PM at series B B2B SaaS, staff SWE at FAANG): [paste]
- Company + interview round type (recruiter screen, hiring manager, technical, behavioral, system design, on-site): [paste]
- My resume / current role context: [paste]
- 2-3 stories I want to land + the competencies they show: [paste]
- Public info about the company / interviewer if I have it: [paste]

Phase 1 — Generate role-specific questions.
- 5-10 likely questions for this round (behavioral / technical / case / system design)
- Each question: the competency it tests + the trap the interviewer is watching for
- Tag by difficulty (easy warmup → hard differentiator)

Phase 2 — Rehearse (rounds of 3).
For each question:
- Ask the question; wait for my answer
- Critique using a STAR rubric (Situation, Task, Action, Result)
- Flag filler ("um", "kind of", "I guess"), vague claims, missed metrics, missing reflection
- Offer one rewrite of the strongest part of my answer

After 3 questions, summarize: what's landing, what's not.

Phase 3 — Behavioral rubric scoring.
For each story:
- Specificity (1-5): named the project, the people, the numbers?
- Conflict + decision quality (1-5): showed the hard moment + the reasoning?
- Impact (1-5): quantified outcome and your contribution?
- Self-awareness (1-5): owned a mistake or a stretch zone?
- Communication (1-5): clear, paced, fielded the follow-up?

Phase 4 — Technical round (if applicable).
- Use the role's standard format (Leetcode-style, system design, case study)
- Watch for: assumption-naming, time management, communication-while-solving, edge cases
- Score against the round's rubric

Phase 5 — Focused practice plan.
- The 3 weakest patterns to drill before the real interview
- One specific story to refine (here's the rewrite)
- Logistics check (sleep, route to office, water, calendar buffer)

Phase 6 — Output.
- Score sheet per round
- Rewrites for my top 3 stories
- A drill list (specific questions to practice on my own)
- A "day-of cheat sheet" with 3 reminders

Feedback signal (after the real interview):
- Which prep predicted what came up?
- Surprises (questions I didn't prep for) — feed into next round's prep
- My energy / pacing notes — refine the day-of plan

Quality bar:
- Critique kindly, not harshly — I'm here to improve, not be judged
- Quote my actual words — vague feedback doesn't help
- If a story doesn't land for the role, say so — don't polish a turd
- Honest about probability — don't tell me I crushed it if I didn't

playbooks.name: Draft a performance review from evidence
playbooks.description: Draft a performance review from goals + peer feedback + 1:1 notes. Get a narrative aligned to a competency rubric.
playbooks.prompt:
Draft a performance review for one of my direct reports.

Inputs:
- Report's name + role + level: [paste]
- Review period: [Q3 2026 / full year / etc.]
- Their goals for the period + outcomes: [paste]
- Peer / cross-functional feedback collected: [paste]
- My 1:1 notes from the period: [paste]
- Our competency rubric (e.g., scope / execution / leadership / craft / collaboration): [paste]
- Calibration constraints (target rating distribution, comp band): [paste]

Phase 1 — Map evidence to rubric.
- For each competency: list 2-3 specific behavioral examples (with dates if possible)
- Mark gaps where I don't have enough evidence — flag for me to fill before drafting
- Identify themes across multiple competencies

Phase 2 — Draft strengths section.
- 3-4 specific strengths, each with a concrete example
- Use behavioral language ("led the X project to Y outcome") not personality ("is a great team player")
- Tie each strength to business / customer impact

Phase 3 — Draft growth section.
- 2-3 areas with concrete behavioral examples
- Frame as "what would unlock the next level" — not punitive
- Pair each growth area with a specific action / project / coaching focus

Phase 4 — Recommend rating + comp.
- Rating against the rubric — calibrated against the distribution
- Honest verdict (don't over-rate to avoid the conversation)
- Comp suggestion if relevant (against the band you sent me)
- A "promotion-ready / on-track / needs improvement" track verdict

Phase 5 — Development plan for next period.
- 2-3 specific goals tied to the growth areas
- Coaching / mentorship plan
- Stretch project recommendation

Phase 6 — Output.
- Review draft (markdown, ready to paste into the HRIS)
- Calibration note for HR / your manager
- Talking script for the live conversation (NOT the same as the doc — softer)
- A list of compliments and growth points I should deliver in person, not in writing

Feedback signal (after the conversation):
- Did the report's self-assessment match yours? (Big delta = poor 1:1 cadence)
- Which framing landed vs which felt blunt
- Follow-up commitments to track over the next quarter

Quality bar:
- NEVER write a review that's softer than what I said in 1:1s — that's surprise-by-paper
- NEVER copy template language — use the report's actual story
- Behavioral examples > personality assessments
- If there's a hard conversation needed, draft it explicitly — don't hide it

playbooks.name: Prep a compensation review against benchmarks
playbooks.description: Run a comp review against Pave + Levels benchmarks. Get per-person raise + equity refresh recommendations with rationale.
steps: Pull current comp + tenure + perf rating
playbooks.prompt:
Run a compensation review against market benchmarks.

Inputs:
- Team comp data (per person: role, level, base, bonus target, equity, hire date, last comp change): [paste]
- Recent performance ratings + flight risk notes: [paste]
- Comp philosophy + target percentile (e.g., 60th of Pave): [paste]
- Total budget for raises + equity refresh this cycle: [paste]
- Benchmark source (Pave / Levels.fyi / Carta / Radford): [paste]
- Stage of company + funding context: [paste]

Phase 1 — Per person: pull current comp + benchmark.
- Current total comp vs target percentile (gap %)
- Levels.fyi range for the role
- Equity outstanding (vested + unvested + cliff status)
- Last refresh date

Phase 2 — Surface anomalies.
- Anyone significantly below band (retention risk)
- Anyone above band (over-paid; calibration check)
- Anyone past the 1-year cliff or vesting acceleration trigger
- New hires whose comp anchor is now stale

Phase 3 — Recommend per-person actions.
For each person:
- Base raise (% and $ amount with reasoning)
- Bonus target change (if any)
- Equity refresh (size + cliff terms)
- Promotion recommendation if applicable
- Comp letter framing (warm but clear)

Phase 4 — Aggregate check.
- Total raise pool used vs budget
- Distribution across performance ratings (top performers should get meaningful skew)
- DEI sanity check: are similar roles / levels getting similar treatment regardless of demographic?

Phase 5 — Flag retention risks.
- People significantly under-market with above-average perf — top priority
- People at cliff inflection — refresh now or risk leave
- People with recent disengagement signals (low NPS, missed 1:1s, vacation drop) + under-market

Phase 6 — Output.
- Per-person comp letter draft (warm, specific, no jargon)
- Team-level summary table (delta % per person, total spend)
- Calibration note for HR / your manager
- A flight-risk list with recommended interventions

Feedback signal (next cycle):
- Did the comp change shift retention as predicted?
- Did under-market people end up leaving anyway? (Comp wasn't the issue.)
- Calibration drift over time — recalibrate annually against benchmark refresh

Quality bar:
- NEVER skip the equity refresh conversation — comp is base + bonus + equity + benefits
- Treat the conversation, not the number, as the retention lever
- Be transparent about how the number was set — not "we're being generous" but "here's the benchmark"
- If you can't fund the right number, say so — and own the retention risk

playbooks.name: Prepare a layoff communications package
playbooks.description: Prepare a layoff comms package: manager script, impacted-employee message, and team re-recruitment talking points.
playbooks.prompt:
Prepare a layoff communications package for a difficult day.

Inputs:
- Business reason (be honest — restructuring / cost reduction / strategic shift / role elimination): [paste]
- Impacted roster (roles, tenure, performance, manager): [paste]
- Severance package details (weeks of pay, benefits continuation, equity treatment, references): [paste]
- Day-of logistics window: [paste]
- Remaining team context: [paste]
- Legal review status: [paste — confirmed by counsel]

Phase 1 — Confirm legal review.
- Has counsel reviewed the impacted list and reasons?
- Has each impacted person's protected class status been considered (WARN compliance, adverse impact)?
- Are the severance terms locked?
If any answer is no, STOP. Get legal sign-off first.

Phase 2 — Draft the manager notification script (15 min, structured).
- Opening (60 sec): "I have hard news. As you've heard / not heard, we've made the decision to eliminate your role. This is effective today. This is not about your performance."
- Reason (60 sec): the honest business reason — no PR-speak
- Severance (3 min): what they're getting (weeks, benefits, equity, references, LinkedIn rec, tooling for job search)
- Logistics (3 min): last day, equipment return, COBRA, when comp lands, who they can reach with questions
- Q&A (5 min): be present for whatever comes
- Close (2 min): thank you for [specific contributions], wish them well

Phase 3 — Per-impacted-employee message (written).
- A personalized note (NOT a template) referencing their specific contributions
- Severance + benefits summary in writing
- Job-search support offer (references, intros, networking)
- HR + manager contact info for questions

Phase 4 — Remaining-team comms (the day after, NOT same day).
- All-hands script: what happened, why, what's next
- Honest framing — don't pretend the layoff didn't happen
- Specific commitment about future (no layoff doesn't return is a promise you can't keep — be careful)
- 1:1 talking points for every remaining manager: how to respond to "am I next?", how to address survivor's guilt, how to re-engage the team

Phase 5 — Day-of logistics.
- Comm schedule (impacted notifications block + all-hands)
- Equipment / access offboarding timeline (immediate after notification, but with dignity — don't lock out mid-meeting)
- Slack / email comms shutdown sequence
- HR support availability for impacted employees
