Phase 6 — Output.
- Manager script (printable, rehearsable)
- Per-employee written package (one folder per person, ready to hand off)
- Day-after all-hands deck + script
- Manager talking-points doc for remaining-team 1:1s
- A 30-day follow-up plan for impacted alumni (don't ghost them — keep relationships warm)

Feedback signal:
- Track impacted alumni outcomes (where they land, NPS of how the layoff was handled)
- Remaining team engagement (eNPS, attrition) over 90 days
- Manager confidence post-layoff — refine scripts if managers report struggling

Quality bar:
- NEVER hide the reason — people see through PR-speak immediately
- NEVER do layoffs over Slack / email if you can avoid it — humans deserve a real conversation
- Severance generosity is a long-term reputation investment — be at the top of market if you can
- Treat impacted employees like alumni who'll be hired back — many will be

playbooks.name: Write a promotion packet for an engineer
playbooks.description: Write a promotion packet from accomplishments + impact + leveling rubric. Get a structured case + 30/60/90 development plan.
steps: Draft each rubric area with evidence
Output the packet + a script for advocacy
playbooks.prompt:
Write a promotion packet for one of my engineers (or any role with a leveling rubric).

Inputs:
- Person's name + current level + target level: [paste]
- Leveling rubric for the next level (paste the rubric or link): [paste]
- Their accomplishments over the last 6-12 months (projects, outcomes, scope, impact): [paste]
- Peer feedback collected: [paste]
- My 1:1 notes + their growth trajectory: [paste]
- Calibration context (your company's promo bar, expected hit rate): [paste]

Phase 1 — Map accomplishments to the next-level rubric.
- For each rubric dimension (scope, execution, leadership, craft, collaboration, impact, etc.): pull the relevant evidence
- Mark dimensions with strong evidence (3+ examples) vs thin (1-2)
- Mark dimensions with NO evidence — these are the gaps to address before submitting

Phase 2 — Draft each rubric area.
Use the "Person, Verb, Task, Impact" structure for each example:
- Person: [name]
- Verb: led / designed / shipped / mentored / etc.
- Task: the specific thing they did
- Impact: the measurable outcome (latency improvement, revenue, team capacity unlocked, etc.)

Aim for 2-3 strong examples per dimension. Quality > quantity.

Phase 3 — Surface gaps.
- Dimensions where they don't yet have evidence — be honest
- A 30-60-90 development plan to fill those gaps before next cycle
- Stretch projects available now

Phase 4 — Calibration check.
- Will this packet hold up against the committee's bar?
- Comparable promotions at your company in the last 12 months — does this person look stronger?
- Any honest concerns (scope is right, but impact is thin? leadership shown, but only with peers, not cross-functionally?)

Phase 5 — Manager advocacy script.
- 3-sentence intro for the committee
- 3 strongest stories to lead with
- Pre-empt the likely objections with a one-line response each
- Specific recommendations from the peer feedback

Phase 6 — Output.
- The packet (markdown, formatted for the committee's template)
- A "still working on" section that's honest about gaps
- Manager advocacy script
- A self-reflection version for the candidate (different framing)

Feedback signal:
- Committee feedback: which dimensions landed vs which raised questions
- If denied: what specifically was the gap? Build the development plan around it.
- For future packets: which evidence types win (technical leadership? cross-functional impact? mentorship?)

Quality bar:
- NEVER submit a packet with no evidence on a key dimension — the gap shows
- NEVER submit if you don't believe — that's a bad bet on their year
- Use their words in peer quotes — committee can smell paraphrased praise
- If they're not ready, be honest with THEM first — submitting a weak packet damages trust

playbooks.name: Review an NDA with redlines
playbooks.description: Review an NDA against your playbook. Get redlines for term, residual, jurisdiction, and risky clauses.
playbooks.prompt:
Review this NDA and propose redlines against my playbook.

Inputs:
- Counterparty NDA (paste full text): [paste]
- My role (sender / recipient / mutual): [paste]
- My playbook (standard positions on key clauses) — if none: use the conservative founder/consultant defaults
- Risk tolerance (we lose this deal if they don't accept terms? or hold the line?): [paste]
- Jurisdiction preferences: [paste]

Phase 1 — Confirm scope.
- Mutual vs one-way (huge difference — flag immediately)
- What confidential info is in scope
- Permitted uses (narrow = good for recipient, broad = good for sender)
- Term (how long the obligation lasts)

Phase 2 — Compare to playbook / defaults.
Standard positions:
- Term: 2-3 years typical, 5 years max for trade secrets
- Definition of confidential info: must be marked or reasonably identifiable
- Residual clause: usually present — but watch the scope (people's heads vs documents)
- Permitted disclosures: lawyers, accountants, advisors with same NDA obligation
- Return / destruction of materials: clear deadline
- Remedies: injunctive relief is standard; specific performance is aggressive
- Jurisdiction: home jurisdiction strongly preferred
- Governing law: matches jurisdiction
- Survival: standard for IP / trade secret clauses

Phase 3 — Surface risky clauses.
- Non-compete dressed up as NDA (red flag)
- Indemnification clauses (NDAs shouldn't have these usually)
- Liquidated damages (uncommon; risk-shifting)
- "Confidential information" defined too broadly (everything we exchange)
- Term > 5 years (unusual outside trade secrets)
- Sub-disclosure restrictions that block normal advisory consultations
- Exclusive jurisdiction in a foreign court

Phase 4 — Draft redlines + fallback positions.
For each risky clause:
- The proposed redline (specific replacement text)
- The reasoning (one sentence)
- A fallback if they push back (next-best position)
- A "deal-breaker?" tag (would you walk?)

Phase 5 — Output.
- A redlined version of the NDA (track changes style)
- A cover note explaining the changes (1 page, plain English)
- A negotiation script for the call (anticipated objections + responses)
- A "minimum acceptable terms" summary

Feedback signal:
- Patterns in redlines accepted vs rejected — refine playbook
- Counterparties that consistently push back on the same clause — surface as systemic
- Time-to-signature pre vs post redlining — calibrate aggressiveness

Quality bar:
- This is contract analysis, NOT legal advice — recommend counsel for non-routine deals
- Be precise about what's red-flagged vs nice-to-have
- Default to mutual when ambiguous — protects you on both sides
- If a clause has unfamiliar language, surface it rather than guess

playbooks.name: Generate ToS + Privacy Policy
playbooks.description: Generate ToS + Privacy Policy for an app or SaaS. Get jurisdiction-aware drafts with cookie + DPA mappings.
playbooks.prompt:
Generate ToS + Privacy Policy for my product. This is a starting draft, NOT a substitute for counsel.

Inputs:
- Product description + URL: [paste]
- User type: [B2B / B2C / both]
- Data collected (auth, PII, payment, usage analytics, files, etc.): [list]
- Third-party processors (Stripe, Segment, OpenAI, Auth0, etc.): [list]
- Target jurisdictions (US, EU, UK, CA, AU, BR, etc.): [list]
- Age restrictions (under 13 — COPPA; under 16 — GDPR; over 18): [paste]
- Refund / cancellation policy: [paste]
- Account-deletion process: [paste]

Phase 1 — Product + data inventory.
- Categorize data: identifiers / commercial / biometric / internet activity / geolocation / sensory / professional / education / inferences
- Map data to source (signup form, payment, analytics, integrations)
- Map data to retention period
- Map data to sharing (sub-processors, advertisers, affiliates)

Phase 2 — ToS draft sections.
1. Acceptance + age requirements
2. Account + responsibilities
3. License grant + IP ownership (yours vs theirs)
4. Acceptable use + prohibited conduct
5. Payment + auto-renewal + refunds
6. Termination (for cause / convenience)
7. Disclaimers + limitation of liability (capped if possible)
8. Indemnification
9. Dispute resolution (arbitration? jurisdiction?)
10. Changes to ToS + notice
11. Governing law + jurisdiction

Phase 3 — Privacy Policy sections.
1. What data we collect (per category)
2. How we collect it (sources)
3. Why we collect it (purposes)
4. Who we share it with (sub-processors + reason)
5. Where it's stored (country) + transfers
6. Retention periods
7. Your rights (access, deletion, portability, correction, opt-out) — per jurisdiction
8. Cookies + tracking technologies (link to Cookie Policy)
9. Children's data
10. International transfers + safeguards (SCCs)
11. Data breach notification
12. Contact for privacy requests (DPO if EU)

Phase 4 — Cookie Policy.
- Cookies in use (per category: essential, analytics, advertising, functional)
- Consent mechanism reference (banner)
- Opt-out path
- Lifetime per cookie type

Phase 5 — Sub-processor + DPA mapping.
- Sub-processor list (vendor, what data, where)
- Identify which require a DPA (any processor of EU/UK personal data)
- Identify which have SCCs in place

Phase 6 — Output.
- ToS draft (markdown)
- Privacy Policy draft (markdown)
- Cookie Policy draft (markdown)
- Sub-processor registry
- A "send to counsel for review" checklist
- An update cadence reminder (annual + on material product change)

Feedback signal:
- Compliance gaps surfaced by counsel review — feed into next draft
- User complaints / DSARs — surface clauses that confuse users
- Regulatory updates that require revisions (e.g., new state privacy laws)

Quality bar:
- This is a DRAFT — every business should have counsel review before publishing
- NEVER copy-paste from a competitor — that creates IP + accuracy risks
- Update annually + on material change (new processor, new data type, new jurisdiction)
- Plain language wins — courts and regulators prefer it; users do too

playbooks.name: Run a SOC 2 Type 1 readiness audit
playbooks.description: Run a SOC 2 Type 1 readiness audit. Get a controls map, evidence checklist, gap remediation plan, and 6-12 week timeline.
playbooks.prompt:
Run a SOC 2 Type 1 readiness audit.

Inputs:
- Company + product description: [paste]
- Scope: [Security only — most common — or Security + Availability + Confidentiality]
- Cloud + infra stack (AWS / GCP / Azure / which services): [paste]
- HRIS + identity provider: [paste]
- Engineering team size + customer count: [paste]
- Vanta / Drata / Secureframe in place? [paste]
- Target audit date: [paste]

Phase 1 — Confirm scope.
- Trust Services Criteria (TSC) included
- System boundaries (what's IN scope, what's OUT)
- Subservice organizations (carve-out or inclusive)
- Period covered (point-in-time for Type 1; period for Type 2)

Phase 2 — Map current controls to TSC.
For each Common Criteria (CC1-CC9) and any included TSC:
- The relevant control statement (e.g., "logical access requires unique IDs and MFA")
- Current state (implemented / partial / missing)
- Evidence location (system, doc, screenshot)
- Owner

Phase 3 — Identify gaps.
- Controls with no evidence
- Controls implemented but undocumented
- Documentation outdated or inconsistent
- Coverage gaps (some services have access controls, others don't)

Phase 4 — Remediation plan.
For each gap:
- The smallest action that closes it
- Owner + deadline
- Effort estimate (S / M / L)
- Risk if not closed before audit

Phase 5 — Critical "table stakes" controls (review explicitly).
- MFA on all admin accounts + production access
- SSO + access reviews (quarterly)
- Background checks on new hires
- Annual security training + acknowledgment
- Vulnerability scanning + patching cadence
- Incident response plan (with last tabletop)
- Change management (PR review + approval requirements)
- Backup + recovery testing
- Vendor / sub-processor risk assessment
- Data classification + handling

Phase 6 — Auditor-ready package.
- Control matrix (TSC → control → evidence → owner)
- Policy library (info sec, AUP, change mgmt, IR, BCP, vendor mgmt)
- Procedure docs (access provisioning, deprovisioning, etc.)
- Sample evidence per control (access review screenshot, etc.)
- A "what auditor will ask" Q&A
- 6-12 week countdown checklist

Phase 7 — Output.
- Controls + evidence matrix (CSV)
- Gap remediation plan + owners + deadlines (Notion / sheet)
- Policy library outline (which docs you need)
- A weekly cadence for the readiness sprint

Feedback signal (during the audit):
- Findings vs predicted gaps — refine the self-audit
- Auditor questions that surprised you — bake into next year's scope
- Time to remediate vs estimate — calibrate next year's planning

Quality bar:
- This is readiness, NOT audit certification — use a real auditor (CPA-licensed)
- NEVER fake evidence — auditors find out and you fail
- Vanta / Drata / Secureframe accelerate evidence collection 5-10x — use them
- The Type 1 is the start. Type 2 (3-12 months of evidence) is where you actually prove the controls operate

playbooks.name: Run a patent prior-art search
playbooks.description: Run a patent prior-art search. Get a ranked list of similar art, claim chart, and a patentability verdict.
steps: Search USPTO + Google Patents + WIPO + non-patent lit
playbooks.prompt:
Run a prior-art search for a patentable invention.

Inputs:
- Invention description (plain English): [paste]
- Field of use + technical domain: [paste]
- Claimed novel elements (in your view): [paste]
- Existing products / patents you know are close: [paste]
- Purpose of search (filing / freedom-to-operate / invalidity / competitive landscape): [paste]
- Geographic scope (US-only / EP / international): [paste]
- Risk tolerance (preliminary / publication-quality): [paste]

Phase 1 — Describe the invention precisely.
- Restate in 3 sentences: what it does, how it works, why it's different
- List 3-5 key technical elements (algorithm, hardware feature, process step)
- List likely IPC / CPC classification codes
- List 10-15 search keywords + synonyms

Phase 2 — Extract searchable claim elements.
For each claim element:
- Functional description (what it does)
- Structural description (how it's built)
- Synonyms an examiner / opposing party might use

Phase 3 — Search the patent corpus.
For each database (USPTO, Google Patents, Espacenet, WIPO PatentScope, J-PlatPat):
- Run claim-element keyword combinations
- Apply CPC class filters
- Date filter (publications before priority date or filing target)
- Capture top 30 hits per database

Phase 4 — Search non-patent literature.
- Google Scholar / arXiv / IEEE Xplore for academic papers
- GitHub for open-source implementations
- ProductHunt / Crunchbase for commercial product disclosures
- Conference proceedings in the field
- Blog posts / company whitepapers

Phase 5 — Rank results by similarity.
For each hit, score:
- Technical similarity to claim elements (1-5 per element)
- Publication date relative to your priority date
- Patent status (active / expired / withdrawn / never granted)
- Geographic coverage
- Citation count (downstream patents that cited it)

Top 10-15 most relevant: enter the claim chart.

Phase 6 — Claim chart per top reference.
- Side-by-side: your claim element vs the prior art element
- Per element: identical / similar / different / not disclosed
- Combined: does this single reference anticipate or render obvious?

Phase 7 — Patentability verdict.
- Anticipation (single reference shows every claim element): YES / NO with reasoning
- Obviousness (combination of references makes it obvious): YES / NO with reasoning
- Suggested narrowing of claims to navigate the prior art
- Risk score (high / medium / low) on filing as-is

Phase 8 — Output.
- Prior-art database (CSV) of all hits with scores
- Claim chart (top 10-15 references)
- Patentability brief (3-5 pages)
- Strategy memo: file as-is / narrow / abandon / consider provisional

Feedback signal:
- USPTO examiner's office action vs your predicted prior art — calibrate next search
- References you missed that the examiner found — surface to next search query refinement
- Claims that survived rejection vs those that didn't — feed into claim drafting

Quality bar:
- This is research, NOT legal advice — engage a patent attorney for filing
- NEVER use only one database — examiners search multiple
- Non-patent literature (papers, code, products) is increasingly important — don't skip it
- Searches >2 years old need refresh — prior art emerges constantly

playbooks.name: Draft a high-level system design doc
playbooks.description: Draft an HLD for a distributed system. Get components, data flow, capacity estimates, and trade-off analysis.
playbooks.prompt:
Draft a high-level system design document (HLD) for a new system.

Inputs:
- Problem statement (1-2 paragraphs): [paste]
- Functional requirements (5-10 bullets): [paste]
- Non-functional requirements (scale, latency, consistency, availability): [paste]
- Constraints (existing stack, team skills, budget, deadline): [paste]
- Known alternatives we're rejecting + why: [paste]
- Audience for the doc (peer review / staff+ review / external): [paste]

Phase 1 — Confirm requirements and scope.
- Restate the problem in your own words
- List the 5 most important requirements + 2-3 nice-to-haves
- Out-of-scope explicitly stated
- Wait for me to confirm

Phase 2 — Enumerate components + data flow.
- High-level component diagram (clients, gateway, services, queues, datastores, caches)
- Data flow: end-to-end for the primary use case (with sequence)
- Storage decisions: which data lives where + why (consistency model, partitioning, TTL)
- Integration points (external APIs, internal services)

Phase 3 — Capacity + cost estimates.
- Read/write QPS at launch + at 12 months
- Storage growth rate + retention policy
- Bandwidth + egress estimates
- Per-component cost (rough): compute, storage, DB, network
- Total monthly run cost at scale

Phase 4 — Trade-off analysis (2-3 architectures).
For each candidate:
- Strengths (what makes it the right choice for some scenario)
- Weaknesses
- Performance characteristics
- Operational burden
- Cost
- Recommendation: which one + why

Phase 5 — Failure modes + mitigation.
- Per component: what happens when it fails
- Blast radius (1 user / 1 region / global)
- Mitigation (replication, retries, circuit breakers, fallback)
- Disaster recovery + backup strategy
- Observability hooks (metrics, logs, traces — what's instrumented)

Phase 6 — Security + privacy.
- AuthN / AuthZ model
- Data classification (PII, PCI, PHI)
- Encryption in transit + at rest
- Audit logging
- Threat model (3-5 likely attacks + defenses)

Phase 7 — Migration / rollout.
- Backward compatibility (if replacing existing)
- Migration steps + dual-write strategy
- Rollback plan
- Phased rollout (% traffic, canary, regions)

Phase 8 — Output.
- HLD doc (markdown, structured for design review)
- A 1-page TL;DR for execs
- ADR stubs for the 3-5 biggest decisions (context, decision, consequences)
- A list of open questions + owners

Feedback signal:
- Design review comments — surface what wasn't clear or wasn't right
- Implementation deltas from the HLD — capture as "what we learned"
- Capacity / cost actual vs estimate — calibrate next HLD

Quality bar:
- NEVER skip capacity numbers — "fast" isn't a requirement
- NEVER write "we'll figure it out later" — surface the open question as TODO
- The HLD's audience matters — exec doc is different from engineer review
- One decision per ADR — don't pile up trade-offs in one doc

playbooks.name: Write an Architecture Decision Record
playbooks.description: Write an ADR (Architecture Decision Record). Get context, decision, alternatives considered, and consequences.
playbooks.prompt:
Write an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) for a technical decision.

Inputs:
- The decision (one sentence): [paste — e.g. "use Postgres + pgvector instead of a dedicated vector DB"]
- Date + ADR number: [paste]
- Author + reviewers: [paste]
- Related design doc or PR (if any): [paste link]
- Background context (5-10 min of conversation that led to this): [paste]

Phase 1 — Title + metadata.
- Title: short noun phrase, decision-focused (e.g., "Use Postgres + pgvector for embeddings")
- Status: [proposed / accepted / deprecated / superseded]
- Date
- Deciders

Phase 2 — Context (the forces in play).
- The problem being solved
- The constraints (skill, budget, deadline, scale, ops capacity)
- The alternatives that were considered (briefly — detail comes later)
- Why a decision is needed now

Phase 3 — Decision.
- The specific choice made
- The reasoning in 3-5 sentences
- The trade-offs accepted

Phase 4 — Alternatives considered (deeper).
For each (typically 2-3):
- What it is
- Why it was attractive
- Why it was rejected (concrete reason — not "felt wrong")

Phase 5 — Consequences.
- Positive consequences (what gets easier)
- Negative consequences (what gets harder)
- Neutral consequences (what changes but not better/worse)
- Risks introduced + mitigation
- What we'd need to see to reverse this decision

Phase 6 — Output.
- ADR markdown file (named like `adr-0042-use-pgvector.md`)
- Save to `docs/adrs/` in the repo
- Update the ADR index (table of contents)
- Cross-reference from the related design doc if applicable

Feedback signal:
- ADRs reversed within 12 months — examine what we missed
- Decisions made without an ADR that bit us later — surface as a process gap
- ADRs nobody re-reads — they were written for compliance, not value

Quality bar:
- ADRs are short — 1-2 pages, not 10
- Use plain language — these are for future-you and new hires
- Write at decision time, not retrospectively
- Mark superseded ADRs explicitly — never delete them

playbooks.name: Design a database schema with ER diagram
playbooks.description: Design a relational database schema from app requirements. Get tables, FKs, indexes, an ER diagram, and migration DDL.
playbooks.prompt:
Design a relational database schema for this application.

Inputs:
- Application description + key user flows: [paste]
- Expected scale (rows in 12 months for each entity type): [paste]
- Read / write ratio per entity: [paste]
- Database engine: [Postgres / MySQL / SQLite / etc.]
- Naming conventions (snake_case, plural tables, etc.): [paste]
- Constraints we must support (multi-tenancy, soft delete, audit log, GDPR): [paste]

Phase 1 — Entity inventory.
- List every entity (User, Account, Order, Subscription, etc.)
- For each: attributes (with types), uniqueness rules
- Mark each as core (load-bearing) vs supporting

Phase 2 — Relationships.
- For each entity pair: relationship type (1:1, 1:N, M:N) + cardinality
- Identify ownership (which side cascades on delete)
- Identify nullable vs required associations

Phase 3 — Normalize to 3NF.
- No repeating groups
- No partial dependencies
- No transitive dependencies
- Flag any intentional denormalization (and why)

Phase 4 — Add keys + constraints.
- Primary keys (UUID vs serial — pick + justify)
- Foreign keys with cascade behavior
- Unique constraints
- Check constraints (enum-like fields, value ranges)
- NOT NULL where required

Phase 5 — Index strategy.
- Per-query index list (start with the top 10 queries)
- Compound indexes for common WHERE + ORDER BY patterns
- Partial indexes for filtered queries (e.g., active rows only)
- DON'T over-index — every index slows writes

Phase 6 — Denormalization (where justified).
- Read-heavy paths (e.g., user feed, leaderboards): consider materialized views or denormalized columns
- Trade-offs: write amplification, consistency model, cache invalidation

Phase 7 — Migration + ops considerations.
- Soft delete strategy (deleted_at column? separate archive table?)
- Audit log (separate table? built into rows?)
- Multi-tenancy (single DB with tenant_id? schema-per-tenant? DB-per-tenant?)
- GDPR deletion (cascade strategy + sub-processor sync)

Phase 8 — Output.
- ER diagram (Mermaid syntax)
- Full DDL (CREATE TABLE statements)
- Migration script (idempotent, with rollback)
- A "top 10 queries" plan + the indexes that support them
- A migration playbook (zero-downtime steps if rebuilding)

Feedback signal:
- Query plans after launch — surface missing or unused indexes
- N+1 patterns surfaced by APM — design opportunities for denormalization
- Schema drift from app code — surface as a process issue

Quality bar:
- NEVER skip foreign keys to "save performance" — fix performance other ways
- NEVER use enum types for fast-changing values — separate lookup table
- Naming consistency matters more than naming taste
- Index reads carefully — measure before adding, not after

playbooks.name: Score an RFP response against criteria
playbooks.description: Score vendor RFP responses against a weighted rubric. Get a side-by-side matrix, flagged risks, and a recommendation.
playbooks.prompt:
Score RFP responses against my evaluation criteria.

Inputs:
- RFP responses (one per vendor, full text): [paste or path]
- Evaluation rubric + weights: [paste — e.g., functionality 30%, security 25%, price 20%, vendor stability 15%, support 10%]
- My must-have requirements (binary pass/fail): [paste]
- Budget + procurement constraints (annual cap, payment terms): [paste]
- Integration / migration requirements: [paste]
- Anti-vendor signals (companies to avoid + why): [paste]

Phase 1 — Confirm the rubric and binary gates.
- Restate weights — do they sum to 100?
- List must-have requirements that disqualify a vendor if missing
- Any tied weights — break with a tiebreaker rule

Phase 2 — Score each vendor section-by-section.
Per response, per rubric section:
- Score 1-10 with reasoning (1 sentence)
- Evidence cited from the response
- Score adjusted for clarity / specificity (vague answers downweighted)
- A "verify with reference call" tag where confidence is low

Phase 3 — Flag non-standard or risky clauses.
- Pricing: hidden fees, auto-renewal traps, price-increase ceilings
- Security: claims without certifications, vague data handling
- SLA: weak commitments, unreasonable cure periods
- Termination: unfavorable terms, long notice periods
- Data: sub-processors not disclosed, no DPA willingness

Phase 4 — Build the comparison matrix.
- Side-by-side per vendor per rubric section
- Total weighted score
- Pass/fail on must-haves
- TCO (total cost of ownership) over 3 years including ramp + onboarding

Phase 5 — Recommend a vendor.
- Recommended pick with reasoning
- Runner-up (and why not #1)
- Vendors to reject (with brief rationale)
- Negotiation levers per vendor (where they're weakest)

Phase 6 — Output.
- Scoring matrix (CSV)
- A 2-page recommendation memo
- A negotiation prep doc with each vendor's pricing flexibility, missing requirements, and reference questions
- A "questions to ask references" list per finalist

Feedback signal (after the contract is signed):
- Vendor performance vs your scoring — calibrate next RFP
- Surprises during implementation — add to rubric for next round
- Negotiation results — what gave way + what didn't (refine leverage)

Quality bar:
- NEVER score based on vendor charisma — only on the response evidence
- Cite the section / page for every score
- Reference calls matter more than the response — schedule them for the top 2
- If two vendors tie, the better-fit POC wins (not the cheaper one)

playbooks.name: Audit cloud spend and recommend cuts
playbooks.description: Audit cloud spend across AWS/GCP/Azure + AI APIs. Get idle resources, oversized instances, and a ranked cut list.
playbooks.prompt:
Audit cloud spend and recommend the highest-ROI cuts.

Inputs:
- Cloud providers + access (AWS / GCP / Azure billing export, Cost Explorer access): [paste]
- AI API providers (OpenAI / Anthropic / Bedrock / etc.) billing access: [paste]
- Last 90 days monthly spend (by service / by tag if available): [paste]
- Total monthly cloud spend: [paste]
- Engineering team size + capacity for remediation: [paste]
- Constraints (workloads we can't touch, compliance, customer SLAs): [paste]

Phase 1 — Pull spend + trend.
- Total spend last 90 days, monthly trend
- Top 10 services by spend
- Top 10 cost centers (tags / accounts / projects)
- Spend growth rate (per service, per month)
- Anomalies (spikes >20% MoM in any line item)

Phase 2 — Identify idle resources.
- EC2 / Compute Engine: low CPU (<10%) for 14+ days
- Load balancers / NAT gateways without traffic
- Unattached EBS / persistent disks
- Old snapshots beyond retention policy
- RDS / Cloud SQL with zero connections
- Unused Elastic IPs
- Forgotten dev / staging environments

Phase 3 — Identify oversized resources.
- Instances with CPU < 30% sustained — rightsize candidates
- RDS instances with low IOPS — downgrade
- Over-provisioned ECS / GKE capacity
- DynamoDB / Bigtable with low utilization
- Memory allocations far above actual usage

Phase 4 — Audit reserved capacity + savings plans.
- Coverage % of compute by reservations / savings plans
- Expiring reservations in the next 60 days
- Underutilized reservations (committed but not running)
- Opportunity to commit to additional savings plans

Phase 5 — Audit AI / API spend.
- Spend per provider over the last 90 days
- Spend per model (GPT-4 vs Claude vs GPT-3.5)
- Top usage by feature / endpoint
- Cache hit rate (if applicable)
- Tokens per request — opportunities for prompt optimization
- Cheaper-model fallback opportunities

Phase 6 — Audit egress + bandwidth.
- Top egress destinations
- Cross-region transfer (often expensive and avoidable)
- CDN coverage gaps

Phase 7 — Rank cuts by ROI.
For each opportunity:
- Estimated monthly savings ($ amount)
- Effort to remediate (S / M / L)
- Risk (zero / low / medium / high)
- Reversibility
- Owner

Top 10 by ROI become the action list.

Phase 8 — Output.
- Audit report (1-page TL;DR + 5-page detail)
- Ranked cut list (CSV with savings + effort + owner)
- Tagging hygiene recommendations (so next audit is easier)
- A monthly tracking dashboard spec
- A "what NOT to cut" list (where saving $X costs you $10X in customer churn)

Feedback signal:
- Realized savings vs predicted — calibrate the next audit
- Cuts that caused incidents — surface and avoid pattern in future
- Spend trend post-audit — is it sticking or creeping back up?

Quality bar:
- NEVER cut without a rollback plan — savings aren't worth a customer-facing outage
- Tag hygiene is the long-term lever — fix tags now and every audit gets faster
- AI API spend is the fastest-growing line item — instrument it properly
- Don't optimize for one-time savings if it kills a savings plan you'll need later

playbooks.name: Learn anything from zero to master
playbooks.description: Run an ultralearning sprint on any skill from zero to mastery. Get a metalearning memo, curriculum, schedule, drills, and a project test.
steps: Phase 1 — Metalearning week (research how to learn it)
Phase 2 — Define the success project + sub-skills
Phase 4 — Schedule the focus blocks + drill prescriptions
Phase 5 — Execute with weekly retrospective + retention layer
Phase 6 — Ship the project + lock in retention
playbooks.prompt:
You're my ultralearning coach for a zero-to-mastery sprint on a single skill. Use Scott H. Young's 9 Ultralearning principles (Metalearning, Focus, Directness, Drill, Retrieval, Feedback, Retention, Intuition, Experimentation), Anders Ericsson's deliberate practice, Tim Ferriss's DiSSS (Deconstruction, Selection, Sequencing, Stakes), and Josh Kaufman's first-20-hours framing where they fit. Hold the line on rigor.

Inputs:
- The skill / topic I want to learn (be specific — "conversational Spanish for travel" not just "Spanish"): [paste]
- My current level (true beginner / hobbyist / intermediate): [paste]
- What "mastery" means TO ME (a concrete deliverable, capability, or test I can pass): [paste]
- Time budget per week (be honest): [paste hours]
- Total sprint duration: [paste — e.g. 3 months, 6 months, 1 year]
- Why I want to learn this (motivation matters for follow-through): [paste]
- Constraints (no in-person tutor / no $X budget / public commitment yes-no): [paste]
- My known weak spots from prior learning attempts: [paste]

Phase 1 — Metalearning (Principle 1). Week 1 only — DO NOT START LEARNING YET.
This is the highest-ROI week of the whole sprint.
- Pull syllabi from the top 3 university or master-level programs on this skill
- Identify 3-5 practitioners at the level I want; read what they wrote about their own learning paths
- Identify the canonical resources (books, courses, mentors, communities, datasets, instruments)
- Map the skill tree: prerequisites + sub-skills + how they compose
- Identify the 20% of sub-skills that produce 80% of the outcome (Pareto — Ferriss "Selection")
- Identify common dead ends (where novices waste months)
- Estimate hours needed at the level I'm targeting

Output of this phase: a "How to learn X" memo (3-5 pages) saved to my workspace. Wait for me to read it before continuing to Phase 2.

Phase 2 — Define the success project (Directness + Stakes).
- The SINGLE deliverable that proves mastery (a shipped app, a 5K race time, a translated essay, a tournament rating, a publishable paper, a sold first commission)
- The 3-5 sub-skills production of that deliverable demands
- Sub-skills ranked by (current ability gap × project impact)
- A public commitment OR external evaluator (Ferriss "Stakes" — accountability matters)

Phase 3 — Build the curriculum (Directness, Principle 3 — the load-bearing principle).
For each sub-skill, prescribe:
- The DIRECT practice activity (the actual skill in its actual context — NOT a proxy like "watch lectures")
- The drill (Principle 4): the smallest sub-component to attack first; what specifically gets isolated and repeated
- The retrieval activity (Principle 5): how I'll test myself rather than re-read / re-watch
- The feedback source (Principle 6): who or what tells me I'm wrong — ranked from highest signal (expert critique, automated test, race time) to lowest (self-judgment)
- Reject any resource adjacent but not direct (Anki cards on Spanish grammar are not Spanish conversation practice — both have a place, but don't confuse them)

The project starts in week 2, not after the curriculum is "done." Direct work compounds.

Phase 4 — Schedule the sprint (Focus, Principle 2).
- Weekly deep-focus blocks (named on the calendar, phone in the other room, single-task)
- Daily drill prescription (15-30 min on the highest-ROI weak spot)
- Weekly project work session (2-4 hours uninterrupted)
- Weekly feedback session (call with mentor, peer review, test run)
- A retention layer: spaced-repetition deck built FROM drill sessions (Principle 7) — not from textbook bullets
- One "rest day" per week (recovery is part of the protocol)

Phase 5 — Execute with weekly retrospective (a loop, every Sunday).
- Skills practiced this week + adherence rate (% of planned blocks completed)
- Drills attempted + accuracy / speed delta
- Project progress + blockers
- Feedback received + what specifically to change next week
- One thing to STOP, one to START, one to KEEP
- Mid-week energy + injury / overload check (if applicable)

Phase 6 — Intuition + Experimentation (Principles 8 + 9). Second half of sprint.
Once basics feel automatic:
- Teach the skill to someone (Feynman technique — verifies mastery faster than self-test)
- Try unconventional approaches: combine two sub-skills, attempt the "weird" project, copy a master then deviate
- Read advanced material with the curiosity of a practitioner, not the anxiety of a beginner
- Compete or perform in public — high-stakes practice compresses learning

Phase 7 — Ship the project (sprint end).
- Deliver the success project under realistic conditions
- Get external evaluation (NOT self-grade)
- Honest assessment: did I reach my definition of mastery?
- If not: gap analysis + extended sprint OR accept current level with grace
- Public retrospective post (optional but accelerates the next sprint)

Phase 8 — Retention (Principle 7). Ongoing after sprint.
- Spaced-repetition schedule for the cards built during sprint
- Weekly minimum maintenance practice
- A stretch project queued to keep applying the skill
- 30 / 90 / 180-day retention checks

Output:
- The "How to learn X" metalearning memo (PDF)
- A full sprint curriculum doc (Notion + PDF)
- Weekly schedule template (.ics file) with time-blocked focus sessions
- Per-sub-skill drill prescription card
- A ranked feedback-source list (free → paid, low → high signal)
- Spaced-repetition seed deck (CSV ready for Anki)
- Sunday review template
- Project brief + success criteria + external evaluator commitment
- A "what to do if I fall off the wagon for a week" recovery script

Feedback signal (the sprint's own learning loop):
- Weekly adherence to focus blocks → calibrates whether the time budget is realistic
- Drill accuracy improvement → surfaces if the drills are right size (too easy or too hard kills motivation)
- Project artifact quality at midpoint vs end → surfaces curriculum gaps
- External evaluation gap from self-assessment → calibrates honest self-judgment
- Retention check at 30 / 90 / 180 days → surfaces what stuck vs what evaporated
- After the sprint: what worked + what wasted weeks → input to the next ultralearning sprint

Quality bar:
- NEVER skip Phase 1 metalearning week — the highest ROI is here, and skipping is the #1 reason sprints fail
- NEVER substitute consumption for direct practice — reading about Spanish is not speaking Spanish
- NEVER drill what you're already good at to feel competent — drill the painful weak spot (Principle 4)
- NEVER re-read or re-watch when you could retrieve — testing beats reviewing every time (Principle 5)
- Get the highest-signal feedback you can afford — bad or slow feedback wastes weeks (Principle 6)
- Embrace failure as data — comfortable practice doesn't produce mastery
- Public commitment + external evaluator beats motivation — design the system, don't rely on willpower
- Pick a clear end date and ship the project — open-ended learning rarely concludes
- This works for: languages, programming, music, sport, math, design, writing, sales, painting, public speaking, chess, anything with a feedback signal
- This does NOT work for: skills with no clear feedback (taste, charisma, intuition-only fields) — for those, mentorship beats self-directed sprints

playbooks.name: Scan for wheel-strategy candidates
playbooks.description: Scan equity universe for cash-secured-put candidates. Get a wheel-fit-scored shortlist with IV rank, delta, and earnings dates.
steps: Filter universe by liquidity + market cap
Score by IV rank + delta + earnings risk
Output strikes + sizing per portfolio rules
playbooks.prompt:
Scan for wheel-strategy candidates (cash-secured puts → assignment → covered calls).

Inputs:
- Account size + max cash per put position: [paste]
- Risk tolerance (delta target — 0.30 conservative / 0.15-0.20 aggressive): [paste]
- Sectors to include / exclude: [paste]
- Minimum stock price + max stock price (for assignment risk): [paste]
- Days to expiration target: [default 30-45 DTE]
- Tax account type (taxable / IRA / Roth): [paste — drives strategy]
- Existing positions + open Greeks: [paste]

Phase 1 — Universe filter.
- Equities with >500K avg daily volume + tight bid-ask
- Market cap > $2B (avoid micro/small-cap assignment risk)
- Optionable with weekly or monthly chains
- Drop names with earnings inside the DTE window
- Drop names with binary catalysts (FDA, merger vote, lawsuit ruling)

Phase 2 — Score each candidate.
For each stock, compute:
- IV rank (current IV vs 52-week range) — target >40%
- IV percentile — target >50%
- Implied move vs expected (skew the agent toward fair-priced premium)
- Delta target match per my risk tolerance
- Dividend ex-date conflict (avoid early assignment on covered call side)
- Wheel Fit Score 0-10 (composite)

Phase 3 — Rank top 10.
For each:
- Recommended strike + DTE + premium estimate
- Max risk (assignment cost) + breakeven
- Annualized return if not assigned
- Cost basis after assignment (would I want to own this stock?)
- A "what kills this trade" line (earnings move, sector rotation, etc.)

Phase 4 — Position sizing.
- Per-name allocation per my portfolio rules
- Total cash committed across new positions
- Aggregate Greeks impact (delta, vega, theta) on portfolio

Phase 5 — Output.
- Ranked CSV: ticker | strike | DTE | premium | max risk | annualized return | wheel fit score | notes
- A "ready to enter" subset I can paste into the broker
- A weekly tracking sheet for open positions (P&L, roll candidates, assignment risk)
- An alert list for when an open position needs action

Feedback signal:
- Per closed cycle: realized return vs expected
- Which sectors / IV rank tiers delivered best risk-adjusted returns
- Assignment rate vs IV rank tier — calibrates delta target

Quality bar:
- This is analysis, NOT financial advice
- NEVER recommend a position you wouldn't take to assignment
- NEVER sell premium against a name you don't want to own
- IRA / Roth: cash-secured only (no margin)
- Watch earnings + binary catalyst dates religiously — surprises destroy wheel strategies
- Realized return on a wheel needs at least 12 cycles to evaluate fairly

playbooks.name: Build a Greek-sized iron condor or credit spread
playbooks.description: Build a defined-risk iron condor or credit spread sized to portfolio Greeks. Get strikes, P(profit), and a roll plan.
playbooks.prompt:
Build a defined-risk iron condor or credit spread on a ticker, sized to portfolio Greeks.

Inputs:
- Ticker + my directional bias (neutral / mildly bullish / mildly bearish / volatility selling): [paste]
- Max risk per trade ($ — typically 1-3% of account): [paste]
- Current portfolio Greeks (delta, gamma, theta, vega): [paste]
- Portfolio Greek limits (e.g., max net delta, max negative vega): [paste]
- Days to expiration target: [default 30-50 DTE]
- Underlying current price + IV rank + expected move: [paste]
- Earnings or binary catalyst within DTE window: [paste yes/no + date]

Phase 1 — Confirm trade premise.
- Why is now the right time (IV rank, technical setup, vol regime)?
- What would invalidate the thesis (earnings, big news, sector flip)?
- Iron condor vs single-side credit spread — which fits the bias?
- If earnings inside DTE, STOP unless explicit earnings-play structure

Phase 2 — Fetch chain + structure candidates.
For iron condor:
- Short call strike (target ~16 delta = ~84% OTM)
- Long call strike (5-10 wider for defined risk)
- Short put strike (target ~16 delta)
- Long put strike (5-10 wider)

For single-side credit spread:
- Short strike (target ~25-30 delta for premium / ~16 for higher P(profit))
- Long strike (defined risk, typically $5 width)

Compute per candidate:
- Net credit received
- Max risk = width − credit
- Max return = credit / max risk
- Probability of profit
- Probability of touch
- Implied move vs strike distance

Phase 3 — Greek-aware sizing.
- Position delta (net of all 4 legs)
- Position vega (typically negative for credit structures)
- Position theta (positive — the payment)
- Aggregate impact on portfolio Greeks
- Reject the trade if it pushes any Greek past my limit
- Suggest contract count that fits both risk budget AND Greek limits

Phase 4 — Entry + management plan.
- Entry order type (limit at mid, not market)
- Profit target (typically close at 25-50% of max profit)
- Stop loss (typically 2x credit received, or test of short strike)
- Roll criteria (short strike tested + DTE > 21? Roll out or down)
- Final close criteria (21 DTE or 25% of max profit — whichever first)

Phase 5 — Output.
- Trade ticket (ready to paste into broker)
- 1-page trade plan (entry, targets, stops, rolls)
- Portfolio Greeks before vs after
- A "what could go wrong" risk list with the action for each

Feedback signal:
- Per closed trade: realized P&L vs expected
- Win rate vs P(profit) calibration over 20+ trades
- Greek limit breaches that needed early management — refine sizing

Quality bar:
- This is analysis, NOT financial advice
- NEVER hold defined-risk positions through earnings unless that's the explicit thesis
- NEVER widen wings to "fix" a tested side — that increases risk
- 21 DTE is the management cliff — gamma risk goes parabolic past that
- Close winners; manage losers; don't pray
- Track your win rate and average winner/loser separately — high win rate with terrible loser ratio still loses money

playbooks.name: Track smart-money crypto wallets for early signal
playbooks.description: Track Nansen-labeled smart-money wallets for early accumulation. Get token alerts with score, supporting data, and a follow/fade verdict.
playbooks.prompt:
Track smart-money wallets and surface early accumulation signals.

Inputs:
- Wallet watchlist (Nansen labels, hand-picked alpha wallets, or Lookonchain feed): [paste]
- Chains to cover (Ethereum / Solana / Base / Arbitrum / etc.): [paste]
- Token universe (top 200 by mcap / new tokens / specific sectors): [paste]
- Minimum signal threshold (number of smart wallets buying / total $ spent): [paste]
- Alert channel (Telegram / Discord / Email): [paste]
- My risk tolerance + position size limits: [paste]

Phase 1 — Detect accumulation events.
For each tracked wallet:
- New token positions opened in the last N hours
- Existing positions added to (>20% increase)
- Coordinated buying (3+ tracked wallets in same token within 24h)
- Time-of-day patterns (Asia / EU / US sessions)

Phase 2 — Cross-check supporting signals.
For each candidate token:
- LP depth + 24h volume change
- Holder count delta (organic vs concentrated)
- Bubblemaps cluster check (insider concentration risk)
- Recent contract activity (mint authority, ownership, function calls)
- Social signal (X / Telegram mentions in the last 24h)
- Recent CEX listings or pending listings

Phase 3 — Risk filter (avoid the trap).
- Honeypot check (sell-side simulation)
- Mint authority not renounced — red flag
- Top 10 holder concentration > 30% — flag insider risk
- LP not locked or unlocking soon — flag exit risk
- Token age < 7 days — flag for extra scrutiny

Phase 4 — Score each signal.
0-100 composite:
- Number of smart wallets buying (more = stronger)
- Total $ spent across smart wallets
- Time-clustered buying (within hours = stronger)
- Holder + LP support
- Risk deductions for any red flags

Phase 5 — Alert + verdict.
For each signal above threshold:
- FOLLOW: high score + low risk + sufficient liquidity to enter
- INVESTIGATE: medium score, needs human review (specific concerns named)
- FADE: smart wallet identified but contract or distribution is shady
- IGNORE: below threshold

Output per alert:
- Token + chain + contract
- Signal summary (which wallets bought, when, how much)
- Risk flags
- Suggested entry tier (small probe / medium / pass)
- Stop-loss + take-profit framework

Phase 6 — Output.
- Real-time alerts to my channel
- Daily digest of all signals (followed + faded)
- Weekly retrospective: signal accuracy + P&L attribution

Feedback signal (closes the loop):
- Per signal: did the token move? Profitable or not?
- Wallet labels that consistently predict moves — promote
- Wallet labels that are noise — demote
- Risk flags that consistently saved you from rugs — strengthen the rule

Quality bar:
- This is analysis, NOT financial advice — crypto is highly volatile and lossy
- NEVER buy a token without verifying the contract address (scams are everywhere)
- NEVER size up because "smart money is in" — they're often wrong too
- Honeypot + insider checks are MANDATORY before any entry
- Position sizing on crypto: typically 0.5-2% of account per signal, max
- Liquidity matters more than alpha — a great signal in an illiquid token can't be exited
- Smart-money tracking does NOT survive once it's widely automated — bias toward fresh wallets, not the labeled ones everyone follows

playbooks.name: Screen a new token for rug-pull and honeypot risk
playbooks.description: Run pre-buy diligence on a new token. Get a 60-second risk audit covering contract, LP, holders, and a go/no-go verdict.
playbooks.prompt:
Screen a new token for rug-pull / honeypot risk before I buy.

Inputs:
- Token contract address + chain: [paste]
- My intended position size: [paste]
- DEX or CEX where I'd buy: [paste]
- Source of the signal (Telegram call / X post / wallet tracker / friend): [paste]
- Time pressure (do I have 60 seconds or 30 minutes to decide?): [paste]

Phase 1 — Contract audit.
- Verify the contract is verified on Etherscan / Solscan / BSCscan
- Mint authority: renounced or active?
- Freeze authority (SPL tokens / Token-2022): present?
- Transfer fees / taxes: what %?
- Blacklist function: present?
- Owner / admin functions still callable: which?
- Proxy / upgradeable: yes/no? (Yes = ongoing risk)
- Recent contract changes (last 7 days): any?

Phase 2 — Honeypot + transfer simulation.
- Simulate a sell of the position size — does it succeed?
- Hidden transfer fees that only trigger on sell?
- Slippage required at my position size
- LP-based sell simulation (will it actually clear?)

Phase 3 — LP + liquidity.
- Total liquidity in USD
- LP token: locked, burned, or wallet-held?
- Lock duration + unlock date
- LP holder distribution (one wallet vs many)
- 24h volume + buy/sell ratio
- Pool age

Phase 4 — Holder distribution + clusters.
- Top 10 holder concentration (>30% = insider risk)
- Bubblemaps cluster: connected wallets (sniper bots, dev team holding multi-wallet)
- New holders in the last 24h (organic growth?)
- Distribution Gini coefficient

Phase 5 — Off-chain signals.
- Project team doxxed?
- Smart contract audit (CertiK, Quantstamp, ZachXBT mention)?
- Telegram + X account age + follower quality
- Website + roadmap age
- CEX listing rumors or scheduled

Phase 6 — Risk score + verdict.
Composite 0-100 across the dimensions. Verdict tiers:
- GO (>80, all checks pass): risk-budgeted entry suggested
- PROBE (60-80, minor concerns): small probe position only, monitor 24h
- WAIT (40-60, real concerns): wait for resolution (LP lock, audit, dox)
- NO (<40, red flags): walk away, no position size justifies the risk

Phase 7 — Output.
- 1-page audit report (top: verdict, body: per-dimension score + evidence)
- A "what would make this go from PROBE to GO" list
- A "what to monitor if I do enter" list (LP changes, owner txns, dump signal)
- A safe entry plan if GO (slippage limit, position size, stop trigger)

Feedback signal (over time):
- Per checked token: did the verdict match outcome 7 days later?
- Which red flag patterns caught actual rugs — promote
- Which "GO" verdicts went to zero anyway — re-examine the methodology

Quality bar:
- This is analysis, NOT financial advice — crypto rugs are real and frequent
- A PROBE verdict does NOT mean "this will pump" — it means "the contract isn't actively malicious"
- NEVER use real money on a token without the audit running first
- Mint authority active + LP not locked + dev wallet large = walk away every time
- Even a perfect verdict doesn't survive a market-wide crash or a coordinated dump
- Position sizing: probe = 0.25-0.5% of account; go = 1-2% max

playbooks.name: Detect cross-DEX cyclic arbitrage opportunities
playbooks.description: Detect cross-DEX arbitrage cycles (A→B→C→A). Get ranked opportunities with expected profit net of gas + slippage.
playbooks.prompt:
Detect cross-DEX cyclic arbitrage opportunities on Solana / Ethereum / Base.

Inputs:
- Chain: [Solana / Ethereum / Base / Arbitrum / Polygon]
- Token universe (top N by liquidity OR a hand-picked list): [paste]
- DEX list (Raydium / Orca / Meteora / Jupiter / Uniswap / etc.): [paste]
- Capital available per cycle: [paste]
- Gas + priority fee budget per attempt: [paste]
- Min net profit threshold to alert: [paste — e.g. >$5 net]
- MEV protection layer (Jito for Solana, Flashbots for ETH): [paste]
- Alert channel: [Telegram / API webhook]

Phase 1 — Pull pool state.
- Current reserves + fee tier for each pool in scope
- Recent fills (last 10-30 sec) to detect imbalanced flow
- Slippage model per pool (constant product or CLMM-specific)

Phase 2 — Find cyclic disconnects.
- For each candidate cycle (A → B → C → A) with my token universe:
- Compute the implied price loop
- If loop > 1.0 (after fees), surface as a candidate
- Account for path with 2-hop and 3-hop cycles
- Filter cycles that cross the same pool twice (no real arb)

Phase 3 — Simulate net profit per route.
- Input amount sweep (find optimal size — typically the point right before slippage kills it)
- Total swap fees across the cycle
- Estimated gas + priority fee
- MEV / sandwich risk haircut (1-3% buffer)
- Net P&L = gross spread − fees − gas − MEV haircut

Drop anything with net P&L < threshold.

Phase 4 — Rank surviving routes.
- Net $ profit
- Required capital
- Number of hops (fewer = lower failure rate)
- Pool depth (more = lower slippage variance)
- Historic confirmation rate (have similar routes confirmed lately?)

Phase 5 — Alert + simulate before send.
For top route:
- Pre-flight simulation against current pool state (5 sec freshness)
- If simulation still > threshold: alert + ready-to-send transaction
- If simulation < threshold: stale data; recompute
- NEVER auto-send without my approval unless I've explicitly enabled it

Phase 6 — Output.
- Real-time alerts (route, expected profit, capital required)
- Daily summary: routes attempted, won, lost, net P&L
- A leaderboard of profitable cycle patterns
- A "killed by MEV" log to refine the haircut

Feedback signal (closes the loop):
- Confirmation rate per cycle pattern
- Realized profit vs simulated — calibrates the MEV haircut
- Patterns that decay (others discovered them) — rotate to fresher cycles

Quality bar:
- This is analysis, NOT financial advice — crypto arb is competitive and capital-intensive
- NEVER auto-execute without simulator confirmation — pool state changes second-to-second
- Gas wars + MEV bots eat most retail "arb" — your edge is in fresh routes, not crowded ones
- A failed arb costs you gas every time — track failure rate as relentlessly as profit
- Most cross-DEX arbs on major chains are already captured by professional bots — the alpha is in new pools or unusual cycles
- If your daily net is negative for 7 days, something in the model is wrong — stop and audit

playbooks.name: Run an annual tax-loss harvest sweep
playbooks.description: Run an annual tax-loss harvest across taxable accounts. Get harvest pairs that avoid wash sale and an estimated tax savings.
steps: Audit all taxable lots for unrealized losses
Check wash-sale across accounts + spouse + IRA
playbooks.prompt:
Run my annual tax-loss harvest sweep (Q4 prep, before December 31).

Inputs:
- All taxable account statements (Schwab / Fidelity / Robinhood / IBKR — lot-level): [paste or path]
- Spouse's accounts (for wash-sale rule across spousal accounts): [paste]
- IRA + Roth + 401k holdings (wash-sale clock applies if substantially identical): [paste]
- My federal marginal tax bracket + state tax rate: [paste]
- YTD realized gains (short-term + long-term): [paste]
- Planned future capital gains or losses I expect to realize: [paste]
- Risk tolerance for the swap period (sell + buy substantially-NOT-identical replacement): [paste]

Phase 1 — Audit all lots for unrealized losses.
- For every position in every taxable account, list every lot
- Per lot: ticker, acquisition date, cost basis, current market value, unrealized loss
- Sort by largest absolute loss first
- Flag short-term vs long-term loss (short-term is more valuable for offsetting short-term gains)

Phase 2 — Identify substantially identical replacements.
For each loss lot you'd harvest:
- The replacement security (similar exposure, NOT substantially identical per IRS guidance)
- Examples: VTI loss → swap to ITOT or SCHB; AAPL loss → swap to QQQ or another tech ETF; SPY loss → swap to VOO with 31-day wait or to IVV with caution
- The portfolio drift the swap introduces (sector, factor, size, geographic)
- Whether to "park" in cash for 31 days or accept the swap drift

Phase 3 — Wash-sale check (THE critical step).
For each candidate harvest:
- Check ALL taxable accounts (yours + spouse) for the same security in the prior 30 days
- Check ALL IRA / Roth accounts for the same security (yes, IRA wash-sales triggered by taxable losses are real)
- Check planned future buys in the next 30 days (auto-invest schedules, dividend reinvestment)
- Check options positions on the same underlying (puts can be tagged substantially identical)
- KILL any harvest where any of these conditions exist

Phase 4 — Estimate tax savings.
For each surviving harvest:
- Loss harvested ($)
- Tax saved at your marginal rate (federal + state)
- Reduction in YTD realized gains (offset)
- Carryforward generated (up to $3k/yr against ordinary income; rest carries forward)

Phase 5 — Build the Q4 execution plan.
- Harvest order (largest tax-saving first)
- Replacement security buy timing (same day, market close)
- 31-day calendar for when you can buy back original (if you want to)
- Auto-invest pause flags + DRIP suspension where needed

Phase 6 — Output.
- Harvest plan PDF (per-lot detail, executable as broker tickets)
- Wash-sale risk audit log (all triggers found + how avoided)
- Estimated tax savings summary (1-page top sheet)
- A 31-day calendar showing when each replacement holds vs returns
- Updates needed to auto-invest / DRIP / contribution schedules

Feedback signal (next year):
- Realized vs estimated tax savings — calibrate
- Patterns: what harvested well vs what fought wash-sale rules constantly
- Whether the swap drift hurt portfolio performance — adjust replacement strategy

Quality bar:
- This is tax planning analysis, NOT tax advice — consult a CPA for complex situations
- The wash-sale rule is BRUTAL — one missed account triggers full deferral
- Watch DRIP and auto-invest religiously — they reinvest at year-end and break harvests
- For substantially identical: VTI and VOO are clearly different (different indices); AAPL and AAPL are not
- Harvest is most valuable when offsetting short-term gains (taxed as ordinary income)
- Capital loss carryforward is a real asset — track it across years
- DON'T harvest at expense of long-term portfolio strategy — the tax tail shouldn't wag the investment dog

playbooks.name: Build a FOMC decision-day volatility playbook
playbooks.description: Build an FOMC-day playbook. Get hawkish/neutral/dovish scenarios with strikes, timing, and a 4-stage volatility roadmap.
playbooks.prompt:
Build my FOMC decision-day trading playbook.

Inputs:
- FOMC meeting date + time (2:00 PM ET press release, 2:30 PM ET Powell presser): [paste]
- Current Fed Funds rate + market consensus: [paste]
- Market-implied probabilities (Fed Funds Futures, CME FedWatch): [paste]
- Current SPY / QQQ levels + recent technicals: [paste]
- VIX level + term structure: [paste]
- My capital allocated to FOMC trade + max loss: [paste]
- My instrument preference (SPY 0DTE / VIX / sector ETFs): [paste]

Phase 1 — Market-implied probabilities.
- Hike / hold / cut probabilities (from Fed Funds Futures)
- Implied terminal rate
- 2024-2025 dot-plot drift vs current
- Where consensus is OVER-confident (the actionable edge)

Phase 2 — Generate scenarios.

Hawkish (rate higher than consensus, OR consensus rate + hawkish language):
- SPY directional bias: down
- VIX bias: spike
- Bond yields (TLT): down
- Dollar: up
- Likely sectors: financials up; growth / tech / housing down

Neutral (consensus rate + balanced language):
- SPY likely range-bound until presser
- VIX deflates after release
- Bonds steady

Dovish (rate lower than consensus, OR rate cut signals, OR worse-than-expected projections):
- SPY: up
- VIX: deflate hard
- Bonds: up
- Dollar: down
- Likely sectors: growth + small caps lead

For each scenario: probability estimate + strike selection + risk caps.

Phase 3 — The 4-stage volatility pattern.
Stage 1 — Compression (10:00 AM - 1:55 PM ET):
- Vol contracts as market awaits
- Best for theta-positive (premium-selling) structures
- Avoid directional bets until decision

Stage 2 — Decision Spike (2:00 PM - 2:15 PM ET):
- Maximum volatility on press release
- 1-3% SPY move within first 15 min is common
- Best for hedged directional or vol-buying structures

Stage 3 — Powell Reversal (2:30 PM - 3:30 PM ET):
- Press conference often reverses initial move
- 60% of FOMC days reverse direction in this window
- Plan around the reversal — don't chase the spike

Stage 4 — Resolution (3:30 PM - close):
- Final positioning, direction confirms
- Best for closing the trade or letting overnight hold

Phase 4 — Pick strikes + timing per scenario.
- Conservative play (defined-risk): credit spread or iron condor positioned for compression
- Directional play: long calls / puts entered AT compression (cheap vol)
- Vol play: long VIX calls or VIX call spread
- Reversal play: enter opposite-side position at 2:30 PM if initial spike feels emotional

Phase 5 — Kill switch.
- Max loss per stage (Stage 2 spike, Stage 3 reversal)
- Mid-day reassessment trigger (if Stage 2 move > X%, recalibrate)
- "Walk away" rules (if VIX dies after Stage 2, kill long-vol positions immediately)

Phase 6 — Output.
- Playbook PDF (1 page top-line + 4-stage details + scenario strikes)
- Pre-market briefing the morning of FOMC (recap of overnight + final probabilities)
- 2 PM "decision live" alert template (script for the reaction)
- Post-FOMC retrospective (what worked + what didn't + which scenario hit)

Feedback signal (over FOMC meetings):
- Per scenario: how often did your probability estimates match reality?
- Per stage: did the timing pattern hold?
- Per instrument: which gave the best risk-adjusted return on FOMC days?

Quality bar:
- This is analysis, NOT financial advice — FOMC days are violent and can blow up accounts
- NEVER size FOMC trades as you would a normal day — assume 2x normal volatility
- NEVER enter naked options into 2 PM — gamma + vega risk is asymmetric
- The "reversal" pattern is statistical, not guaranteed — manage stops accordingly
- Consensus probability can be wrong — but trading against consensus needs explicit thesis
- If you can't articulate the EDGE in your scenario probabilities, don't trade FOMC — just watch

- Watchlist names with notable pre-market move

- Slack message with TL;DR + key levels

playbooks.name: Run a daily trade journal and EOD review
playbooks.description: Run a daily trade journal + end-of-day review. Get P&L attribution, discipline checks, and a weekly pattern report.
playbooks.prompt:
Run my daily trade journal + end-of-day review.

Inputs:
- Today's broker statement / fills (Alpaca / IBKR / TastyTrade / Robinhood export): [paste or path]
- My setup taxonomy (tag each trade by setup type — momentum, mean reversion, earnings play, swing, etc.): [paste my tags]
- My trading rules (max risk per trade, max trades per day, no FOMO entries, etc.): [paste]
- Account size start of day: [paste]
- Premarket plan I wrote (what I said I'd do): [paste]
- This week's running stats (win rate, avg R, P&L): [paste]

Phase 1 — Ingest fills + categorize.
For each filled trade today:
- Ticker, entry time, exit time, P&L
- Tag by setup (from my taxonomy)
- Tag by quality (planned / opportunistic / FOMO / revenge)
- Tag by execution (clean fills / chasing / slippage hit)
- Note any rule violations

Phase 2 — Compute session stats.
- Number of trades + win rate
- Average R-multiple won vs lost
- Largest winner + largest loser
- P&L attribution by setup tag
- Time-of-day distribution (am I better at open? midday? close?)

Phase 3 — Discipline check.
- Did I follow my pre-market plan? (binary yes/no per planned trade)
- Did I take any unplanned trades? Why?
- Did I size any position above my rules?
- Did I hold a stop that I should have honored?
- Any revenge trade signature (entered another trade right after a loss)?

Phase 4 — Pattern review.
- The setup that performed best today + why
- The setup that lost the most + why
- Surprise patterns (unusual sector, unusual time)
- Lessons specific to today (a market regime detail to remember)

Phase 5 — Write the journal entry.
Sections:
1. Headline (1 sentence — was it a good day or a bad day, and what made it that?)
2. Stats (numbers from Phase 2)
3. Wins (3 trades that worked + WHY they worked)
4. Losses (2-3 trades that didn't + WHY they didn't)
5. Discipline grade (A-F with reasoning)
6. Tomorrow's plan adjustment (one specific thing to do differently)

Phase 6 — Sunday: weekly retrospective.
- 7-day stats roll-up
- Setup leaderboard (which earned, which lost)
- Win rate by tag, by time of day, by market regime
- 3 wins to repeat next week
- 3 losses to NOT repeat next week
- A "what would have improved this week's P&L by 20%" thought experiment

Phase 7 — Output.
- Daily journal entry (Notion / Obsidian markdown)
- Weekly retrospective PDF (Sundays)
- A running setup leaderboard updated daily
- A monthly P&L attribution by tag
- An annual "what I learned" memo (end-of-year)

Feedback signal (closes the loop):
- Setups consistently positive over 30+ trades — promote
- Setups consistently negative over 30+ trades — DROP, not "try again"
- Discipline grade trend — declining = burnout coming
- The patterns the journal kept surfacing — bake into rules

Quality bar:
- This is performance analysis, NOT financial advice
- NEVER fudge the numbers — the journal is for me, not for show
- Discipline grade is binary truth — don't soften it
- A losing day with discipline = a good day in the long run
- A winning day with bad discipline = a bad habit forming
- Win rate alone is meaningless — average R-multiple is the real edge metric
- Track the same stats relentlessly — drift kills comparison over months
